 § 281. Method of Payment 

When the State permits a number of individuals to limit their legal liabilities by forming through association a legal entity called a corporation, with its members whose stock is fully paid for, free from personal obligations for the corporate acts, some provisions should be and are made to guarantee that the corporate group actually has the assets the charter calls for.¹ Texas has inserted such a safeguard in its constitution, and statutes have been enacted declaratory of the constitutional purpose.2 

Article 12, section 6, of the Texas Constitution provides: "No corporation shall issue stock or bonds except for money paid, labor done or property actually received, and all fictitious increase of stock or indebtedness shall be void." 3 The effect of these provisions is to require each shareholder to pay par value for his stock, or the stated consideration if the stock is no-par stock. The purpose of these provisions is to prevent the fraud-

It goes without saying that a partner is liable for the debts of the firm while he is a member, even though when he bought an interest in the firm all parties intended to incorporate. Freeman v. Huttig Sash & Door Co., 153 S.W. 122, 105 Tex. 560, Ann.Cas.1916E, 446.

Civ.St. art. 1353 provides: "No corporation shall issue any stock whatever, except for money paid, labor done which is reasonably worth at least the sum at which it was taken by the corporation, or property actually received reasonably worth at least the sum at which it was taken by the company. corporation which violates any provision of this article shall, on proof thereof in any court of competent jurisdiction, forfeit its charter, permit or license, as the case may be, and all rights and franchises which it holds under, from, or by virtue of the laws of this State." A contract whereby stock is to be issued under circumstances violative of the statutory and constitutional provisions is illegal and unenforceable by the corporation.5 

The constitutional and statutory provisions with reference to payment in cash do not give much difficulty. The Supreme 

Court has held that money paid does not mean money to be paid and thus stock can only be issued for money already received." 

This holding does not prevent a subscriber from contracting to pay for his stock in installments, so long as the stock is not issued until the consideration is fully paid. Similarly, under the "labor done" provision, an attorney may subscribe for shares to be paid for with professional services needed by the corporation.8

Much litigation has arisen over what constitutes "property actually received" and the value to be placed on such property.

 § 282. 

Property 

Since property may be taken in payment for capital stock, it might be well to ascertain just what property may be taken. 

Although this subject is treated more extensively later, it may be broadly stated that a subscriber's note is not "property actually received" within the provision. But a note secured by a valid first mortgage on land owned by the subscriber, reasonably worth twice the amount of the note, is "property actually received," when used to pay for stock in an insurance company.10 

Land may be taken by the corporation in exchange for stock, where the land is fairly and reasonably worth the sum at which it is valued and it is not ultra vires for the corporation to purchase the land.11

But a transfer of land to the corporation for stock which is largely in excess of the actual value of the land does not constitute a payment for the stock so far as the rights of creditors are concerned.12 Even though the affidavit to the charter recites that the stock was paid for in cash, where as a matter of fact property was conveyed to the corporation for its stock, no one except the State or a creditor who had been injured by that irregularity can complain.13 And where the stockholders paid

Though it is held that an unsecured note is not "property" within the contemplation of the constitutional provision, it is also held that "securities" may be used in payment for stock, and are not inhibited by the constitution or the Texas statute.23 The court said: "The distinction between the word 'securities' in its general signification, as apparently used in this contract, and the notes of the obligor is that 'securities' are property already existing, the possession and ownership of which is fixed in the obligor; while the notes of such obligor do not become 'securities', property, until they have passed from him into the hands of another, who holds as a possessor and owner. His own note, as long as it remains in his possession, is not a security. And when delivered by him to a third party, covering an obligation then existing, it is only a continuation of that obligation. It cannot be property owned by him passing to such an obligee." It seems apparent from this language that the Texas courts make a distinction between a stockholder's note and the note of a third party, holding that the note of a stockholder is merely another form of expressing his promise to pay for his stock, while a note of a third party is "property" received by the corporation when assigned to the corporation by the stockholder.

§ 283. 

Is a Note Property? 

Since a corporation by the constitutional provision may issue stock only for money paid, labor done, or property received, under which of these heads does a promissory note of a stockholder come? Such an instrument, although a promise to pay money, is not money, nor is it labor done; therefore it must be "property" or else it is a prohibited return for corporate shares.30 

In discussing whether a note is property it must be remembered that the Constitution of Texas only prohibits "the issuance" of stock until fully paid for. Therefore, where a note is given for stock, if it is understood that the stock will not be "issued" to the subscriber until the note is paid, the contract is valid and not illegal.31 This question is discussed in detail in the chapter on "Capital Stock and Issue of Stock." 

The courts of Texas, like the courts of many other states, might have avoided a great deal of difficulty by adopting the view that a promissory note given in exchange for corporate shares is "property" within the meaning of the constitution. They did not adopt this view, however, and the cases in this state are almost unanimous to the effect that an unsecured note of a stockholder is not property.32

For many years the fact that the note is secured by a mortgage on real property, of sufficient value to provide ample se-

The court held a secured note was not property within the meaning of the constitution, using the following language: "Undeniably, in the broad sense a note is property in the hands of the payee. So, in a literal sense, is everything property which is capable of ownership. All forms of choses in action are property in the same sense the right to recover a debt, the right to recover damages for breach of a contract, unsatisfied judgments, and other similar kinds of actionable demands. But the framers of the 

Constitution never intended that property of that nature should constitute the capital of a corporation. The term "property" was used in that section of the Constitution in no such sense. It means property readily capable of being applied to the debts of the corporation. As a rule, it should be property of the kind adapted to the charter uses of the corporation and which it may legally acquire." 35

Several recent cases of far-reaching importance must be considered in connection with the doctrine of the above case. But under the established rule of decision in this court, that contract rights transferred to a corporation in payment for stock are, to the extent of their value, 'property actually received' by the corporation. Cole v. Adams, 92 Tex. 171, 46 S.W. 790—a decision whose soundness cannot be controverted-a subscriber's note secured by a valid first mortgage upon real estate, accepted by the corporation in payment for stock, cannot be held as other than property in the full sense of the Constitution. The corporation thereby obtains something more than the mere promise of the subscriber to pay. It obtains the right to have the land appropriated to the payment of the note. This is a valuable right, a property right, as fully so as any contract right, and, in general, as valuable as any such right. 

The corporation receives it and owns it. It constitutes a distinct asset in its hands; recognized, generally, as one of the most stable, desirable, and easily convertible forms of property, as instanced by the Legislature's Act authorizing the capital of such corporations as this one to consist of such mortgages." "The right acquired under such mortgage is clearly property, and the law was therefore one within the power of the Legislature to enact." 

39. 222 S.W. 961, 110 Tex. 529. Although in this case the Court said that in Washer v. Smyer "we held the naked note of a subscriber" is not property yet in Washer v. Smyer the corporation involved was an insurance company and the stockholder's note was "doubly secured." The 

Moseley case was decided in 1920 and the Washer case in 1919. 12

Prior to this case, the doctrine that a secured note was property had been refused.40 The court in the Pierce case 41 intimated that the statute was probably unconstitutional, but the contrary to this proposition was definitely held in the last paragraph quoted from the Moseley case. Penland v. Schramm 42 was a case in which a secured note had been given for stock in a corporation other than an insurance company, hence one not coming under the statute set out above. Still the court held that if a note secured by a mortgage is property as to one corporation, it should be held to be property as to all, and that it did not matter whether or not the security was double the amount of the indebtedness. To quote from the opinion: "We think it immaterial that the Moseley case arose under the 

[Ver- 

provisions of Article 4711, Revised Statutes non's Ann.Civ.St. art. 4705]. If a secured note is not 'property' received within the meaning of the Constitution, said article is unconstitutional. The court expressly held that this article was not unconstitutional. The fact that this article, in effect, recognizes that notes secured by mortgage on real estate of double the value of the note, exclusive of improvements, is 'property' within the meaning of the Constitution, is immaterial, for the reason that the same would be 'property,' if at all, though less than double the amount of the note secured." 

The Penland case seems sound. The Constitution does not make a distinction between insurance companies and other corporations. If under the constitutional provision a secured note is not property, the statute is unconstitutional, or, as said in that

In Shaw v. Korth, Tex. Civ.App., 26 S.W.2d 351, a note was given for stock that the bank had organized to take over some frozen assets of the bank, and the bank purchased the note. It was not shown whether the stock was issued to the maker of the note. The Court held the banking

case, if it is not already property, the statute cannot make it so. 

If the note is property as to one, when properly secured, it is property to all corporations, especially those that have authority to invest their funds in secured notes. There seems to be little difference in selling the stock of a corporation for cash and then investing the proceeds in mortgages, and in selling the stock outright for such consideration. The ultimate result is the same. 

There is a distinction between insurance companies and other corporations, as the capital stock of an insurance company must of necessity be invested in revenue-bearing securities, of which mortgages represent the most desirable type. The capital stock of ordinary corporations is invested in equipment designed to be used in making profits for the company. But merely because different types of corporations carry on different types of business requiring different investments of their capital assets, seems to be no sufficient reason to call a note property, when owned by an insurance company, and refuse to call it property when taken for stock of other corporations. The whole matter is determined by the answer to the question as to whether or not the Legislature has the power to define what is, and what is not, property, since the Constitution provides how subscribers may pay for their stock.

In view of the fact that many other states, having constitutional provisions similar to those of Texas, have held without the aid of a statute that secured notes are property, it is time for our courts to put this matter on a common sense basis. In the face of the above constitutional provision, even the Supreme Court of Texas has not the power to say that a secured note is property as to insurance companies by reason of the above statute, but not property as to other companies. Of course, that court has the power to say that notes doubly secured are property as to all corporations. But will the court be so arbitrary? 

And the court has power to say that only a secured note is property; that an unsecured note, being merely another promise of the stockholder, is not property within the meaning of the above constitutional provision. Since the opinions of the Supreme 

Court in Cole v. Adams and General B. & C. Ins. Co. v. Mose- 14

ley,that court should now say that a secured note of a stockholder is property to the extent of its actual value; and hold that where such a note is given for stock the shareholder has paid for his stock to the extent of the actual value of the secured note. To prove the value of the note is a question of fact, and often difficult, as is true in most cases where property is given in payment of stock. In a recent case a Court of Civil Appeals decided that even though the original note is illegal where it was not secured, it becomes valid by a subsequent mortgage of personal property to secure it.44 And a Federal Court decided that payment of such a note validated the transaction.45 In view of the fact that the court decided that a secured note was property because it furnishes some security in addition to the stockholder's mere promise, it would be difficult to prove that an unsecured note is property within the definition of that term as laid down in the Moseley case. The Moseley case, furthermore, expressly recognized the doctrine of Washer v. Smyer, as to unsecured notes.

As the Supreme Court refused a writ of error in the Brownfield-Hudson case, and especially as the facts did not show that the note was doubly secured, it seems fairly certain that our courts now hold that a secured note is property even though the security is less than the face of the note. Just how small the security may be as compared with the amount of the note and yet be "property" remains an unsettled question. The Supreme

Court has yet to decide whether a secured note is property as to all corporations or only as to those corporations that have authority to invest their assets in secured notes.

Valid Credit Transactions 

A few cases in which stock has been issued on credit and not coming within the prohibition of the Constitution should be briefly noticed. In Lone Star Life Insurance Co. v. Pierce,46 

money was borrowed from the corporation and a note given therefor, secured by a deed of trust. The money was used to purchase stock in the corporation. It was held that this was not a prohibited transaction, if the transaction was actually what it purported on its face to be, and the whole proceeding was not merely a colorable method of securing the stock of the corporation on credit. The fact that the money was used to purchase stock would not affect the result, the court stated, if the transaction was bona fide and the person to whom the loan is made is one that could rightfully borrow from the company. 

Where the subscriber makes a bona fide loan from another corporation and with the money or credit thus obtained actually pays for his stock in the plaintiff corporation, the transaction is valid even though the officers of the plaintiff assisted the subscriber in obtaining the loan and subsequently purchased the note from the lending corporation.47 Where the subscriber borrows money from a third party and with this money pays the corporation fully for his stock, the subscription agreement is valid and enforceable even though he pledges his stock to secure the loan.48

Where an officer of a corporation procures the issuance of stock to a fictitious person, and, as attorney for the fictitious person, transfers the stock to himself, paying therefor with forged securities, the corporation, on the discovery of the fraud, could either cancel the stock because of the fraud, or treat him as the stock subscriber, and require him to pay therefor. Texas Constitution was amended in 1904 providing for the organization of banking companies in Texas, certain parties began the operation of a bank under the above special act. The court held that even a receiver of the purported bank could not recover on the subscription contracts of "the stockholders." The reason for these holdings, as stated by the court, is that "we are not aware that it has ever been held that persons dealing with a corporation are bound to take notice of the manner in which it has attempted to exercise its powers. But it is well settled that they must take notice of its powers." "Persons dealing with a corporation are not charged with knowledge of the facts, but they are charged with knowledge of the law. All men are charged with that knowledge. That is why all men are subject to the law. Creditors cannot blind themselves to the law. They must, like everyone else, take notice of it. If they deal with a concern reputed to be a corporation but whose existence as a corporation the law prohibits, they are bound to know that under the law it has no corporate powers and can exercise none. They are held to know that it can not issue stock and that subscriptions for its stock are therefore without consideration and unenforceable. Being held to this knowledge under a universal principle, how can they claim to have been deceived into giving credit upon the faith of such subscriptions? They can make no such claim because they are not innocent and have not been misled. They are in the position of having dealt with the reputed corporation fully aware of the illegality of the transaction, and they cannot be prejudiced, therefore, by the assertion of its illegality. 

Creditors can not be misled by a subscription to stock of a reputed corporation whose existence the law prohibits, and which it was accordingly without authority to issue. This is so because they are bound to take notice of its powers. Such a transaction does not present merely an illegal exercise of a lawful power-a thing resting in the facts, as to which the law does not impute knowledge to third persons. The proposed stock is wholly void and the transaction unenforcible because of the entire absence of any power in the corporation to issue the stock—a thing determined 

24

Ch. § 286 

by the law, and as to which it imputes knowledge to all persons." 70

In both of the above cases the purported stockholders should have been estopped to deny their liability to creditors. In the first case the Court overlooked the fact that it did charge the creditors with notice of a very material fact, and that was that the original charter provided for only $100,000 of stock. In the second case the Court charged the innocent creditors with knowledge that the charter was tendered by a special act of the Texas Legislature in 1871 instead of under the general incorporation statute passed after the Constitution was amended in 1904. Unless the above cases are overruled the Court will hold that the overissued stock certificate is void even in the hands of an innocent pledgee or purchaser for value, and the corporation would not be liable to such a holder in damages. Such a result would be the height of injustice and not in accord with the better holdings.80

If the subscriber obtains money or other property from the corporation by fraud and transfers such property to the corporation in payment of the amount due by him on the subscription contract, the Court will presume that in reconveying the property to the corporation he intended to compensate the corporation for his fraudulent acts, and, therefore, the corporation, its receiver, or creditors may recover the balance due the company on the subscription agreement.81

That distinction is clearly erroneous and should not be followed by the Texas Supreme Court when the question again arises.86 The question may not arise very often in Texas as under the general incorporation statutes all of the stock must be subscribed before the Secretary of State will approve the charter.87 Yet under the no-par value statute and under Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. arts. 1310 and 1311, corporations may still be organized in Texas with only part of their stock subscribed when the charter is approved by the Secretary of State. Certainly there is more reason for implying the condition where the subscription was made before the charter was obtained than where the subscriber agreed to buy stock of a corporation then in existence. A subscriber to the capital stock of a corporation may be bound on his subscription contract, even though the purpose clause of the charter includes things not specifically included in the subscription agreement provided the additions in the charter are implied in the subscription agreement.88 

The forfeiture of stock for the non-payment of an installment due thereon, is void unless the forfeiture complies with the statute providing for forfeiture which sets out certain requirements, such as notice in writing to the stockholder.89

A corporation cannot levy assessments on the holders of fullpaid stock, unless power to do so is conferred by the charter or the articles of association or a valid statute. This is held by the 

Texas Supreme Court, the following language being used: "Stock upon which nothing has been paid may be called nonassessable and may be so treated; not legally, however, under our Constitution. But 'paid up, nonassessable stock' can only mean stock that is made nonassessable by reason of the fact that the amount for which it calls has been fully paid." 90

In Texas there is a statute which specifically exempts the stocknolder in a corporation from further liability, after he has fully paid par for his stock.91 Therefore, where the petition merely alleges that the defendants were the principal shareholders of the corporation, for which the plaintiff rendered services, it does not state a cause of action against the shareholders.92

In Texas, it is held that an order appointing a receiver to take charge of the "whole property" of an insolvent corporation will empower him to sue for and recover unpaid subscriptions to the corporation. Title to the property of an insolvent corporation vests in the receiver or the trustee in bankruptcy in trust for the benefit of creditors, and it is his duty to compel delinquent subscribers to pay the balance due, and with that fund, discharge the claims of the creditors.21 There is language in the Chemical 

Company case 22 that the trustee in bankruptcy or the receiver alone can sue to collect unpaid subscriptions, and the creditor cannot sue therefor. This seems to be in conflict with the language in the Mathis case,23 which dealt with the action by the creditor against the single delinquent shareholder. The language in the Chemical Company case has the support of the authorities.24 As stated by the court in the case of Thomason v. Miller,25 whether or not the trustee in bankruptcy can sue on bonus, discount or watered stock depends on the theory of liability. 

Under the fraud theory, there would be no right in the trustee in bankruptcy or the receiver, but the right of action is personal to the subsequent creditors who have been defrauded.

According to the opinion of one Court of Civil Appeals in Texas that part of the contract which provides that the subscriber to the capital stock of a corporation will not be required to pay the full amount of the stock subscription is void as a matter of law, and no suit in equity to cancel such contract is necessary. In this connection the Court of Civil Appeals said: "It follows, therefore, that under the Constitution and laws of Texas any contract between a corporation and the subscribers for its stock, that the latter will not be required to pay the full amount of their stock subscriptions, is void as a matter of law, and when that fact is established a proceeding in equity to cancel such a contract is not required." 27 But if the stockholders know that the stock has been issued for less than par the contract between the corporation and the stockholder is not void and it cannot be set aside by the corporation.28 If a subsequent creditor did not know the stock was issued for property worth less than the par value of the stock such creditor may compel the payment of the difference if such is necessary to satisfy his claim. The trustee in bankruptcy or receiver can recover the agreed consideration for the stock. Therefore, if the stockholder promises a definite amount of money or property and does not perform his promise even the corporation can recover the amount the stockholder agreed to pay. That contract right is an asset of the corporation. If the stockholder agrees to give property for his stock and refuses or neglects to transfer the property to the company, the latter, or its receiver or trustee in bankruptcy, has a right to recover the appraised value of the property and not merely its actual value.2 29

Necessary Parties 

30 When the court has authorized the receiver or the trustee in bankruptcy 31 to file suit to collect unpaid subscriptions, the question of determining who are necessary parties becomes an important one. There have been very few Texas cases on this point but the case of Mathis v. Pridham,32 in which Judge Williams wrote the opinion, gives a good discussion of the questions here presented, and also indicates the attitude of the Texas court in that connection. The excerpt below also brings out the distinction between the suit in which a marshalling and accounting of the assets is obtained and the suit in which a single creditor seeks satisfaction of his debt out of the unpaid subscription of a stockholder: "In its general structure and purpose it is an equitable proceeding in behalf of all the creditors of an insolvent corporation, after the appropriation of all its tangible assets to the debts, against subscribers to its capital stock, to have an accounting and a contribution from the defendants of such proportion of their unpaid subscriptions as might be found necessary to satisfy the debts. In this character of suit it is essential to the completeness of the remedy that the amount of the indebtedness of the corporation, the amount of unpaid stock in the aggregate, the amount due from each stockholder, and the proportion thereof necessary to discharge the debts, should be definitely and finally ascertained. It might also become necessary to ascertain who, among the subscribers, are solvent and who insolvent, in order that the solvent ones be required, as far as their subscription suffice, to contribute enough to make up the deficiencies arising from insolvency of the others. It is apparent, therefor, that, in order to render certain and uniform justice to each creditor and each stockholder, they should all, as far as practicable, be brought into court. Accordingly we find the rule that equitable suits of this character must be brought by and for the benefit of all the creditors and against all delinquent subscribers to the stock of the corporation who are solvent and 

30. Mathis v. Pridham, 20 S.W. 31. Stevens v. Davenport, Tex.Civ.

within the jurisdiction of the court so well established by authority that we need only to refer to some of them. Cook, Stocks, Sec. 206, and note; 2 Mor.Corp. Sec. 897; Beach, Priv.

Corp. Sec. 700, and authorities cited. These authorities commend themselves to our judgment as being sound, and as indicating the true doctrine on the subject. It certainly should be within the power of creditors of an insolvent corporation, or their representative, pursuing the trust fund, which the law declares unpaid subscription to capital stock to be, to bring all the parties necessary to a full adjustment of their rights before the same court, in one suit, and secure an adjudication which will settle all their rights and liabilities. The principles and practice of equity afford such a remedy, which in no wise conflicts with our statutes regarding venue, but is embraced within the scope of the fourth exception to article 1198 [Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 

1995]. Authorities which maintain the right of a creditor to sue an individual stockholder to recover an unpaid subscription and apply it upon his debt do not conflict with the rule above laid down. In such suits, an accounting and marshalling of assets and distribution of all of the proceeds is not sought, but a single creditor seeks satisfaction for his debt out of the unpaid subscription of one stockholder. Some authorities deny his right to do so, and hold that the remedy in equity is exclusive. Others admit the right of the creditor to maintain such an action, but none of them in America, so far as we have examined, deny the right of all the creditors to join all delinquent members of the corporation in one proceeding such as that now before us. Some of them hold that the joining of all the stockholders from whom subscriptions are due is not essential, but others (and, we think, the better ones) hold that in so comprehensive a proceeding as a suit for an accounting and a determination of the pro rata part of the indebtedness which each subscriber shall pay all must be joined, as far as known, unless they are insolvent, or beyond the jurisdiction." 33

rably: "Under the trust fund theory the liability is absolute and each stockholder is liable ratably for the deficiency between what he paid in money or property and the par value of the stock he received. Under the holding of Mathis v. Pridham all solvent stockholders within the jurisdiction of the court, who are liable under this theory are necessary parties where the action, as here, is to satisfy the balance due creditors in the final winding up of the corporation's affairs. Under the fraud theory there is no right of action in the trustee in bankruptcy, but the right of action is personal to the several creditors who may show themselves defrauded." 35

As a matter of fact the law should not be so technical as to render the receiver impotent to recover, where the Hospes doctrine is followed. As is contended throughout this text, the Texas statute is so plain our courts should not hesitate to follow "the absolute liability" theory. If they finally reach that conclusion there would be no doubt but that the receiver or trustee in bankruptcy could recover on bonus, discount, or watered stock for all creditors-whether prior or subsequent-as the liability would run in favor of the corporation. Even where the Hospes doctrine is followed the receiver, or trustee in bankruptcy, should be permitted to recover since a great many cases hold that the receiver represents the corporation "and creditors." If he is not permitted to recover for creditors in most receivership and bankruptcy proceedings the rights of the creditors will never be enforced since the expense of suits to prove the liability of the shareholders would be too expensive and their outcome too hazardous for individual suits by the creditors. As a practical matter, it is almost impossible for the creditors to get together and combine their efforts in a single action. Defenses Available to Stockholders 

It is the established rule in Texas that the rights of a stockholder who has been induced to purchase stock by the fraudulent misrepresentations of the corporation or its agents are subordinated to the rights of those who, without any knowledge of such fraud, have subsequently become creditors of the corporation.39 Of course, if the rights of creditors are not involved, the stockholder may rescind. But the contract is merely voidable, not void, and until he rescinds it is binding.40 If he does not attempt to rescind before the insolvency of the company, in a suit by a receiver, he cannot set up the fraud as a defense to the action for the balance of the subscription price where the rights of subsequent innocent creditors have arisen. His right to rescind is subordinate to the rights of such creditors as is fully explained in another chapter in this text.41

Davis v. Burns 42 is a leading Texas case on this point. There the subscription was induced by fraud, and it was held that the subscriber could not have the stock cancelled although he tried to do so before the company became insolvent. The court held that his right to cancel was subordinate to the rights of those who without knowledge of the fraud and before repudiation by the subscribers became creditors of the corporation; and the fact that the creditors did not know of the subscription did not affect their right to recover, through the receiver. This seems to be another application of the fraud or holding out theory. This rule was also applied in Burleson v. Davis.43 Since then the rule has never been questioned. The rule was first intimated in Mathis v. Pridham,44 in which certain stockholders were induced by fraudulent representations to subscribe to the capital stock of a corporation, and they pleaded these facts, against the action of the receiver to recover from them the unpaid portion of the stock. Judge Williams said: "There was no error in sustaining the exceptions to the answer; admitting the facts, if timely set up, would have availed against the company they could not be of any avail in this proceeding as a defense against creditors." 

If the rule of Weatherford M. W. & N. W. R. Co. v. Granger 45 to the effect that a promoter cannot be an agent of an unborn corporation is followed literally, a stockholder could not rescind his subscription agreement even though the promise was induced by fraud where the agreement was made before the company received a charter. The Commission of Appeals, however, refused to be bound by logic rather than justice, and held that a fiduciary relation exists between the promoter and the subscriber; hence permitted the subscriber to rescind.46 Of course, the subscriber's right to rescind is subject to the rules discussed in this section.

 § 292. 

Set-Off of Debts Due Stockholders 

The general rule is that if the corporation is indebted to the stockholder who has not paid all of his subscription, he may set off the amount of the debt against the action for the balance due on his subscription, if the corporation is solvent. But it is well settled that if the corporation is insolvent, stockholders who are also creditors cannot set off such a debt against their liability for stock, but they must pay in full the amount due thereon, and then share pro rata with the other creditors in their class. 

If the set-off were allowed after the corporation became insolvent and had ceased business, the stockholder-creditor would be given a preference.47

The right of set-off allowed by the Federal Bankruptcy Act of July 1, 1898, does not apply to creditors of a bankrupt corporation who are also shareholders and indebted to the corporation on unpaid stock subscriptions. As authority for this proposition, a Texas court quotes the following from Bausman v. 

Kinnear, C.C.A.Wash., 79 F. 172, 24 C.C.A. 473: "A stockholder, who is also a creditor of a corporation has no right to set-off as against his unpaid subscription, after the corporation has become insolvent, and a suit in equity has been brought to wind up its affairs and distribute its assets. The unpaid stock is held to be a trust fund for the purpose of paying the debts of the corporation, and as such it must be distributed among the creditors pro rata. The debt due to a stockholder is entitled to no preference over other debts, and he cannot require its payment by way of set-off to the exclusion or postponement of other claims. The reason usually assigned for this rule is that the debt owing by the stockholder to the corporation after insolvency and that owing from the corporation to him are not in the same right, the former being a debt payable to a trust fund. The decisions upon this proposition appear to be unanimous." 48 Some

Cochran case 53 gives an excellent discussion of the problem here presented. In a Civil Appeals case a judgment creditor in pursuance of Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1345 attempted to force an attorney who had subscribed for stock in the defendant company to pay the balance he owed the company for his stock. Before the motion was made to force the attorney to pay the balance he owed the company, the corporation had agreed to allow the attorney to credit on the balance due the amount the company would owe the attorney as fees for attending to the company's legal business. The attorney was allowed to set off the amount of his services actually rendered against the amount of the unpaid subscription.54 The court stated that the rule of the Cochran case 55 did not apply and based its decision on the contract. 

In the opinion the court said: "Appellant's concluding proposition is that to allow appellee the value of his services would be to award him a preference, which she says is denied him, both at law and in equity, citing in support of her proposition among other decisions, Cochran v. Monteith, 221 S.W. 1055 (T.C.A.), where the rule contended for by appellant is announced and where it is said: "The decisions upon this proposition appear to be unanimous.' But the facts from which this rule is deduced are not the facts of this case. We do not have before us, as a matter of law, the balancing of the stock subscription against the account for legal services. In other words, these facts do not raise at all the issue of set-off. On the contrary, the issue is one simply of recognizing and enforcing a specific contract that the services rendered should be so compensated. Witt v. Nelson, 169 S.W. 381 (T.C.A.), involved to some extent the legal proposition before us. There Nelson advanced funds to his corporation necessary to keep it a going concern, and after its insolvency, when he was sued for his unpaid stock subscription, asked credit for the amount so advanced. Statutory Liability 

Sometimes the statute creating the liability of stockholders specifies the time within which an action must be brought by creditors to enforce the same. Where this is not the case the limitation depends upon the nature of the liability. If it is contractual, the clause of the statute relating to actions on contract is generally held to govern. If the liability is penal, the case is governed by the clause relating to actions upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture.67 66

Enforcement in Foreign Jurisdiction 

Ordinary statutes of limitation are treated as laws of procedure, and as belonging to the lex fori, as affecting the remedy only, and not the right. But if a statute which creates a right of action also limits it, as is commonly the case with statutes imposing upon stockholders liability to creditors, the right will be enforced subject to the limitation even in a foreign state or jurisdiction.72 On the other hand a state has the right to enact a statute of limitations applicable to actions to enforce the liability of stockholders in foreign as well as in domestic corporations, and such a statute of limitations will be enforced in an action against a stockholder in a foreign corporation, both by the courts of the state and by the federal courts sitting in the state in cases brought therein.73

As we have seen, the statutory liability of stockholders is generally regarded as contractual, so that the right of action is barred by the statute limiting the right of recovery on contracts.74 It has been held by the Supreme Court of the United 

States, however, that the liability of stockholders in a national bank to creditors is not to be regarded as contractual, so as to make applicable the limitation prescribed by a statute of Washington for an "action upon a contract or liability express or im-

 § 296. Constitutional and Statutory Provisions against Fictitious 

Payment

Texas, like a number of other states, has provided that no corporation "shall issue stock or bonds except for money paid, labor done or property actually received, and all fictitious increase of stock or indebtedness shall be void." 80 Most states have held that this provision did not intend to make the validity of every issue of stock or bonds by a private corporation depend on the inquiry whether the money, property or labor received therefor was equal in value to the par value of the stock or bonds so issued.81 Such is the attitude of the Texas courts. They treat stock issued at below par as unpaid subscriptions, as far as the rights of creditors are concerned.82 The liability to pay the difference between the par value of the stock and the sum at which it was issued is imposed by law. 

The provision that all of such "fictitious increase of stock or indebtedness shall be void" presents a very difficult question. 

That all stock issued below par in Texas does not fall under the "void" provision of the constitution may be seen by a quotation from Judge Williams' opinion in the case of Mathis v. Pridham: 83

The better rule is that even when stock is issued for nothing, the creditors may enforce an obligation to pay for the stock, since the agreement to take it gratuitously is invalid, and by reason of our constitutional and statutory provisions a legal obligation is imposed on the stockholder.90 It would seem that the same rules would be applicable to both stock and bonds, since both are mentioned in the constitutional provision. Yet such is not the case. The rule in many states is that bonds may be legally issued for less than their face value.91 A number of states have declared that not only stocks, but also bonds must be issued for "money paid, labor done, and property actually received." Even so, it has been held that this does not prevent the corporation from selling its bonds at the market price or the best price it can obtain for them." 92

If the stockholders fully paid for their stock when it was issued to them, they would not be liable for any further assessments merely because the directors made an honest mistake of judgment in the purchase of property needed by the company, even though the property was purchased from a stockholder.93 Clearly the stockholders would be liable for the difference between what the directors paid for the property and its actual value if they were guilty of fraud or bad faith in purchasing the property. If the purchase is from a co-director, the strict rules of 

Tenison v. Patton 94 will apply to the contract of purchase. Since some promoters of corporations seem to think that it is lawful merely to simulate a payment for the stock of the company, our courts will scrutinize very carefully such transactions and set them aside where there is evidence of fraud or bad faith. 

Some promoters do not hesitate to make an affidavit that the stock has been fully paid for where the subscriber gave a check for the amount of his subscription which was returned to him as soon as the charter is approved by the Secretary of State. 

Such flagrant violations of the law will be severely dealt with by our courts, and if the same result is attempted by fully paying for the stock and purchasing property from the shareholders at a conscious overvaluation, the courts will not hesitate to condemn such practices and hold the stockholders liable to creditors of the company for the difference between the simulated purchase price and the actual value of the property.

§ 297. What is Fictitious Increase? 

As a safeguard against unwarranted and unauthorized issuance of stock, the framers of the constitution provided that stock should not be issued except for money, labor, or property. This clause has given rise to much confusion and to inharmonious decisions. The framers of the constitution went further, however, and provided that all "fictitious increase of stock shall be void." The purpose of the framers doubtless was, in the first place, to forbid issuance of stock without par value being received, and, secondly, to provide a penalty, in that the person accepting a "fictitious increase" would not share in the profits and control of the corporation. Leaving aside for the moment a definition of what constitutes "fictitious increase," and looking to the decided cases, we find practically no cases involving the rights of shareholders, who have not paid par for their stock, to share in the profits or control of the corporation. The constitutional provision against "fictitious increase" has been invoked 

97. Tex.Civ.App., 286 S.W. 285, writ 98. Pacific Am. Gas. Co. v. Miller, of error refused. et al., Tex.Civ.App., 76 S.W.2d 833. 56

Ch. § 297 

against creditors as a protection to persons who have been enjoying the rights and privileges of a stockholder. The erstwhile stockholder asserting that his certificates represented "fictitious increase" of stock and by the constitution are void, and thus no liability attaches to him.

With this introduction in mind, let us turn to a survey of the cases in an endeavor to discern the meaning the courts have given to "fictitious increase" of stock. 

In Mathis v. Pridham 99 the court intimates that "fictitious increase" means overissue of stock. That is, issuing shares representative of an amount beyond that authorized by its charter. 

The court held that issuing shares for less than par value was not a "fictitious increase" of stock.

At one time our statute on increase of capital stock provided that the amount of capital stock could only be doubled, and any attempt to increase above this amount would be void.¹ Under this statute a corporation filed an amendment to its charter attempting to increase its stock from $100,000 to $1,200,000. In 

Kampmann v. Tarver, the receiver of this corporation sued the subscribers who purchased this increase and who had not paid their subscriptions. The court held that there was no liability on the subscribers to pay, as this was an increase beyond the amount allowed by the statute.

It, therefore, seems fairly well settled in Texas that if the increase is an over issue of stock the stock is "fictitious" and even a creditor cannot recover against the subscriber. Another question that has been discussed by the Texas cases is whether stock that has been issued without the receipt or promise of consideration is fictitious. The courts 3 have held that this is not a fictitious increase of stock, and have stated that creditors could

There are three theories on which liability of stockholders to creditors on account of discount, bonus or watered stock is predicated: the trust fund theory, which originated in Wood v. Dummer; 33 the fraud or holding out theory, originated by the case of Hospes v. Northwestern Mfg. & Car Co.; 34 and the statutory liability theory.35 The main distinction between the first two rules is that in the Hospes doctrine, based on fraud, actual or constructive, creditors whose claims arose prior to the subscription in question cannot benefit thereby because they did not rely on the fact that the full price would be paid for the stock; and the same applies to creditors who dealt with the corporation with notice of the agreement with the stockholders. At present the 

Hospes doctrine is the most popular. The old trust fund theory is breaking down. Ballantine prefers the following rule: The liability should rest on the obligation imposed "by statute or common law upon original subscribers and purchasers with notice to make a contribution to capital for the benefit of creditors as an incident of membership in the corporation." 36 As the constitutional and statutory provisions are so plain, it is the opinion of the writer that this theory of liability is the most satisfactory and the one that most courts will finally adopt. The claim against the stockholder should be considered one of the assets of the corporation that prior or subsequent creditors, with or without notice, should be permitted to rely upon for the satisfaction of corporate debts.37

From the language in the decisions of the Texas courts it is difficult to ascertain just what theory the liability of subscribers in these cases is based on. For years the Texas courts have automatically recited the trust fund theory, but an examination of the decided cases reveals the fact that this theory, if it ever in fact existed in this state, has been abandoned so far as the liability of subscribers for unpaid subscriptions is concerned. The trust fund theory is clearly fictitious as a corporation does not hold its assets in trust for its creditors any more than an individual. A few cases in which the trust fund theory has been stated are found in the note.³ 38 There are many more to the same effect. In fact, there are very few cases dealing with corporation law in Texas wherein this antiquated doctrine was not reiterated somewhere in the opinion. But regardless of how often this statement has been repeated, the Hospes doctrine is in fact being applied. Then, quoting from the Burleson case,42 the court said: "It is well established ** that the rights of stockholders who have been induced to purchase stock by the fraudulent representations of the corporation or its agents are subordinated to the rights of those who, without any knowledge of such fraud, have subsequently become creditors of the corporation." 43 

The authority of these cases has never been questioned. Thus it will be seen that the Texas courts, apparently unaware of the difference in result which logically follows the applications of these two theories, purport to predicate the subscriber's liability on the theory that the capital stock constitutes a trust fund for the benefit of creditors; but when the results that the courts reach are analyzed, it is obvious that at least insofar as the problem of determining which creditors may enforce and profit by the liability of the subscriber, the Hospes doctrine is applied. 

The following language from Burleson v. Davis 44 is an illustration of how the courts confuse the trust fund theory with the Hospes doctrine: "In such case the subscriber to the capital stock of the corporation by his own act has induced the subsequent creditors of such corporation to believe that the capital stock subscribed by him has been or will be paid in, and will remain a trust fund to which subsequent creditors may look for security. The stockholder-plaintiffs herein subscribed to the stock of the Union Trust Company with a view of making a profit on the investment. By such act on their part they invited the depositors to deposit their money with said trust company, and thereby represented that their subscription to the stock was bona fide, and would remain in the vaults of the company to meet any demands that might be made by the depositors. They now by their acts say to the depositor: "True, we made such representations and pledges to you, but we now seek to repudiate the pledges so made by us, because we were induced to do so by fraudulent misrepresentations made to us.' The courts treat a promissory note exchanged for stock as just another evidence of the stockholder's promise to pay, and say that when creditors are concerned, the stockholder is estopped to assert the illegality of the transaction and the courts enforce the agreement without regard to the time when the creditors' rights arose.46 This is an admirable result and doubtless should be the rule applied in a majority of other situations. For as said in Thompson v. First State Bank,47 "creditors dealing with a corporation have the right to assume that its capital has been or will be paid in accordance with law." 

Where stock has been issued for cash at less than par value, as a gift or bonus or for overvalued property, what are the creditors' rights? Under these circumstances if the trust fund doctrine were applied there would be no res and consequently nothing for the creditors to recover. Under the fraud or holding out theory, those creditors whose rights arose subsequent to the illegal transaction, and who relied upon the representation that the stock was legally issued, could recover. As a matter of fact, few, if any, creditors inquire as to the amount of capital stock that has been issued when they give credit to the company. 

They rely more on the financial rating of the company. In an endeavor to apply a rule of thumb to a given fact situation some courts have presumed that the subsequent creditor relied upon the fact that the stock had been legally issued. This presumption, even though not in accord with the actual facts, reaches a just result. But such reasoning will not protect a creditor whose rights arose prior to the issuance of this stock. It is true that the court cannot even presume that the prior creditor relied on a transaction that was not even contemplated at the time his debt

§ 301. Rights of Third Persons with Respect to Notes Given for Shares-Creditors

A very strong argument which has never been answered by any of the decided cases, can be made against the position taken by the Commission of Appeals. In the Texas cases cited above, especially in the case of Mitchell v. Porter 75 the court reasons that the creditor should recover the amount agreed to be paid as surplus because he is estopped to deny liability. As a matter of fact no question of estoppel is involved since the stockholder has made no false representation and in practically all cases there has been no reliance on the stockholder's promise to pay above par for his stock. In most cases the creditor knows nothing of the stockholder's promise until long after credit is given the corporation. As a matter of fact there is no question of estoppel involved in these cases. Under the holding of our Supreme Court the contract is illegal. 

As we have already seen, even though the contract is illegal and not void, the creditor may recover against the stockholder. 

On what basis? There can be no reason for recovery except the obligation imposed by the law. Since the contractual obligation is illegal and, therefore, must be discarded, the only legal obligation imposed by the law is that the subscriber must pay par for his stock. If this reasoning is logical even the creditor should not be permitted to recover the amount the subscriber agreed to pay to the surplus of the company. This argument seems unanswerable unless the contract is divisible. In many of the cases the contract is clearly not divisible as the subscriber simply agrees to pay a lump sum for so many shares of stock.

It was stated that the evils designed to be prevented by the Constitution did not warrant the holding that the subscriber can, by his own wrong in violating the constitution, escape the payment of his note. The court correctly concluded that the constitutional provision is to protect the public, and was not meant to make the innocent suffer rather than the guilty. In Zielinski v. Hernig 80 it is said: "The protection thrown around the innocent purchaser of commercial paper, in our judgment, and in so far as can be legitimately accomplished, should be strengthened by our courts, and the vitality of same should not be impaired without a clear necessity, or a legislative enactment demand that it should be done."

The modern trend is to hold that the implication of a statute that a certain obligation is illegal is not enough to render the instrument unenforceable in the hands of a holder in due course, simply because the transaction out of which it arose is not sanctioned by the Constitution or statutes. As stated in Washer v. 

Smyer: 81 "There is an essential difference between prohibiting a certain form of transaction-making it unlawful, and declaring that it, with all securities issuing out of it, shall be utterly void. 

It is a distinction familiar in the law." The security of commercial transactions and considerations of public policy require that innocent purchasers be protected. It seems that regardless of whether a note is property or not, the innocent holder should be protected as against one who has given his solemn obligation to pay, although it is given in violation of law. 

Even if no recovery is allowed in favor of the innocent purchaser as against the maker of the note, he is entitled to recover against the corporation, where the note is indorsed by the corporation. By the indorsement, the genuineness of the instrument has been guaranteed.82

A distinction has been drawn between the first elause of Article 12, section 6, of the Constitution, and the last clause of that section. The first clause provides that stock shall be issued only for money paid, labor done, or property actually received, but does not declare what the effect of a violation of the provision shall be. In the last clause, however, it is expressly stated that all fictitious increase of stock shall be void. This is the distinction made by some of the cases in order to allow recovery on notes given for stock in the hands of an innocent purchaser.83 

Perhaps the best statement of the distinction is found in Smith v. Ideal Laundry Company,84 where this language is used: "The distinction made by the founders of the Constitution between the unlawful issuance of stock or bonds for an inadequate or no consideration, and the fictitious increase of stock or indebtedness, is just and right, for the first may involve a lack of business acumen, but the second involves fraud and moral turpitude. The former may involve such negligence and lack of business sense as to render the act voidable; the latter is criminal, and renders the transaction void."

Whether a certain transaction in its inception is void or merely voidable, has a direct bearing on the rights of subsequent parties. It is believed the excerpt above properly construes the constitution. This is borne out by the following passage from Washer v. Smyer: 85 "The word 'void' is used but once in the constitutional provision, and that, it is to be noted, is not in the clause which prohibits the issuance of stock for other than money, property or labor. It is in the distinct clause which says that all fictitious increase of stock or indebtedness shall be void. 

While the term is found in that clause of the section, the framers of the Constitution avoided its use in the other. It must be assumed that they did so deliberately." 83.

§ 303. Rights of Innocent Purchaser of the Stock 

Where stock is issued for the illegal note of a stockholder and sold to an innocent purchaser, the stock becomes valid; and the corporation must recognize the assignee as a stockholder.87 

§ 304. When is Property Overvalued? 

The courts of America have adopted different rules for determining the liability of the shareholders for overvaluing property given for stock of a corporation. Some courts have adopted the "true value rule", which in short is that payment for capital stock is no payment except to the extent of the true value of the property; and if property is taken at an overvaluation, the shareholder is liable for the deficiency.88 Other states have, however, applied a less strict rule, called "the good faith rule." 

Under this latter rule the valuation put on the property by the directors is conclusive in the absence of a showing of fraud or intentional or reckless overvaluation.89 Some of the courts have

The conflict between the Adams case and the Peden case was noted in the recent case of Thomason v. Miller,³ and it was there observed that the Peden case was decided after the enactment of Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. arts. 1308 and 1309, which require an affidavit showing the manner in which stock subscriptions are paid, and a description and value of the property which is taken in payment for the stock, charge the Secretary of State with the duty of ascertaining the correctness of the stated valuation, and confer on him authority to refuse the charter if the property is overvalued; while the Cole case was decided prior to the statute. 

If this is a valid reason for the differences in the two decisions, it would seem that the Peden case, that is, the good faith test, is the law in Texas. But a careful perusal of the Peden case discloses that there is a question as to whether the language on this point is dictum or decision. The Thomason case takes no stand on the conflict.

§ 306. Liability of Transferor and Transferee of Bonus, Discount, or Watered Stock 

In determining the liability of the vendor and vendee of certificates of stocks of a corporation one must keep in mind whether the liability is based on watered stock or on the liability of one who has not fully paid the agreed consideration for the stock. It goes without saying that in either case the vendor remains liable if the transfer was fraudulent.13 If the transfer is not fraudulent and the liability is based on the agreed consideration for the stock, the transferee is liable if he purchased with notice that the entire consideration had not been paid for the stock. In such a case the transferor is not liable as a novation was effected by the transfer of the stock to one who purchased with notice. In the very nature of things the stock of a corporation is transferable. Therefore, as long as the transfer was not fraudulent, the corporation has agreed in advance that it will release the transferor and accept the liability of the transferee in lieu of that of the transferor. However, if the transfer is to a purchaser without notice a novation is not effected and the transferor remains liable for future calls and the transferee assumes no liability.14 In the case of bonus, discount, or watered stock the liability of the transferor and transferee depends upon what doctrine of liability is recognized by the law of the state which applies to the case under consideration. Under the New 

Jersey and Delaware doctrine of "absolute liability” both the transferor and transferee with notice are held liable on bonus, discount, or watered stock.15 A court in New York held that the transferor is liable on bonus, discount, or watered stock where

It seems clear that the distinction discussed in the preceding paragraph should be made. A casual reading of the cases cited in this section will reveal how unsatisfactory the authorities are. All of these questions, with the exception of the actual decision in the Park-Rich Case, remain unsettled in Texas. The text books say that a novation has been agreed to where there is a sale of partly paid stock to a solvent party with notice; and some cases hold that a joint tort has been committed where there is a sale of bonus, discount or watered stock to a purchaser with notice or knowledge. 

The Texas courts will be faced with perplexing problems when these questions arise. In the first place do we, in determining the liability of the stockholder, follow the “absolute liability” or the "Hospes" doctrine? Suppose in the partly paid for stock there is an agreement that the transferor will remain liable and that the vendee assumes no liability, will the courts enforce this agreement? In Texas, if the stock is issued before the agreed consideration is paid the "issue" is illegal. Unless the stock certificate is made out and delivered to the purchaser or subscriber, it would be very difficult to have an innocent purchaser without notice that the purchase price has not been fully paid. But if it is "issued" and the holder is recognized as the owner before it is fully paid for, the issue is illegal. These questions must be considered by the Texas Courts in determining the above questions as to the liability of the vendor and vendee in the sale of (1) partly paid for stock and (2) bonus, discount or watered stock.

As the authorities are so confusing the Texas Supreme Court is free to adopt a sane solution of the most troublesome of the

Capital Stock and Issue of Stock even though the certificate of stock is filled out, the stock has not been issued unless the subscriber is recognized as the "owner" of the stock, such as permitting him to vote or receive dividends. If he has merely a contract to subscribe and has agreed to pay certain installments for his stock the contract is lawful so long as the stock is not issued until fully paid. In all cases of this kind it seems difficult on principle to say that the corporation has agreed in advance of full payment to enter into a novation with any solvent person to whom the subscriber assigns his rights. The rule of contract law is that one can assign one's rights but not one's obligations. 

Some authorities say that the stock of a corporation is assignable; and, therefore, a novation is effected as soon as the corporation issues a new certificate to the assignee of the subscriber. There is some reason for that conclusion where it is lawful to issue a certificate of stock to a subscriber who has only partly paid for his stock since the issuance of a new certificate to the assignee may be some evidence of an agreement by the corporation for a novation.

Even that is an extension of the rules of contract law. If A owes B and the latter assigns his rights and "obligations" to C who assumes the debt, after B "accepts" C as the principal debtor A remains a surety, and a novation is not effected unless there is a special agreement by which A is released. Where the promoters have been exceedingly careful in the selection of solvent reliable subscribers, and a certificate of stock is not issued to the subscriber, even the acceptance of payments from the assignee

The text writers have been too liberal in asserting that the transferor is released where the transfer was not made to escape liability even though the transferee is not as solvent nor as substantial a person as the transferor.28 Most text writers and law review case notes make no distinction between the liability of the transferor in the case (1) of the transfer of stock that had been fully paid for but to which stock there is a statutory liability, such as bank stock under the old statutes, and (2) the transfer of bonus, discount or watered stock to a purchaser with knowledge.29

Where a statutory liability attaches to the stock the transferor is usually released from liability twelve months after the transfer. In such a case the transferee would become liable even if he had no knowledge of the statute. As the corporation received par for such stock, the only question involved is the meaning of the statute which imposes the liability. Under the statute is the vendor liable for twelve months after the assignment? Aside from that question which the statute makes plain, the only issue under the usual statute is, who owned the stock when the liability arose? So it seems evident that a distinction should be made in the above two cases. At least the cases should not be confused, and it should not be argued that because

Suppose the owner of partly paid for stock sells his rights "and obligations" to a solvent person, but the assignee is not as solvent nor as reliable as the assignor; and the corporation refuses to accept the assignment where the assignee knows that the stock has not been fully paid for. Would a court, in a state where the stock can be legally issued before it is fully paid, compel a transfer of the stock on the books of the company; and in a subsequent case hold that a novation was effected by the transfer? If the text writers and cases mean to say that only where the corporation voluntarily recognizes the transfer realizing that an offered novation is tendered, no complaint can be urged against their contention that the transferor is released. 

Too often the statement is made that a mere "transfer to a solvent person with notice" releases the transferor.

If the transferee cannot force the secretary to make the transfer where the directors realize that the transferee is not as reliable as the transferor, no serious objection could be made to the conclusion that a novation is effected as soon as the corporation has issued a new certificate. The authorities seem to say that as soon as the transferor has surrendered the old certificate to the secretary and requested a transfer a novation has resulted so as to relieve the transferor of liability. In Section 

6105 of Fletcher, Cyc. Corporations (Per. Ed.) it is said: "The general rule is that a transfer of stock which is not registered or deposited for registration does not relieve the transferor from liability to or for the benefit of creditors of the corporation for any balance that may remain unpaid on the shares. However, it is sufficient to relieve the transferor from liability under this rule, if he has done everything which the law requires him to do in order to secure the transfer on the books, although the transfer has not in fact been registered because of the neglect or refusal of the proper corporate officers to register it." However, in two fairly recent California cases the reason for the difference in liability is clearly stated.44 In Rhode v. Dock-Hop 

Co.45 the court said: "It is apparent that, when one accepts partially paid stock, which does not purport to be anything else, he does so, or must be taken to do so, upon the understanding that it is answerable upon call for the unpaid balance upon it, and that he as its owner must respond to such a call. When he enters into relationship with the corporation as one of its stockholders owning stock of that character, he assumes as an incident to the relationship, the obligation to respond to calls upon him for further contributions to the capital of the company until such capital is full paid in. ** * "But where a person accepts the ownership of stock which purports to be fully paid, a very different situation is presented. 

It cannot be said of him for a moment that he accepts the stock and enters upon the relation of stockholder to the corporation upon any understanding that his stock is liable for further calls on capital account, or that he, as an incident of his ownership and consequent relationship, assumes any such obligation. On the contrary, it is evident that he accepts the ownership of the stock and enters upon the relationship of stockholder with just the contrary understanding. What, then, is the principle upon which the holder of watered stock is, under any circumstances, held obligated to supply substance instead of water, to make good what it is pretended the corporation received but did not? 

The answer to this question is not in doubt. The stockholder is held upon the principle that one giving credit to a corporation is entitled to rely upon its ostensible capitalization as the basis for the credit given, and that, when the corporation issues watered stock and thereby assumes an ostensible capitalization in excess books in the opinion, reversed Park v. Rich, Com.App., 212 S.W. 947, 216 

S.W. 146. 

44. The reason is also emphasized in 25 Col.L.Rev. 408. 

45. 194 P. 11, 184 Cal. 367, 12 A.L.R. 437. 94

of its real assets, the transaction necessarily involves the misleading of subsequent creditors, and, whether done with that purpose actually in mind or not, is at least a constructive fraud upon such creditors. "Such, however, is not the situation of the stockholder owning shares ostensibly fully paid but not so in fact. He owes the corporation no duty to make good the difference, and there is no obligation on his part which is an asset of the corporation or which the corporation may enforce. 

"Upon the plainest principles, therefore, he cannot be held liable unless he was either a party to the transaction in the first instance or has in effect in some manner made himself a party since. "It is essentially one to compel the defendants to make good a false representation in defraud of the plaintiff; a suit to enforce an alleged personal liability, not a suit to enforce a lien or claim against the stock in the hands of the defendants. As an element of such a cause of action against the defendants, they must be shown either to have participated in the making of the representation or in some manner to have assumed responsibility for it. The mere fact that they received their stock as a gratuity does not show either. The fact may still be that they knew nothing about the representation and had no part in it, and cannot justly be held responsible for it in any way. "In view of the necessity for a new trial, there are three further points which should be determined for the guidance of the court and parties. The first of these is as to what is necessary in order to show that the defendants, acquiring, as they did, their stock by way of transfer from Knapp, assumed responsibility for the fraudulent representation involved in the issuance of the shares as fully paid; is it enough to show that they acquired their stock with notice or knowledge that it was issued for a consideration fictitious in part, or must something more be shown? 

As to this, we think it sufficient that it appear that when the defendants accepted their stock they had notice or knowledge of its real character. We can see no reason why one who accepts stock with notice or knowledge that it is but partially paid, al- 95

§ 

Ch. 8

though issued as fully paid, should not be held to assume the same responsibility which he would assume if the stock were issued for what it really is, partially paid stock. He knows, or should know, its real character, and should be charged as if its ostensible character were what it really is. 

And in Spencer v. Anderson 40 the court said: "In considering the questions presented by the defense of the statute of limitations, it is important to keep in mind essential differences between actions by a creditor of a corporation to recover upon the stockholders' unpaid subscriptions, on the one hand, and actions by such a creditor to recover from stockholders who have received bonus or watered stock, upon the other hand. Some of these differences are clearly pointed out in Rhode v. Dock-Hop Co., 184 

Cal. 367, 194 P. 11, 12 A.L.R. 437. Actions of the first class sound exclusively in contract, while the gist of the actions of the second class is tort. The two classes of actions present many points of similarity, and the failure to distinguish between them has led to unfortunate confusion, particularly in the earlier cases. 

Both are creditors' bills in equity, both are actions by a creditor of a corporation, seeking the aid of equity for the satisfaction of his claim out of assets not reachable by the ordinary processes of the law, and in both (but for different reasons) the plaintiff is required to allege and prove the recovery of a judgment against the corporation and the return of execution nulla bona (or that the corporation has become insolvent). But here the similarity ceases. "It also follows that a creditor cannot recover against the holder of bonus or watered stock unless the latter has participated in the fraud, or has ratified it by accepting the stock with knowledge thereof."

In the quotation from the first of the two California opinions the court stated that the main reason for holding the purchaser of watered stock with notice liable to creditors is that a false representation of the condition of the company's affairs is made to the creditors of the company; that all who are implicated 

46. 222 P. 355, 193 Cal. 1, 35 A.L.R. 822. 96

in that wrong are liable to creditors without notice of how the stock was paid for when it was originally issued; that one is a party to the wrong "who accepts stock with notice or knowledge that it is but partially paid" and that such party "assumes the same responsibility which he would assume if the stock were issued for what it really is, partially paid stock." In the second of the two cases the court said that the transferee of watered stock is liable if he "participated in the fraud, or has ratified it by accepting the stock with knowledge thereof."47 Both of these opinions intimate that a purchaser, or donee with notice, becomes liable even for debts of the corporation incurred before the transferee became the owner of the stock. This point has not been decided by the Texas courts. If the reason for the liability of the holder of watered stock is that he has made a false representation that the creditor expressly or impliedly relied upon, how can it be said that the transferee is liable for debts created before he purchased the stock? It may be just to hold him liable for obligations created after he became the owner of the stock, but it is difficult to understand why he should be liable for obligations incurred before he purchased, or became the donee, of the stock. If by fraud A was induced to sell on credit his horse to B for $100.00, and B sold the horse to C, a purchaser with knowledge of the fraud, would any lawyer contend that C became liable to A for the purchase price where A elected not to rescind the trade? The liability of the purchaser with notice should be put on a more rational basis than has been urged by the courts up to this time.48

Another point that has never been decided in Texas is the liability of the transferee with notice who is a purchaser or donee from a prior innocent purchaser without notice. The statutory liability of stockholders in banks and other corporations is discussed in another chapter in this text.50 

In the case of partly paid stock the rights of the creditor is derivative. In other words, his rights are worked out through the right of the corporation to sue for the balance of the agreed consideration for the stock. In the case of watered stock, in those states that follow the fraud doctrine, the subsequent creditor without notice has an individual right to compel the stockholder to pay the difference between the par value and what he paid for the stock if he is unable to collect the amount due from the corporation. Where the creditor's suit is derivative; in other words, where he is suing in the right of the corporation, the stockholder can interpose any defense that would be valid if he were sued by the corporation.52 The stockholder is not discharged from his liability to the corporation where he pays the amount due to the creditor even though he pays the creditor after the latter has a right to bring a creditor's bill against the stockholder. He owes the amount to the corporation and is not discharged by a payment to the creditor of the amount due to the creditor.53 

From what has been said it seems evident that in the case of partly paid-for stock when the claim is barred against the corporation, it is also barred so far as the creditor's suit is concerned.54 However, in the case of watered stock the corporation has no cause of action against the stockholder. In other words, the rights of the creditor against the holders of watered stock is a personal action and limitation does not begin to run until the creditor has exhausted his remedy against the corporation.
