In most cases credit is extended to a corporation on the basis of a financial statement and its financial reputation rather than on the amount of its "capital stock." The company may have a small capital, yet if it has a large surplus and undivided profits its borrowing capacity is much greater than if it has a large "capital stock" which is greatly impaired. However, the stockholders would not be personally liable for the debts of either corporation if the stock was fully paid for when it was first issued. On the other hand, let us suppose a case where the "capital stock" of an oil company is $100,000. The subscribers took all the stock for oil leases worth only $50,000 when the entire stock was issued to them. Later an oil field was developed on the company's property and the original subscribers sold their stock for one million dollars to A, B and C who knew that the stock was originally watered to the extent of $50,000. In the heyday of the company's business plaintiff lent the company $50,000 but he did not know that the original stock was watered. 

When the plaintiff gave credit to the company its assets amounted to ten times its "capital stock," but when the plaintiff's debt matured the assets of the corporation were not sufficient to pay its obligations. Under the law of most states A, B and C would be liable to the extent of $50,000 if it became necessary to collect that amount to pay subsequent creditors without notice that the original stock was watered, even though the stock "was issued" twenty years before the company became insolvent. So the liability of the original subscribers and subsequent purchasers with notice is not bottomed on a misrepresentation that the clear assets of the corporation equal the amount of the company's "capital stock" when credit is extended to the corporation, but on a false statement that when the stock of the com-

In Trinity Portland Cement Co. v. Naylor the court held that a creditor 59 could not bring a creditor's bill against shareholders for the unpaid balance of their stock subscriptions where the company was thrown into bankruptcy and the plaintiff had accepted sixty per cent of his claim under a composition agreement. 

The court said that Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1345 applied only where the creditor had obtained a judgment against the corporation and the execution returned nulla bona. In the opinion the court said: "It is plain that the right there given a creditor of a corporation, to a levy of execution on the property of a stockholder who has failed to pay into the corporation the amount of his stock subscription, does not arise until judgment has already been recovered by the creditor against the corporation and no property belonging to it can be found out of which the judgment may be satisfied. In other words, that right is given to no one but a judgment creditor; and the specific mention of a judgment creditor without giving a similar right to all general creditors whose claims have not been reduced to judgment implies an exclusion of the latter from the benefits of that statute under the rule 'inclusio unius est exclusio alterius.' To hold otherwise would be to do violence to the most elementary rules of statutory construction."

The creditor must proceed at law and not in equity where he seeks to hold the stockholders liable for unpaid subscriptions under Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1345. The creditor must make the motion specified in the above article in the court where he obtained judgment against the corporation.65

Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1395 provides: "No stockholder shall be liable to pay debts of the corporation beyond the amount unpaid on his stock." In the case of Peden Iron & Steel Co. v. 

Jenkins 66 the court assumed that the above statute applies to watered stock. In that case the only claim of the creditor was that the oil lease transferred to the company for its stock was over-valued, and, for this reason, it was sought to hold the stockholders individually liable for the difference between the real value of the lease and the par value of the stock. The court did not discuss the question in detail as the lower court held that the lease was not overvalued. However, if the court had been of the opinion that the above statute does not apply to watered stock, it could have affirmed the ruling of the district court in a very few words. The above article of the Texas statutes is very similar to article 1345 as to the liability of the stockholder for "unpaid stock."

The troublesome question that has not finally been settled by the Supreme Court of Texas is, do both of the above articles impose a personal liability on the stockholder not only in the case where he has not fully paid the agreed consideration for his stock, but also where the stock is watered? Under article 1395 the court may impose an absolute liability on the stockholder to the full extent of "the amount unpaid on his stock" when the corporation is dissolved. As a matter of fact, under the Texas statutes which clearly make unlawful "the issuance" of watered stock, the Texas courts should impose an absolute liability on the subscriber as in New Jersey, Delaware and Illinois, and not follow the holding of Scovill v. Thayer 67 in holding that the contract between the shareholder and the corporation is binding on the company; since that is a "common law" decision, and not in harmony with our present statutes. At least one of the 

Texas Courts of Civil Appeals reached that result, and the reasoning of that opinion is unanswerable.68 Since article 1345 applies only where the creditor has obtained a judgment against the corporation, and article 1395 applies only after the corporation has been dissolved, in all other cases it is necessary for the Supreme 

Court of Texas to decide whether Texas follows the Hospes doc trine or the absolute liability doctrine. The liability of a subscriber on a legal or illegal contract of subscription under the above two articles where he agreed to pay above par for his stock is discussed in § 863 in the chapter on Dissolution of a Private Corperation.

Carman Co.,⁹ the Supreme Court of Colorado held that the statute fixed an absolute liability on the stockholder even though watered stock was issued to him. In that case the subscriber was given one share of common stock for each share of preferred stock for which he paid par value. The court held that the subscriber was liable even to creditors who knew that the common stock was issued as a bonus, and it is evident that the court would have held the subscribers liable even to creditors whose claims arose before the defendants subscribed for the bonus stock, if that question had been involved in the case. In the opinion the court said: "It would therefore appear that Frink is liable 'to the extent of the unpaid portion of his stock.' But since he made no contract to pay anything for this common stock and there is no evidence of its value, his counsel contend there is no basis in the record on which 'the unpaid portion of his stock,' if any, can be determined; hence there could be no recovery. But the liability is statutory, arbitrary and definite. Par value seems to have been the measure contemplated by the Legislature. No other is suggested. "It is said that the Zott Company's reports to the secretary of state disclosed its practice of issuing common stock as a bonus on preferred, as did its financial statements, and it is contended that this constructive notice bound creditors, and since they could not have been misled into any belief that this common stock had been, or would be, paid for, no reason remains for permitting them to hold such stockholders under the statute. But there is no evidence that the Carman Company or its assignors had, or should have had, knowledge of the financial statements, and the reports to the secretary of state are too indefinite to convey the information that Frink acquired his common stock without consideration. Regardless of these facts, however, the statutory liability is unconditional, and in such case notice and knowledge are immaterial.”

§ 307  § 307. Issue of Additional Stock by a Corporation Financially Em barrassed

If the market value of the stock of the corporation is below par, the corporation must either issue new stock at less than par or borrow, if it needs money. By the weight of authority there is no liability on the subscriber when a corporation becomes embarrassed and issues an increase of its capital stock in good faith at the best price it can obtain, although such stock is sold for less than par.70 One Texas case has recognized this rule. The court in Witt v. Nelson "¹ said: "In considering the cases wherein it has been held that unpaid subscriptions to capital stock is a trust fund for the benefit of creditors, it must be kept in mind that there is a distinction between stock subscribed for the purpose of organizing the corporation and stock sold by an organized corporation for the purpose of enabling it to pay its debts or to carry on its business. In the former case it is held upon equitable grounds that the subscription is a contract to pay the full par value of the stock, if it becomes necessary to do so to protect creditors; in the latter case the purchase is a contract to pay only the price agreed upon, if the same be the fair market price of the stock purchased. 

In the instant case, the purchasers of stock sold for the purpose of enabling the corporation to continue its business, and not for the purpose of increasing its investment, or enlarging its plant, were not subscribers to the stock in the sense that subscribers are required to pay the full par value of their stock." The Witt case seems to be the only 

Texas case that has dealt with this point. 

Since the Supreme Court refused a writ of error in the Witt case, apparently Texas follows the rule of Handley v. Stutz. The court in Witt v. Nelson gave three distinct grounds for refusing to hold the subscribers liable and the Supreme Court by refusing

 § 342. Restrictions and Regulations of the Transfer of Shares 

Even though a shareholder may transfer his shares of stock, the right of transfer is subject to reasonable regulations and restrictions. There are various methods by which the transfer of shares is legitimately restricted and regulated.¹ 

Aside from all other restrictions, the transferee must have the legal capacity to purchase and hold shares of stock. A married woman in Texas has the legal capacity to acquire and hold stock.5 The rules of contract law apply to a purchase of stock by an infant, and consequently an infant may repudiate his duties as a shareholder at any time before he attains majority, or within a reasonable time thereafter; but if he fails to take advantage of his opportunity within a reasonable time after he becomes of age, he will be held liable as a shareholder. In Texas a partnership may hold stock in a corporation. The legal capacity of a corporation to purchase and hold its own stock or the stock of another corporation is discussed elsewhere.8 6

One method employed by many states to restrict and regulate the transfer of shares is by enactment of a statute for that purpose. There are no statutory restrictions in Texas on the transfer of shares but Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 1334, specifically regulates the transfer. It provides: "The stock of any corporation created under this title shall be deemed personal estate, and shall be transferable only on the books of the corporation in such manner as the by-laws may prescribe." But if the registered of the corporation's assets, nor is a sale of all the stock of a corporation a sale of the physical properties of the corporation. Presnall v. Along with the latter class of by-laws are those which regulate the mode of transfer. Their purpose is not to prohibit the transfer of shares but to protect the corporation itself. The court in Seeligson & Co. v. Brown," in referring to by-laws requiring that the stock be transferable only on the books of the corporation, said: "As they are intended merely for the protection of the interests of the corporation no effect is given to them further than is necessary to effect that purpose. It is necessary that an incorporated company should have the means of knowing who are stockholders and members in order that they may know to whom dividends are to be paid, and who are entitled to vote upon the stock; and where the company has a lien upon the stock for debts due to it from a stockholder, that it should have the means of preventing a transfer in derogation of its own rights. To secure this knowledge and to enable corporations to avail themselves of their liens upon the stock of the company without danger to the rights of purchasers, these clauses are usually inserted in their charters or form a part of their by-laws". A very interesting problem arises in a situation where an officer of a corporation purports to sell and transfer shares of stock which he allegedly owns in the said corporation, but actually the officer has either previously sold or pledged his stock to third persons. In the case of Williams v. Terminal Hotel Co.,20 the president of the corporation sold to the plaintiff fifty shares of stock purporting to be the stock owned by the president, but in reality the stock was an overissue because all the authorized shares had been previously issued. The court refused to allow the purchaser any recovery from the corporation on the theory that he was guilty of negligence in not demanding a right to inspect the books to determine whether the transfer had been made on the books. The Court cited the case of Moores v. Citizens' 

National Bank of Piqua 30 and followed the reasoning of that case. The contrary view is set down by the Missouri Court in 

National Bank of Webb City v. Newell-Morse Royalty Co.31 

There is no doubt in the writer's mind that the Missouri case and the authorities cited therein in support of the decision will mete out justice more often than the Texas holding. Webb City v. Newell-Morse Royalty Co.34 343. The Effect of the Dissolution of the Corporation 

Upon the dissolution of the corporation, the shareholder loses his power to transfer the legal title to his shares of stock. The most that he can transfer is an equitable right to share in the assets of the corporation after all debts of the corporation have been paid. 

66 * * * the dissolution of the corporation put an end, immediately, to the transferable nature of the stock. And it thus reduced the interests of the stockholders to mere equitable rights to their several distributive shares of the corporate funds, upon. principles of equal justice and equity among all the stockholders, after paying all debts and expenses. * * And this right to a distributive share of the estate being a mere chose in action, the owner thereof cannot assign it to a third person, so as to give the latter any greater or other interest therein than the assignor himself possessed." 35 No Texas cases discuss this point.

§ 344. Making the Transfer Effective at the Domicile of the Cor poration

Another interesting aspect to the transfer of shares of stock is involved where the corporation is domiciled in one state, and the transfer is made in another state in which both parties may reside.37 However, no matter where the certificate is acquired, the person acquiring the certificate will be recognized as the owner since the certificate is a representative of the shares. The 

Restatement of the Conflict of Laws recognizes that shares of stock may be subject to the jurisdiction of the domicile of the corporation or to the jurisdiction of the state where the certificate is located.38 Corporate shares of a non-resident may be levied upon by service upon the corporation. In some states where the certificate is treated as personal property, it may be attached in the state where it is located.39 The rule of making

§ 345. Sales Contract-Rights and Remedies 

A contract involving the transfer of shares of stock is governed by the general rules of contract law.42 If the offer to sell was made in jest and was so understood by the offeree, there would be no contract of sale even though the offeree went through the formality of accepting the offer. If the offer was made in jest, but the offeree thought it was made seriously and as a reasonable person had a right so to conclude from all the overt manifestation of intent on the part of the offeror, there would be a contract.43 The contract of sale must be supported by consideration. But, if there was no fraud involved in the sale of the stock, mere inadequacy of consideration would not be sufficient to invalidate the contract.44 The contract need not be in writschaft V.

"If the stock contracted to be sold is easily obtained in the market, and there are no particular reasons why the vendee should have the particular stock contracted for, he is left to his action for damages. But where the value of the stock is not easily ascertained, or the stock is not to be obtained readily elsewhere, or there is some particular reasonable cause for the vendee requiring the stock contracted to be delivered, a court of equity will decree a specific performance and compel the vendor to deliver the stock." 89

As a general rule, by the weight of authority in America, specific performance of an agreement to sell specific stock will be decreed if the shares are not readily obtainable in the open market.⁰⁰ But in a small minority of the States, specific performance is not decreed, even though the shares cannot be purchased in the open market.91 If an owner of shares of stock misrepresents the value of the stock by positive statements of facts, the purchaser of said stock can recover damages if the stock is of less value.92

§ 347. The Method of Transferring Shares 

The method of transferring shares has been previously touched upon in discussing the validity of the regulations and restrictions in transferring shares. Prior to the passage of Vernon's Ann. 

Civ.St. art. 1334, in the absence of a by-law or provision on the certificates requiring the transfer of shares to be made on the books of the company, the legal title passed by the transfer and delivery of the certificate by the person to whom it was issued. 

An early case said that "a share of stock in a corporation, unlike land, may be sold by parol, or pass by delivery of the certificate of stock, by which its ownership is evidenced. 

But at the time the 26 certificates were issued to Condit and at the time of the sale to Le Page, the company was a joint stock company and not a corporation, and there was no rule or by-law which required its stock to be transferred upon its books or otherwise providing the manner of sale. This being true, in the absence of any rules or regulations of the company governing the sale of its stock, the legal title, in our opinion, passed by the transfer and delivery of the certificate by the person to whom it was issued." • Prior to the passage of article 1334, it was fairly customary for the by-laws of the corporation to provide that the shares of stock are transferable only on the books of

In section 851 Machen says: "Transfers of shares are governed by the same principles whether, as in England, they are separate and distinct from the share-certificate or whether, as usually in the 

United States, they are endorsed upon it. Indeed, a transfer of shares in an English company endorsed upon the certificate would be quite as valid as if it were written upon a separate paper; and, conversely, in 

America, a transfer disconnected from the certificate has the same effect as if endorsed upon it. The 

American practice is one of convenience merely. § 348. Transfer by Delivery of the Certificate 

In a majority of states gifts of stock are valid without any written assignment." The Texas case of Shaw v. McMillan 12 the items of stock purchased by appellee for appellant are three receipts for subscriptions to stock that were not formally transferred by the original owners. The want of indorsement showing the transfers of these three receipts for subscription is urged as an objection by appellant as showing a want of ownership and title in the stock, and that such transfers should have been made by the original owners in order to pass the title thereto. "The evidence shows that the presentation of these receipts to the secretary of the association without a written transfer from the original owners entitled the holders thereof to the certificates of stock they represented. The evidence further shows, that such certificates would have been issued to the holders whenever the stock was presented to the secretary. It is also shown that these receipts, the evidences of the right to so much stock in the concern, were purchased by appellee for the use of appellant. This question, like the others presented in this record, is without merit."

Ch. § 348 

In Texas, mere delivery without indorsement has been considered as insufficient to pass the legal title.14 This view is supported by Machen. He says: "Apart from express statutory authority, a corporation has no power to create shares which shall be transferable merely by delivery-in other words, to issue certificates certifying the bearer to be the holder of the shares represented thereby. To do so is impliedly prohibited by statutory provisions requiring the company to keep a register of shareholders—a provision which could not be complied with if shares were made transferable by mere delivery of the certificate. To be sure, in America, after a certificate is indorsed in blank, it passes from hand to hand much in the same way as commercial paper payable to bearer; but whilst in this way as between successive holders of the certificate, title to the shares passes by mere delivery, yet the legal title the only title which the company is bound to recognizeremains in the registered holder." 15 

14. Wagner v. Marple, 31 S.W. 691, 10 Tex.Civ.App. 505, writ of error refused. The legal title remained with Marple (the pledgor) and this because of the absence of any transfer by indorsement by him. The mere delivery of the stock as a pledge would not pass the title to the pledgee. It would indeed create a right in the bank as pledgee by virtue of which it could resort to equity if its security was in any way threatened. Davis v. Hardwick, 94 S.W. 359, 43 Tex.Civ.App. 71. It is undisputed that the stock in question had been transferred in blank by appellant so as to constitute it a pledge and, in a very important sense at least, to pass the title under the authorities.

The facts that Hardwick received the stock, causing it to be marked "cancelled" and new stock to be issued in his own name, did not, of themselves, necessarily amount to either a conversion or to the transfer of the absolute title. Such use was entirely consistent with the reciprocal rights of pledgor and pledgee. 

15. 1 Machen, Modern Law of Corpo rations, § 852. See, 6 Thompson, Cor poration, § 4330 (3rd Ed.). The pass ing of the title to stock by a mere delivery of the certificate is governed by the same principles that have been frequently applied to notes, bonds, certificates of deposit, life insurance policies, and ordinary written contracts generally. And on this theory it has been held that a stockholder may transfer to another a complete equitable title to his stock by mere delivery of the certificate without complying with the forms required by the corporation.  § 349. Transfer without the Delivery of the Certificates 

There is a conflict in other states as to whether a transfer is good without the delivery of the certificate.16 Machen says, "In view of the principles which are stated below as to the function in corporate conveyancing of the company's share register, the simplest method of effecting a transfer of shares might be thought to be a mere entry in the books of the company without the execution of any previous transfer.” He further states: "Even if, as in some of the American States, a contract for the sale of shares be deemed to be within the Statute of Frauds, yet an actual transfer on the books of the company even without any writing signed by the transferor would be effective; the 

Statute of Frauds applies only to contracts for sale of personal property and not to transfers completed by delivery, for which an entry in the company's books is in the case of shares of capital stock the only possible substitute or equivalent.” 17 

The Texas cases say that the possession of the certificate is not absolutely necessary to have title to the stock.18 In a cor-

poration the certificate of stock is not the stock itself; it is but a muniment of title, an evidence of the ownership of stock. It is not necessary to a subscriber's complete ownership of the stock. 

He becomes a full stockholder certainly where he has performed his obligation and possesses all of a stockholder's rights, even if no certificate is issued to him at all.19 In Presnall v. Stockyards 

Nat. Bank,20 the court said: "It is generally agreed that shares in an incorporated company are the aliquot parts of the capital stock, and merely give to the owner a right to his share of the profits of the corporation while it is a going concern and to a share of the proceeds of its assets when sold for distribution in case of its dissolution and winding up. The shares do not give their owners any right in the property itself of the company. 

That remains in the artificial body called the corporation. The right of the individual shareholder, according to the amount put into the fund of the corporation, is therefore of an incorporeal nature, though of value, not capable of manual delivery then the nature of a share certificate issued by the corporation * is merely the symbol, or paper evidence, of property, and stands on a similar footing with that of other muniments of title."

§ 351. Uniform Stock Transfer Act 

The Uniform Stock Transfer Act, which has been adopted in a large number of the states but not in Texas, provides in Section 1: "Title to a certificate and to the shares represented thereby can be transferred only, (a) By delivery of the certificate indorsed either in blank or to a specified person by the person appearing by the certificate to be the owner of the shares represented thereby, or (b) By delivery of the certificate and a separate document containing a written assignment of the certificate or a power of attorney to sell, assign, or transfer the same or the shares represented thereby, signed by the person appearing by the certificate to be the owner of the shares represented thereby. Such assignment or power of attorney may be either in blank or to a specified person. *

§ 353. Registration-Status of a Stockholder 

It is important for the transferee to register his shares so that he may claim the status of a stockholder.37 Giving the corporation notice would have the same effect.38 Registration or notice is necessary for the stockholder to receive his dividend or to vote at the meeting of the stockholders. In one case the court said that if the corporation had notice of plaintiff's claim to the dividends and the plaintiff prayed for an injunction to restrain the company from paying the dividend to the person in whose name the stock stood, both the corporation and the person credited with the ownership of the stock would be liable for any dividend thereafter paid unlawfully to the accredited owner.39 Registration is necessary to enable a stockholder to hold office where the statute, the by-laws, or the charter provides that one must be on the books of the corporation. "It is apparent that the rule which holds stockholders disposing of their shares of stock to a strict compliance with the regulations prescribing the method of making transfers is based upon the principle of estoppel. Presumably those who extend credit to a bank do so, partly, at least, upon the solvency and financial standing of its shareholders; and the records of the corporation are expected to furnish a correct list of those shareholders. But the principle of estoppel in pais applies only when the party against whom it is invoked has failed to do that which it was his duty to do in order to prevent a deception. If there has been no culpable neglect or failure on the part of the selling shareholder to do what is legally required of him in order to have the transfer entered of record as required by the by-laws of the corporation, there is no basis for an estoppel." 

In Adams v. Texhoma Oil and Refining Co.,48 a stockholder of a joint-stock association sold his stock, but the transfer was never recorded on the books of the company. 

The court refused to hold the former stockholder liable as a partner on the ground that the statute which requires the stock transfers to be made on the company books is for the benefit of the company or the corporation, as the case may be, rather than for the benefit of innocent purchasers of stock or creditors.

The court in Shaw v. Green,49 held the former shareholder's executor liable on an assessment on the theory that the bank corporation was insolvent within one year from the date on which the transfer of shares was recorded on the bank's books, even though the sale of the bank stock was made by the shareholder before the bank became insolvent.

§ 357. Rules with Respect to Levy, Garnishment and Attachment 

The common law rule that shares of stock cannot be levied on, garnished, or attached 58 has been changed by statute in Texas. Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 3795 provides for levy as follows: "A levy on the stock of any corporation or joint stock company is made by leaving a notice thereof with any officer of such company." 59

Any levy not in compliance with this article is void. Machen says there are two elements of negotiability and that certificates of stock are negotiable in the sense that they cut off equities. Since the element of estoppel is often present, the certificates: of stock are often spoken of as quasi-negotiable. Cook says: "Indeed, to such an extent has the law of estoppel been applied to protect a bona fide purchaser of stock, that, excepting in cases of certificates transferred in blank and lost or stolen without negligence on the part of the owner, a bona fide purchaser is protected now in almost every instance where he would be protected if he were purchasing a promissory note or other negotiable instrument."71

This tendency is due to the fact that it is becoming more and more the custom to deal with the certificates as if they were bills and notes and to transfer them without going through any formalities excepting to endorse and deliver them. The bona fide purchaser takes the shares free from any secret trust. 

For example, in the case of Anderson v. Waco State Bank,72 a wife directed her husband to purchase shares with money belonging to her separate estate. Without her knowledge, he had the certificate issued in his own name, and he assigned it to a bank, which had no notice that it had been purchased with funds of the wife, as collateral for a loan to himself. The court said that since both the real owner and the bank had equal equities and since the bank also had the legal title, it would prevail. which the transferee had no notice." 

He says that they are not negotiable in the sense that the transferee gets a better title than the transferor had.

 § 359. Loss of Title by Estoppel 76 

In the recent case of Phillips v. Citizens' National Bank "" one

Wilson endorsed in blank a certificate for twenty-five shares of the stock of the Shear Company and pledged it to Phillips as security for a loan. Phillips lost the certificate, and the finder returned it to Wilson. Wilson then pledged it to the Citizens' National Bank, which had no notice of Phillips' lien. Upon default by Wilson, the bank foreclosed and bought in the stock at the sale. In a suit by the bank against the corporation to establish its ownership of the certificate, Phillips was interpleaded, and the respective rights of Phillips and the bank were therein adjudicated. On Appeal the Court of Civil Appeals held that the claim of the bank was not subject to the lien of Phillips.78 The court stated that assuming both parties are innocent the loss should fall on Phillips, whose act made the loss possible. Further, based on the jury's finding that Phillips was negligent in losing the certificate, it said that it would only be equitable to put the loss on the party whose negligence made it possible. The Commission of Appeals in the principal case reversed this decision, holding that stock certificates are personal property, that they are not negotiable, but subject to the ordinary rule of caveat emptor in their sale and assignment. The court agreed that negligence of the legal holder of a certificate may give rise to an estoppel, but decided as a matter of law that the mere fact that Phillips lost the certificate was not evidence of negligence.

The authorities are uniformly in accord with the principal case in holding that stock certificates are not negotiable instruments such as bills and notes.79 Stock certificates like ordinary chat-

The courts have been unable to adopt any specific terminology that adequately classifies or describes the legal status of a stock certificate as a commercial instrument. A number of authorities refer to them as "quasi-negotiable."86 It has been said that they possess "a species of negotiability although of a peculiar character," or that while "neither in form nor character negotiable paper they approximate to it as nearly as practicable."88

At first blush it may seem that these rules represent a more liberal application of the doctrine of estoppel than that applied to the transfer of ordinary chattels. Obviously, entrusting possession of a chattel to a pledgee or other bailee confers upon him no "indicia of ownership" or "apparent authority" which is considered sufficient to estop the owner from asserting title. But where possession is accompanied by some affirmative authority from the owner the case is quite different. The distinction is stated thus by a leading authority:99 "But if the owner of an ordinary chattel [italics mine] entrusts to another, not merely the possession of the property, but also written evidence, over his signature, of title thereto, and of an unconditional power of disposition over it, the case is vastly different. There can be no occasion for the delivery of such documents, unless it is intended that they shall be used, either at the pleasure of the depositary, or under contingencies to arise. 

If the condition is not expressed on the face of the instrument, 

the case cannot be distinguished in principle, from that of an agent who receives secret instructions qualifying or restricting an apparently absolute power."

A practical illustration of the import of the above quotation is found in the situation where one purchases a chattel through an agent and knowingly allows the agent to take the bill of sale in his own name and to retain possession of both the chattel and the bill of sale. In such a case a bona fide purchaser for value from the agent would clearly be protected.¹ It seems that allowing an agent to hold possession of a chattel along with such a bill of sale and allowing a bailee or pledgee to hold a certificate indorsed in blank are analogous situations. From its very nature a certificate indorsed in blank purports to invest in the holder "an unconditional power of disposition"; and although the certificate 

99. McNeil v. Tenth National Bank, 46 N.Y. 325, 330, 7 Am. Rep. 341, 343. Arkansas

529, 194 Ark. 1002.

is not the property itself (share of stock), but only a "muniment of title" thereto, it seems that transferring such a certificate indorsed in blank to an agent or bailee might be called intrusting to another "not merely the possession of the property but also written evidence over his own (owner's) signature of title thereto." Viewed from this angle the problem ceases to be one of negotiability or "quasi-negotiability," and becomes purely a question of estoppel.

A limitation has been placed on this doctrine by the Massachusetts Supreme Court in the case of Scollans v. Rollins,³ where it was held that delivery of a sealed envelope containing certificates indorsed in blank to a broker for safe keeping was not such an entrusting of the certificates which would raise an estoppel. 

Justice Holmes suggested that the broker's opening of the envelope and appropriating the certificates was similar to a "carrier's breaking bulk." The court was obviously employing the distinction between "custody" and "legal possession" created by the common law courts in larceny cases. Larceny required that the offender obtain possession with the animus furandi,* and in order to embrace the act of breaking bulk and appropriating goods within the definition of that crime, the courts held that a bailee of articles in bulk had only custody of them and that possession was first acquired upon breaking the container.5 The 

Massachusetts court acting on the strength of some precedent in that state extended this principle to a case of certificates handed over in a sealed envelope; and by so doing materially restricted the free transferability of stock certificates. There is ample authority for the proposition that bailing a sealed envelope should not be treated as a bulk bailment even in larceny cases." of a certificate in a sealed envelope is not an entrusting of possession of the certificate is entirely inconsistent with and repugnant to the underlying principle of estoppel governing these stock transfer cases. Is there any greater "indicia of ownership" conferred where the certificate is unenclosed than where the owner seals it before handing it over? In either case the physical power of disposal is given over a certificate indorsed in blank which in itself imports authority to transfer in the holder. 8

The same court on a previous hearing stated that if possession of the stock certificate enabled the bank (bailee) to make representations of ownership such possession was obtained by commission of a crime against the plaintiff, who, it seems, not being legally required to anticipate a crime, would not be estopped. 

But is it not just as much a crime against the owner for the bank by selling the certificate to appropriate to its own use his certificate handed to it unsealed? The reasoning of the court would be just as applicable to the latter situation. Yet, in such a case as we have seen, the great weight of authority, including the Massachusetts courts, does estop the owner from asserting title as against a bona fide purchaser for value without notice. 

The problem raised by the above decision may be one of great importance. To say the least, it is not unlikely that business men may seal their stock certificates when depositing or pledging them. No other authority has been found directly on the issue. 

It is believed that if the point is ever raised in a Texas court, the problem will be viewed not as one requiring an employment of the nice distinction of common law larceny cases, but rather as one raising principles of estoppel. The trend of the decisions clearly indicate that the courts are steadily adopting a more liberal policy toward the stock certificate as a commercial instrument, and the propriety of such a policy can hardly be questioned in view of the important role played by such instruments in the business world.

Pomeroy lays down the rule that if the stockholder obtains a certificate by forgery and then gets a new certificate issued to him that he would be protected.10 This is not the view in Texas. There is no estoppel created against the corporation where there is forgery.11 Some cases say that where the certificate is indorsed without authority the same principle applies.12 

§ 361. Two Grounds for Estoppel 

There are two grounds utilized by the courts as the basis for estoppel. One is negligence, and the other, which also has been mentioned, is the situation where the owner allows another person to appear to have certain powers of disposing of the shares of stock. The innocent purchaser or pledgee is protected where the owner intrusts the indorsed certificate to another even though the owner is not guilty of negligence. It is usually where the owner entrusts a person with the shares.¹ In Strange v. Houston & T. C. Ry. Co.,¹4 the court said that having thus given to

 § 362. Corporation's Liability-Forged or Unauthorized Transfer 

Where there is no element of estoppel and the corporation recognizes a forged or unauthorized transfer and registers it on the books, the corporation may be sued in conversion for damages,22 by the original owner but not by the party to whom the new certificate was issued. The stockholder may, instead of suing at law for damages, ask for equitable relief to restrain the transfer of shares on the books to those claiming them and to require the issuance of new shares to the plaintiffs.23 The corporation is bound to find out whether the signature of the transferor is genuine,24 the fact that it acted in good faith is no defense. There is a duty on the corporation to see that the original certificate is not outstanding.25 The corporation is not liable to one holding a mere equitable unregistered title unless there have been sufficient circumstances to put it on notice.26

 § 363. Remedy of True Owner against the Transferee 

The true owner also has a remedy against the transferee. He may join him with the corporation, and recover the certificate.27

He may maintain an action for damages against the transferee even after the stock has been sold to another person.28 However, in Texas the owner has no right of action against a bona fide purchaser of a new certificate issued by the corporation,29 but if the corporation has no treasury or unissued stock and sufficient stock cannot be bought to satisfy plaintiff's demands, the innocent purchaser should be forced to surrender his stock to the true owner. In such case the purchaser has a claim against the corporation as is discussed in a subsequent section in this chapter. 

364. The Rights of the Defrauded Transferee 

The transferee who has been defrauded does not have an action against the corporation unless there has been collusion between it and the transferor. The issuing of new stock on the faith of forged or unauthorized transfers creates no estoppel against the corporation.30

§ 366. Agent Guilty of Conversion 

Where a person acts as agent for a person who claims to be the owner of the stock but who does not have title, the agent is guilty of conversion in selling it whether he has notice or not of the lack of his principal's title.37 

§ 367. Fraudulent or Unauthorized Transfers by Trustees 

Another large group of cases involves fraudulent or unauthorized transfers by trustees. Whether a trustee passes good title to the stock to the transferee depends upon the attending circumstances. As a general rule, where the trustee appears upon the books as the absolute owner, the transferee gets good title.38

The defendants invoked the aid of Article 12, § 6 of the Constitution which provides: "No corporation shall issue stock or bonds except for money paid, labor done or property actually received, and all fictitious increase of stock or indebtedness shall be void," and then claimed the unpaid part was fictitious. Article 12, § 6 of the Constitution provides that no corporation shall issue stock except for money paid, labor done, or property actually received. If subscribers to the stock of a corporation cause the books of the corporation to show the stock fully paid up and the stock has not been fully paid for, they are guarantors of the balance due regardless of a transfer. The Commission of Appeals said that there was no evidence of want of good faith on the part of the transferees. It further said that parties dealing with this stock in the hands of the certificate holders had the right, and the creditors dealing with the corporation were authorized, to assume that the transactions between the original subscribers and the corporation were free from any vice and that the contract of organization had been legally and fully carried out. 

Since the subscribers had made affidavit that the stock was fully subscribed and paid and had the stock issued as fully paid and non-assessable and had represented in the sale of the stock that it was fully paid, the purchasers paying full face value therefor, the question of their good faith in the sale of the stock was immaterial on the question of their liability for amounts unpaid on their stock.58 The different theories upon which a stockholder is liable to creditors where the stock is issued at a discount or for

 § 376. Rights of Pledgee 

The pledgee of stock has an absolute right to the pledgor's pro rata share of proceeds resulting from the sale of the assets of the corporation. This right of the pledgee has priority over the claim of the pledgor's surviving widow for a year's allowance and expenses of the last illness of her deceased husband.83 The pledgee of the stock of a corporation has an equity in the assets of the company and can prevent the corporation or its stockholders from the removal of the assets of the corporation out of the place designated as the place where the company will conduct its business in the charter of the company. Therefore, if the officers are attempting to remove the assets to a place other than that described as the company's place of business in its charter the pledgee has a right to object to such removal, and if the defendant promises to pay the debt due the pledgee if the latter will withdraw his objection to the removal of the company's assets the promise is based on consideration and is a primary promise and, therefore, is enforceable even though the promise is not in writing.81

If the pledgor did not indorse the stock certificate in blank, and did not give the pledgee authority to sell it, the purchaser from the pledgee did not get title, especially where the pledgee erased the special indorsement to him and forged the name of the pledgor to the indorsement. And an option given the pledgee in the indorsement on the certificate to purchase two years later other stock of the pledgor did not authorize the pledgee to sell the pledged stock.85

The pledgee can sell the shares pledged to secure a note if the obligation is not paid at maturity, and he can agree with the pledgor to credit dividends allocated to the pledged stock on the obligation.86

Ch. § 411 

 § 411. Who are Promoters-Their Functions 

A "Promoter" is one who brings together the persons who become interested in the enterprise, aids in procuring subscribers, and sets in motion the machinery which leads to the formation of the corporation itself. The term involves the idea of exertion for the purpose of getting up and starting a company, and also the idea of some duty toward the company imposed by or arising from the position which the promoter assumes toward it. "It is a term of business, and not of law, usefully summing up, in a single word, a number of business operations familiar to the commercial world by which the company is brought into existence." 

The term does not necessarily imply that the promoters become members of the corporation, but in a majority of cases they become stockholders of the subsequently formed company and take an active part in determining the financial status of the company at the beginning of its existence. In Old Dominion Copper Mining & Smelting Co. v. Bigelow 2 Justice Rugg said: "The word 'promoter' has no precise and inflexible meaning in this country. 

In England it is defined by statute. St. 7 & 8 Vict. c. 110, § 3. see also St. 30 & 31 Vict. c. 131, § 38. But even there the duties of promoters as fiduciaries to the company are matters of commonlaw cognizance. Erlanger v. New Sombrero Phosphate Co., 3

App.Cas. 1218, 1269. In a comprehensive sense 'promoter' includes those who undertake to form a corporation and to procure for it the rights, instrumentalities and capital by which it is to carry out the purposes set forth in its charter, and to establish it as fully able to do its business. Their work may begin long be-

In this respect he is held to the high standards which bind directors and other persons occupying fiduciary relations." 3 

412. The Prospectus 

Ordinarily one of the promoter's functions is the preparation of a document called a "prospectus," the purpose of which is to acquaint people in general, and more especially prospective investors, with the merits and advantages of the new corporate enterprise. A prospectus has been defined as a "document published by a company or a corporation, or by persons acting as its agents or assignees, setting forth the nature and objects of an issue of shares, debentures, or other securities created by the company or corporation, and inviting the public to subscribe to the issue." It has been held by the House of Lords that the purchaser of shares in the market upon the faith of a prospectus, which was not received from the promoters or those who are answerable for it, cannot by action upon it so connect himself with the promoters as to render the latter liable to him for the misrepresentations contained in the prospectus, as he could have done if it had been addressed to him personally, or if he had bought stock directly from the company in reliance on the statements in the prospectus.5 This case draws a distinction between

Most assuredly no lawyer doubts that the promoter of a company, whether he is a director or not, who knowingly issues or sanctions the circulation of a false prospectus naturally tending to mislead and to induce the public to purchase its stock or other securities, should be responsible to all those who purchase directly from the company in reliance thereon." But if the prospectus contains no false statements the plaintiff cannot recover damages because her stock became worthless on account of the depression rather than her reliance on any statement in the prospectus.

Should any person other than the one that the guilty party intended to influence be permitted to recover? Some courts of 

America have extended the English rule. In Downey v. In Texas innocent misrepresentation is fraud. It is a tort, and, therefore, the injured party may affirm the contract that was induced by innocent misrepresentation and recover the damages that he suffered, or he may rescind the contract by placing both parties in status quo.11

Ch. 413 

 § 413. The Orthodox Rule 12 

Perhaps the leading case discussing the ambit of a fraudulent representor's responsibility is that of Peek v. Gurney.13 The directors of a corporation were being sued for damages resulting to the plaintiff because of reliance on misrepresentations contained in a prospectus. The purpose of the directors in making the misrepresentations was to induce members of the public to purchase stock from the company. Although the plaintiff purchased some stock of the company in reliance on the misstatements, he was not an original allottee, having purchased the stock from an allottee of the corporation. Lord Cairns, relying upon two previous cases, denied the plaintiff a recovery. This holding was based upon the rule that a representor is responsible only to those whom he desired to influence by the misstatement in the manner that occasioned the injury. There are two distinct parts to this rule limiting a defrauder's responsibility: first, there must have been a desire or purpose to influence the action of the particular plaintiff or class of people to which the plaintiff belongs; and second, there must have been a desire or purpose to influence him in the manner that occasioned the damage. Lord 

Cairns gave an illustration of the second part of this rule: 14 "I put the case of a person having built a house and desiring to sell it. He comes to me and wishes me to purchase it; he describes it as a highly advantageous purchase, and makes state ments of the fact to me with regard to the house which are untrue and are misrepresentations; but I decline to purchase and our overtures come to an end. He subsequently sells it to some

Professor Keeton, while a graduate student at the Harvard Law School, spent a great deal of time and research on the Law of Fraud. He has published several excellent articles in the Texas Law Review on that subject. This, and several sections following. with very few changes and additions, were taken from his article in 17 Texas Law 

Review, pages 5-26.

other person, upon what terms I know not. That other person completes the purchase, and that other person desiring to raise money or mortgage applies to me to lend him money. I lend him money upon a mortgage of the house." 

Lord Cairns was of the opinion that the mortgagee should not be permitted a recovery under the facts set out above, because although the representor desired to influence the representee, he desired the latter to purchase the property, not to take a mortgage on it. Moreover, it might be argued that the second part of this rule could be regarded as necessary to deny the plaintiff a recovery under the facts of Peek v. Gurney because the statement was communicated to the general public and was for the purpose of inducing anyone to purchase an allotment of shares. 

It is believed that the results of the cases will disclose that a majority of the courts have reached conclusions inconsistent with the requirement that the representor must have made the statement for the purpose of inducing reliance on the part of the complainant or the class of people to which he belongs. The rule is honored with lip service by most of the courts, but in decisions where the question is of importance, i. e., where the representor would not be liable under the rule, it has been discredited. If, however, such a rule represents the view of most courts, why should liability for fraudulent misrepresentations be so limited when liability for acts intended to produce bodily harm to some one is not so limited? Lord Cairns adopted this rule because he felt that liability should cease somewhere and that a fraudulent representor should not be liable ad infinitum, and he could think of no other way of drawing the line where responsibility should cease. The writer is not willing to maintain that a fraudulent representor should be held for all consequences and to anyone who happens to suffer loss by reliance on his misrepresentation, but it is submitted that the ambit of responsibility should not be limited by the rule that the assertion must have been made for the purpose of inducing action on the part of the one who relies on it. 192

Ch. § 413 

Two reasons have been suggested as a means of justifying a precept which would in some measure limit a fraudulent representor's liability.15 In the first place, it has been said that a fraudulent representor is not even morally accountable to everyone who happens to rely on his misstatement; and in the second place, it is contended that the ordinary affairs of life would become unsafe under a rule holding the representor for all consequences and responsible to everyone. At least two social interests are being considered by these suggestions.16 When it is said that a fraudulent representor is not morally accountable to everyone, the reason is perhaps because society seeks to guarantee to each individual a minimum social existence, and even a person who has committed a wrong is entitled to a chance to live decently. The idea seems to be that although some innocent people will suffer a loss, it is better to let those suffer than to ruin a representor by making him responsible to anyone who might rely on the misstatement. This may be the reason why a different rule prevails as to the causal relation necessary to liability for intentional invasions of interests of personality and property and as to the causal relation necessary to liability for intentional invasions of interest in not being cheated. The amount of damages that the plaintiff can recover is sometimes much greater where the defendant has been guilty of fraudulent representations than it is where he has been guilty of other tortious acts. A letter of recommendation addressed to one person could be used any number of times to an indeterminate number of people.

The social interest underlying the second reason is the social interest in furthering the general social and economic progress.¹7 

For example, to hold accountants responsible to anyone who might rely on a false certification concerning the balance sheet of a corporation might prevent an important social function from being performed by responsible people. This is a much stronger 

15. Cooley, Torts (3d Ed.1906) 94016. Pound, The Theory of Judicial 942. 

Decision, 36 Harv.L.Rev. 940. 

2 HILDEBRAND TEX.CORP.-13 193 

17. 36 Harv.L.Rev. 940.

§ 

Ch. 10

argument to limit a negligent representor's liability than to limit the liability of dishonest people. It has always been difficult for the author to attach much weight to the foregoing reason in the case of a liar. That honest men will be deterred from engaging in certain activities because of the possibility that although they may act honestly, the courts will mistakenly find that they acted dishonestly is not likely. So often, also, to hold a representor responsible to a different person from the one whom he intended to cheat does not increase the amount of damages assessed against him. Where, for example, the misrepresentation is in respect to the condition or value of a chattel, it is indeed difficult to see why the representor should not be liable to any remote purchaser who happens to rely on the misstatement for the economic loss occasioned thereby. The damage is limited and is seldom more than the difference between what he paid for it and what it would have been worth had the representations been true. 

The suggestion is made, however, that some limitation on the class of people who can take advantage of the misrepresentations is desirable even where the damage assessed against the representor cannot be more than a definite amount because of the limits of effective legal action. The further removed a person is from the misstatement, the less the likelihood of reliance thereon, and it may be that justice cannot be administered successfully so as to permit anyone to recover who could prove reliance thereon. There would be only a slight chance, if any, of rebutting the plaintiff's assertion that he acted in reliance on the defendant's statement. (There is, therefore, some justification for not holding a person liable to anyone whom he happens to cheat merely because he intended to cheat some one, even though an actor who intends to injure one person in a certain way is liable to anyone whom he happens to injure in that way.) 

§ 414. Methods of Delimiting Representor's Liability 

Admitting, however, that there should be a limitation somewhere on the fraudulent representor's responsibility, the method suggested by Lord Cairns is not the only way so to limit it. 

There are a number of different possibilities that might be sug- 

2 HILDEBRAND TEX.CORP. 

194

Ch. § 414 

gested and have actually been announced in the cases, usually by way of dictum, but sometimes as the rule applicable to the controversy in question. These different possibilities will be discussed in advance in order to facilitate a discussion of the results reached by the courts: (a) It is often asserted both by courts and commentators that a representor is responsible only to those that he intended should rely on the misstatement complained of.18 This manner of expressing a representor's liability is ambiguous because of the double meaning of the word "intention" as used in this connection. An actor may be regarded as intending a result if he knows that the result will be produced by his conduct, even though he does not desire it.19 And a person will be regarded as having known that the plaintiff would rely on a misstatement, if he believed to a substantial certainty that the plaintiff would rely on it. 

For example, an actor cannot be held liable for false imprisonment unless he intended to imprison someone. But this necessary intention exists under the Restatement of Torts where the act is done either for the purpose of imposing confinement or where the actor knows that confinement will result. Lord Cairns adopted the former meaning in Peek v. Gurney,20 i. e., the representor must have an intention to induce reliance in the sense of a purpose to induce such reliance. It does not follow, however, that because some courts have used the term intention to mean desire or purpose, some of the courts have not used it with the double meaning already suggested. It is therefore suggested

that a representor could be, and has in some cases been held, liable to those he knew would rely upon his misstatement, as well as to those he desired should rely on it. Such a rule would result at least in some extension of a representor's responsibility without making him liable to anyone who happened to be injured in reliance upon his misstatement. Suppose, for example, A makes a false statement in the presence of X and Y for the purpose of inducing X to buy stock in Z Corporation; he knows also that Y will rely on it, although he does not desire Y's reliance. According to the language of Lord Cairns in Peek v. Gurney and the dicta in many cases, X could recover even though A did not think X would be induced to rely on the misrepresentation, whereas Y could not recover even though A was substantially certain Y's reliance would take place. (b) Commentators have asserted quite frequently that a representor is responsible to anyone that it is reasonable to expect would rely on the misrepresentation.21 It is therefore urged that the proper inquiry is, was the representation reasonably calculated to induce reliance on the part of the plaintiff? There seems, however, to be little, if any, authority holding a fraudulent representor responsible solely because he should have foreseen that the plaintiff might rely on his misrepresentation. But there is dictum in some cases to that effect, and it is at least another possibility for measuring the extent of a fraudulent representor's responsibility. 

21. Sugarland Industries v. Parker, Tex.Civ.App., 293 S.W. 609, writ dismissed; Green, Deceit, 16 Va.L.Rev. 

749; Harper, Torts, § 218, where the author states: "The defendant is liable to the particular person whom he intends to defraud and to anyone whom he might reasonably suppose might be harmed by his misstatement." A case which was cited in support of this text is Wheelwright v. Vanderbilt, 138 P. 857, 69 Or. 326.

This case denied a recovery and so is not much authority for the proposition that a representor is responsible to anyone who he could reasonably foresee would reply, even though he did not intend such reliance. Moreover, the statement of the case is to the effect that the representor is liable to anyone whom "he may reasonably be supposed to have intended." That is quite different from saying that the defendant is responsible to anyone he could reasonably suppose would be so affected. See, Foix v. Moeller, Tex.Civ.App., 159 S. 

W. 1048, writ refused. 196

Ch. § 414 

(c) The suggestion has been made that a representor should be responsible to one he believed would rely on his statement, even though when he made the statement, he did not desire such person to rely thereon, nor was he convinced that such a person would rely thereon. There are cases which seem to indicate that such a precept is being applied. (d) It is believed that no one of the three possibilities suggested can explain the results in many of the decisions. It seems that the actual results of the cases can best be explained by the following rules. A fraudulent representor should be responsible to anyone to whom the statement is directly communicated, provided the latter is justified in regarding the statement as addressed to himself: a fraudulent representor should be responsible to anyone who received the statement through a third person, provided the latter had the actual or apparent authority to communicate it. It will at once be noted how these rules differ from that of Lord Cairns in Peek v. Gurney. It is an objective rather than a subjective test. Liability to the plaintiff depends not necessarily upon whether the defendant desired the plaintiff to rely, or knew that the plaintiff would rely, or even believed that the plaintiff would rely, but upon whether the statement, as reasonably construed, should be regarded as addressed to the plaintiff. 

It is conceivable that a representor would desire the person to rely on a statement even when not addressed to him, and if so, the representor should be liable to that person. If the representor authorized the repetition of the statement to the plaintiff, he should be responsible even though he did not know or desire that it would be communicated. The fact that he knew or believed that it would be communicated is not conclusive of responsibility, but if he knew or believed that the representee intended to pass it on to the plaintiff, such knowledge on his part would usually be sufficient evidence of authorization to the representee to publish it. Such a circumstance ought at least to create a presumption which would shift to the representor the burden of going forward with the evidence. Knowledge of the fact that the representee would communicate the misstatement to the plaintiff was regarded by Justice Cardozo in Ultramares Corporation v. 197

§ 

Ch. 10

Touche 22 as an important factor in measuring a fraudulent representor's responsibility. It would seem that such a circumstance is of importance because of an implied authority conferred on the representee to communicate the information to others.23 

The assertion is often made that the misstatement must be made with the intent that it should be communicated, and this form of expression was also used by Justice Cardozo.24 Here, also, the word "intent" is subject to the same double meaning that it has when used in the expression that the representor must intend reliance on the part of the plaintiff. Justice Cardozo evidently meant by intent to communicate the misstatement, either knowledge that it would be communicated or desire to have it communicated.

The rule which is suggested here seems to have been in the minds of two of the judges in Peek v. Gurney. There, Lord 

Chelmsford in his opinion made the following observations: "It appears to me that there must be something to connect the directors making the representation with the party complaining that he has been deceived and injured by it;

There is not much likelihood that people will rely on statements addressed to others, but wherever a misrepresentation is addressed to the plaintiff, there is usually a strong probability of reliance. 

§ 415. Manner of Communicating the Misrepresentation 

In general there are two ways by which a misrepresentation comes to the knowledge of the complainant. The statement may

According to Pollock, a misrepresentation must be made "with the intent that the plaintiff shall act upon it, or in a manner apparently fitted to induce him to act upon it." What 

Pollock means by "apparently fitted to induce him to act upon it" is not clear, but it would seem to the author that if the statement as made by the representor was addressed to the plaintiff, then necessarily it was "apparently fitted" to induce him to act, or if the plaintiff relied upon a statement addressed to him by a third person who had been apparently authorized by the representor to communicate it, then the representor's original assertion was "apparently fitted" to induce the plaintiff to act upon it. 199

be communicated to the plaintiff without the intervention of any third person, or at least without the intervention of a person who is not the representor's agent; or the misstatement of the representor may be communicated to the complainant by a third person for whose conduct and action the representor is not responsible. Any number of cases can be found for the proposition that a misrepresentation need not be communicated to the particular person complaining, so long as the defendant intended that it be communicated to him and that he rely thereon. Moreover, the fact that the representor himself communicated the false statement to the plaintiff is clearly not controlling as to his liability. The manner, therefore, by which the injured person received knowledge of the misrepresentation has never been regarded as a controlling circumstance. For convenience in discussion, however, these two general types of cases will be separately treated. 

§ 416. Communication to Representee Made Directly 

In the first category would fall those cases where a corporation or its officers have issued a prospectus or circular letter containing fraudulent misrepresentations and this prospectus comes to the attention of the injured party by means employed by the representor for that precise purpose; those cases where a misstatement is made to a person in one capacity, and he relies on it in another and different capacity; and those cases where the statement is made in the presence and hearing of the complainant, but with a desire or purpose to influence another who is also present. As an illustration of the last-mentioned group of situations, one case showed that a representor was engaged in selling stock to one Brannon and the misrepresentation involved was made directly to him, but the proof disclosed that it was made in the presence and hearing of the complainant. The latter purchased stock from the representor in reliance on the assertion. 

The court held the representor liable for this injury because "to all intents and purposes the representation was made to the plain- 200

Ch. § 416 

tiff." "28 In this case, as well as in Peek v. Gurney, the statement came to the knowledge of the plaintiff without the intervention of any third person. In neither case was the statement addressed to the plaintiff or class of people to which the plaintiff belonged. 

In neither case was there a purpose on the part of the representor at the time of the statement to induce action on the part of the plaintiff. But there is one very important difference in the cases. In Peek v. Gurney the plaintiff did not negotiate with the defendant, whereas in the above case he did; this very circumstance, it is believed, justifies the court in reaching a different result.

If the representor is responsible only to those whom he desired should be influenced by his misstatement, then even if the fact that the representor knew that the plaintiff was relying on it is sufficient evidence to justify the inference of a desire to induce the latter so to act, the fact of knowledge is certainly not conclusive of such a desire. If, for example, evidence was offered to show that the purpose was to get Brannon to purchase a large block and that the representor permitted the plaintiff to be deceived rather than disclose the truth, would a court be justified in considering the evidence or would it be immaterial? If the evidence is held to be immaterial, then the court is necessarily holding that a purpose to deceive is unnecessary. Should a court hold that the evidence is immaterial, such a ruling would still be consistent with a precept limiting the representor's responsibility to those he intended should rely on his misstatement. Moreover, the holding would also be consistent with the view that a representor is at least responsible to anyone who is justified in regarding the statement as addressed to him. This is true because even though the statement could not be regarded as addressed to the plaintiff when made, if the circumstances are such that the representor knows that the plaintiff is relying on his assertion and the plaintiff realizes that the representor is aware of this reliance, then the plaintiff is justified in treating the statement as ad- 

28. Southern States Fire and Casu alty Ins. v. Cromartie, 61 So. 907, 908, 181 Ala. 295; See also, Alexander v. Beresford, 27 Miss. 747, 61 Am.Dec. 538. 201

§ Ch. 10 

dressed to himself as well as another. The situation is exactly the same as if the representor had repeated the statement to the injured person upon the latter's request. It is a continuing representation. If, however, the original statement by a reasonable construction cannot be regarded as addressed to the plaintiff, then he cannot recover for injury arising out of reliance thereon at a subsequent time in the absence of circumstances which will amount to a tacit or implied in fact misrepresentation addressed to him.

Under the facts of Peek v. Gurney it is possible to argue that the representor knew when he made the statement that some one in the general class to which the plaintiff belonged would rely on it. As previously stated, a person has knowledge that something will happen when he has no substantial doubt but that it will occur. Therefore a rule holding the representor responsible to one that he knew would rely would result in the imposition of a greater liability in some instances than would a rule making the representor liable to all those to whom the statement would be regarded as addressed. Where false statements are contained in a prospectus and these statements can be regarded as addressed to the public for a particular reason only, the courts have quite generally followed Peek v. Gurney where some member of the public has relied on the statement.for another reason.29

The language in these cases is similar to that used by Lord Cairns' in Peek v. Gurney, limiting a representor's liability to those whom he desired to deceive. Where the statement comes to the knowledge of the plaintiff without the intervention of any third person, the apparent purpose of the representor will be controlling on the question as to whether the misstatement was addressed to the plaintiff, and in all of the prospectus cases the apparent purpose and the actual purpose were the same. In no way are these cases inconsistent with a rule which

§ 417. Misrepresentation to One in One Capacity Who Relied upon it in a Different Capacity There are several cases where a misstatement has been made to the representee in one capacity but he relies on it in another and different capacity. Where a statement is addressed to a person as an agent and he relies on it in his individual capacity, the result has always been to deny any recovery to the representee, on the ground that the representor to be liable must have intended the representee to act upon it in a matter affecting himself.30

These cases would be consistent with almost any rule suggested unless it is said that a representor should be liable to anyone he should realize would rely on his misstatement. In none of these cases does it appear that he desired the agent to rely on it personally or even believed that he would, and the transaction which was induced by the misrepresentation was not made between the agent and the representor, but between the agent and some third person. In the case of Wells v. Cook 31 the defendant sold the plaintiff, as agent of his brother, a herd of sheep, representing that the sheep were free from disease. 

The sheep were diseased, and thereafter the plaintiff purchased the sheep and others from his brother. The disease was contagious and was communicated to the rest of the flock. The court refused a recovery on the ground that the statement was not made with the intention of inducing the plaintiff to purchase. 

It is to be noted that in this case the plaintiff suffered a property loss in addition to the economic loss of getting something much less valuable than he expected. The case seems to have made no distinction between physical damage resulting from reliance on a misrepresentation and economic loss resulting there-

Where a person does an act with intention to cause bodily harm or property damage, he is liable to anyone who suffers it. 

In another case the defendant made false representations in the sale of land, and the court held that an undisclosed principal could not recover for these misrepresentations in an action of deceit.32 It seems to be well settled that an undisclosed principal can sue for breach of a warranty; 33 why, therefore, should he not be allowed to sue in an action of deceit where the statement does not amount to a warranty? 418. Communications Made to Representee by Means of Credit 

Agency

The extent of a fraudulent representor's responsibility has been discussed more often in situations where the misstatement was not communicated directly to the injured person, but came to his attention through its repetition by some third person. The original assertion of the fraudulent party cannot be considered as addressed to the injured person unless the third person was authorized either by the representor himself or some rule of law to repeat it to such a person and for such a use. 

Probably the most frequent example of a complainant being allowed a recovery even though the misstatement was not made to him personally, is where he has relied upon a report of a commercial agency, which report was based in whole or in part upon misstatements of the representor.38 Most of these cases involve instances where a subscriber to the agency has either made a 38.

§ 419. Communications Made Indirectly to Representee Which are Required by Law

There is a large number of cases dealing with misrepresentations made by officials of a corporation concerning its financial condition to some department of the state or federal government in reports which are required by law. The object of requiring such information is usually set out in the statute, and if not, it is generally apparent. The knowledge of the representor as to the purpose for which the information is desired, is an important fact to consider if the ambit of the representor's responsibility extends only to those he intends should rely on the misstatement. 

Occasionally, the fact that the representor knew or must have known the object of the desired information has been emphasized in the judicial opinions. The defrauder's knowledge, however, of the object of the law does not determine conclusively his purpose. There is a substantial difference between these cases where the representor must furnish this information to the state or suffer penalty and those cases where the representor misrepresents his information to commercial or credit agencies. Where the information is required to be furnished, the declarant's only object may be to induce the government officials to act in reliance thereon in order to prevent the imposition of a penalty imposed by statute, or for the purpose of inducing the agent of the state to approve the charter of the corporation.
