In Texas, before the Secretary of State is authorized to approve the charter of the proposed corporation, the full amount of its authorized capital stock must be subscribed and fifty per cent thereof paid in cash or its equivalent in property or labor. 

An affidavit of those who execute the charter is furnished to the Secretary of State showing who subscribed for the stock of the corporation and how much was paid by each subscriber.50 If the charter is approved, it is filed in the office of the Secretary of State and is open to inspection by the public.51 For this reason the Secretary of State is authorized by law to show the charter to any interested party. Those who execute the charter are charged with notice of the law. Suppose that in the affidavit it is stated that fifty per cent of the capital was paid for in money and property worth the par value of the stock and that this statement is false. If the text discussed in the foregoing paragraphs is correct, any creditor or stockholder of the company who was deceived by the affidavit should be permitted to recover the damage that he suffered by reason of the falsity of the affidavit. 

The courts have said that in the above situation the company has no cause of action for the falsehood; therefore, the receiver of the company or the trustee in bankruptcy would have no cause of action, and he must sue in the right of the corporation. However, each individual creditor or purchaser of the stock of the company who knew of and relied on the false statement has a personal claim against those who made the false representation to recover their damages. The general rule is that a third 52

The action is misconceived, and there can be no recovery in this case though the fraud was admitted on the record in the terms in which it is charged.

Justice Gould, in allowing the plaintiff to recover, makes a distinction between a public and a private misrepresentation. § 420. Issuance of Invalid Stock by Corporation 

There are a number of cases in deceit arising out of an issue of what purports to be genuine stock but which is in fact invalid. 

The usual case involved a fraudulent overissue.58 This fraudulent overissue has been made for the purpose of raising money and for the purpose therefore of inducing the purchase of stock from the corporation. theory, but is the corporation or its officers liable in deceit to subsequent bona fide purchasers of the stock as well? One of the early cases on this question was Shotwell v. Although the representor did not desire anyone except original purchasers to rely on his statement, he knew that whenever stock of the company was sold, a certificate would be delivered to the purchaser as evidence of title. If in a case of this kind he does not know that others will rely, he at least believes that such reliance will occur. 

Moreover, the representation that the stock is genuine is clearly addressed to any subsequent purchaser thereof. Subsequent cases have adopted the same result, a result which is inconsistent with the rule of Lord Cairns in Peek v. Gurney.60 61 In a case similar to those just mentioned, an officer of a corporation issued unpaid certificates of stock to X for the purpose of permitting X to obtain a loan from a certain person, not the plaintiff. The certificate was used to obtain a loan from the plaintiff, and the plaintiff was allowed a recovery. The question involved in this case is similar to the one presented where a person accepts a bill of exchange drawn on his principal without authority to do so, or where the courts have permitted a remote indorser, who has purchased in reliance on the acceptance, an action for damages against the representor.62 In the absence of evidence showing a contrary purpose, the object of the acceptor is to induce anyone dealing with the payee to rely on the acceptance so that the payee can realize his money. Of course, the acceptor may know that others will rely on it in subsequent transactions, or if he does not know others will rely, he at least knows that there is a likelihood of reliance by others, but this is not sufficient to show that such was his purpose. A statement made in an article of commerce, a muniment of title, a negotiable instrument or similar document-one of the exceptions-is addressed to all persons who may in the ordinary course of business have occasion to deal in a business transaction with such articles. 

As to statements required by law-the other exception-the purpose of the legislature is important rather than the actual or apparent purpose of the representor, because the representee is justified in treating the statement as addressed to himself, irrespective of the attitude of the representor. The frequent reiteration of the so-called general rule announced in Peek v. Gurney cannot but cause uncertainty, because it is a deformity in the law of deceit.

The Securities Act was passed by the Texas Legislature in 1935.65 It provides that certain persons, corporations and other associations must obtain permission from the Secretary of State before they attempt to sell their stocks, bonds, and other securities.66 It also provides that dealers and salesmen or agents of dealers must register with the Secretary of State before they can legally sell securities that come within the provisions of the Securities Act. The statute also empowers the attorney general to enjoin the sale of stocks or bonds by corporations, joint stock companies or other persons, if the issuer is about to employ any device, scheme or artifice to defraud or to obtain money or property by means of any false pretense.67 A company that wishes to issue securities must furnish the Secretary of State with a copy of any prospectus or advertisement or other defered because of reliance on the representation in a transaction for guidance in which the report is required to be made available."

The issuer must also set forth. in detail its plan of organization and must show the cost and actual value of property that it proposes to receive in payment for its stocks or bonds. The Act also makes it a crime for any dealer, agent or salesman, principal officer or employee to sell or offer for sale or solicit subscriptions to stock of the issuer without being registered as provided in the Act. If the issuer wishes to sell its own securities, it becomes a dealer and must comply with the provisions of the statute applying to dealers.68.

It also makes it criminal for any of the above parties to make any false statement of fact in any advertisement, prospectus, letters, telegrams, etc., which contain an offer to sell any of the securities of the issuer. It also makes it criminal to employ any fraudulent practice in the sale of any securities."⁹ In other words, the Securities Act attempts to prevent fraud in the sale of any securities in Texas by local or by foreign corporations or joint stock companies; but it does not attempt to determine the rights of the injured party, if he is defrauded in the purchase of the securities. There are so many exceptions to the statute set forth in Section 3 of the Securities Act and so many exemptions of the securities that come within the provisions of the statute as shown by Section 23 of the Act, that the common law rules discussed in the foregoing sections still apply to most companies organized in Texas.70

The Texas Securities Act is undoubtedly constitutional. The courts have many times declared that the regulation of the sale

For instance, in Section 24 it is provided that if the dealer, agent or salesman wishes to appeal from the decision of the Secretary of State in refusing to approve for sale his securities, he may proceed to affect an appeal to the courts in a manner provided in this Act for similar appeals. In neither case is the issuer or the dealer asking that he be permitted "to register" as an authorized dealer. That seems to be the only remedy specifically provided for by Section 28 of the statute.

By Section 7 of the Securities Act, Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 

600a, § 7, it is provided that, "The total expenses, including organization expenses and all commissions paid to salesmen of any proposed company, as herein defined, shall not exceed twenty (20) per cent of the total amount of capital sought to be employed in such proposed company."

By Article 12, Section 6 of the Texas Constitution it is pro vided: "No corporation shall issue stock or bonds except for money paid, labor done or property actually received, and all fictitious increase of stock or indebtedness shall be void.” In the case of Weatherford Ry. Co. v. Granger," the Supreme Court of Texas held that under the above constitutional provision the promoter is not entitled to any compensation for labor performed before the company was chartered unless "the statute which authorizes the corporation provides that the corporation, when formed, shall pay the necessary expense of promoting the scheme." In other words according to the Granger case, while it is true the stock may be issued for labor done, the labor must be performed for the corporation after its charter has been approved by the Secretary of State. In the above case the Texas

Supreme Court stated that an attorney is not entitled to any compensation even for preparing the charter of the company. 

The constitutional provision means that the labor must be performed for the corporation. As a general rule, if the promoters of a company do not have sufficient confidence in its success to bear the attorney's fee for the preparation of its charter and the necessary expense in obtaining subscriptions to its stock and other necessary expenses of incorporating the company, they should not form the company.

Under constitutional provisions identical with the Texas Constitution the courts of some of the American states have held that the "labor" must be performed "for the corporation." One of the leading cases on the question is Kirkup v. Anaconda

Amusement Company.76 In that case the court held that a contract by the promoters to pay the plaintiff a ten per cent commission, or that per cent of the stock for selling the stock of the company before the charter was obtained, is unenforceable." 

The capital of the corporation should not be impaired by preincorporation expenses before its business career has begun. If the Texas Supreme Court extends the holding of the Granger case to its logical conclusion, the Court will affirm the holding reached by the Montana Court in the Kirkup case, and, therefore, it will hold that no stock can be "issued for labor" unless the "labor" is performed for the corporation. If that is the meaning of Article 12, Section 6 of the Texas Constitution, the above quotation from the Securities Act, which authorizes the taking of twenty per cent of the stock of the company for pre-incorporation expenses, is unconstitutional. The general incorporation statutes of Texas form a part of the charter of corporations organized under those statutes. In the Granger case in a dictum the court said that the corporation would be liable for pre-incorporation expenses if the statute which authorizes the incorporation provides, "that the corporation, when formed, shall pay the necessary expenses of promoting the scheme." The only case cited in the Granger case in support of the above statement is an English case. In England there is no written constitution whose mandates are superior to the acts of Parliament. For this reason the English decision should have no weight with the American courts.78 If this dictum is followed and if twenty per

 § 421. The Texas Securities Act-Constitutionality 

In the recent case of Kadane v. Clark,80 the Texas Supreme 

Court held that the Texas Securities Act is constitutional. In upholding the act, the court followed, by comity, the opinions of the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals, which had previously upheld the act in two cases.8 81 Kadane v. Clark is the first case under the new Securities Act to come before the Texas Supreme Court.82 In this case plaintiff was a geologist suing for a commission for procuring a purchaser for certain oil and gas leasehold interests, but he had not registered under the Texas Securities Act. The court held that an oil and gas lease is a security within the meaning of the Securities Act, and that a contract for a commission made by one who had not registered as a dealer in violation of the Securities Act is unenforceable. The two cases in which the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals upheld the 

Securities Act, Atwood v. State 83 and Muse v. State are both similar to Kadane v. Clark in that the defendant in each case was dealing in oil and gas leasehold interests, and in each case the conviction of the defendant under the Securities Act was affirmed. A case by one of the courts of civil appeals in 1938 also upheld the constitutionality of the Securities Act, holding that a contract made in violation of the act is unenforceable.85 Several

91. In the Texas Securities Act, Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 600a, the broad definition of "security" in section 2 includes any "certificate or instrument representing any interest in or under an oil, gas, or mining lease, fee, or title." This provision is not usually found in security acts. 

In Fowler v. Hults, Tex.Com.App., 161 S.W.2d 478, 482, the Commission of Appeals held that one employed to obtain oil leases from land owners are not "dealers" within the meaning of the original Securities Act.

Whether they are under the amendments by the Forty-seventh legislature was not decided. Acts of Reg. 

Sess. 47th Leg. (1941) ch. 363, p. 593. 

In this opinion the court said: “All the provisions of the Act above quoted and referred to relate to sales and sellers of securities and not to purchasers or buyers. Nowhere in the

Act is there any language which might be construed as disclosing an intention to require purchasers of securities to register or to prohibit one from buying securities without registering, unless it is the words 'or dealing in any other manner in any security or securities' in the definition of the term 'dealer' in subdivision (c) of section 2, and substantially the same phrase in section 30 above quoted. "A dealer is defined as a person 'who engages in this State 

in selling, offering for sale or delivery or soliciting subscriptions to, or orders for, or undertaking to dispose of, or to invite offers for, or dealing in any other manner in any security or securities within this State.' The phrase 'or dealing in any other manner' is one of general words following particular and specific words all of which relate to selling or undertaking to sell, and under the rule of ejusdem generis must be held to include only acts or activities of the same kind as those specifically enumerated, there being no clear manifestation in the 

Act of a contrary purpose. Farmers' & Mechanics' Nat'l Bank v. Hanks, 104 Tex. 320, 324–327, 137 S.W. 1120, Ann.Cas.1914B, 368; Thomas v. State, 129 Tex.Crim. R. 628, 91 S.W.2d 716.

Had the Legislature intended to require buyers of securities to register, its intention would, or certainly in a penal Act should, have been manifested more clearly than by the use of the word 'dealing' following particular and specific words all relating to selling. "If the plaintiff in error Fowler as a condition precedent to the performance of the services for which he was employed by defendant in error Hults, procuring the execution of the oil and gas leases by the land owners, were required to register as a dealer under the Securities Act, then any person employed by an oil company, or other prospective lessee, to obtain or assist in obtaining oil and gas leases from land owners would be required to register as a dealer in securities before entering upon the performance of his duties. There is in our opinion no language in the Act to justify that construction of it and that construction is not necessary to the accomplishment of the declared and obvious purpose of the statute."

 Article 12, § 6, of the Texas Constitution provides: 

"No corporation shall issue stock or bonds except for money paid, labor done, or property actually received, and all fictitious increase of stock or indebtedness shall be void."

It has been suggested in the Texas Law Review that by reason of the above constitutional provision, the above quoted part of Sec. 7 is unconstitutional, because under identical prohibitory provisions New York and Delaware held illegal the issuance of stock for promotion services, and because the Texas case of Weatherford, M. W. & N. W. Ry. v. Granger ⁹7 held that no implied promise could be imputed to a corporation to pay for services of a promoter or corporator rendered before the corporation came into existence; and, the writer in the Law Review said, therefore an express promise to pay for such services would be without consideration in absence of a novation, and would ordinarily be ultra vires if there was a novation.9 98 Whether stock can be issued for pre-incorporation labor has not been definitely decided by the Texas Supreme Court. It would seem that this statute does not contemplate the issuance of stock to a promoter merely because he is the main promoter who decided to organize a corporation to carry on some business. Also, as a matter of policy, it would seem that stock should not be issued to a promoter for merely going about and getting subscriptions. If the promoter has a new idea, he may get it copyrighted or patented and transfer such rights to the corporation in payment for stock. But he should not be issued stock for his services in getting subscriptions, for if he has any faith in the corporation he is forming, he should be willing to contribute any such services in order to get the corporation, which he is sponsoring, organized. Therefore it would seem that if this statute is held to be constitutional, stock could be given in payment of such services as legal services, auditing and accounting services, and so forth, but could not be issued for conceiving the idea of organizing a corporation nor for obtaining subscriptions to the stock of the corporation. Where there are several promoters, all are liable in damages for the fraud of an agent employed by them to effect the sale of the corporate securities. The prospectus must be couched in clear phraseology and free from misleading or tricky phrases.  423. Theories of Corporate Liability 

Several theories have been advanced in different states to fix the liability of corporations on the contracts made by their promoters. Ratification, adoption, continuing offer accepted, and novation have all been considered. Strict ratification is impossible as it presupposes the existence of a principal at the time the contract is made.17 Texas courts have approved the idea of adoption. The prior execution of the contract by the opposite party is held to be sufficient consideration for the subsequent adoption.18 Though the courts recognize that this is the proper basis for corporate liability, all real distinction between it and most of the other theories has been torn down and there remains only a hairline of difference in reasoning. Courts which generally follow adoption or ratification, will, when proper facts present themselves, say that there has been a novation. If the courts determine that the facts present a case of novation, the result will be different in many cases from those where an attempt is made to base conclusion on adoption or ratification. In the case of novation, assent of the third party is required, and the promoter is released from liability.19

Adoption cannot have the effect of relating back to the time the contract was made, as does ratification of the unauthorized acts of an agent. At that time there was no corporation, hence no principal.20 In this respect adoption resembles novation.

§ 425. Continuing Offer 

The courts that hold the corporation liable on the ground of "adoption" should look upon the contract between the promoter and the third party as a continuing offer to the corporation. 

Some courts do consider the contract between the promoters and the third party as a continuing offer to the corporation. In Kirkup v. Anaconda Amusement Co.27 the court said: "The adoption of such a contract is on the theory that the contract made by the promoters is a continuing offer on the part of the other party to the contract unless withdrawn by him, and that it may be accepted and adopted by the corporation after it is created." This sufficiently overcomes the somewhat unusual result of allowing a hitherto third party to step in and by its own affirmative act become liable on and benefit from a contract which had already been made.28 The phrase "continuing offer" imparts the idea that after organization, the corporation will have power either to accept or reject the offer. For this reason a promise cannot be made to the corporation until it is organized. The courts, however, are more interested in meeting out justice to the parties than following the conclusion to which a slavish adherence to the rules of contract law would lead them.31 

§ 426. Meaning of Taking the Benefits with Their Burdens 

It is conceded that by accepting the benefits of a contract made by its promoters, the corporation adopts not only the beneficial, but also the burdensome part of the contract. It takes the contract cum onere. The question arises whether by so accepting the benefits, the corporation also adopts incidental promises connected with the main contracts. For instance, a fee agreed to by the promoter to be paid an attorney for drawing a contract which the corporation has adopted. In Weatherford, M. W. & N. 

W. Ry. Co. v. Granger 32 the plaintiff, an attorney, sued for professional services rendered in preparing a bonus contract whereby the corporation was to build a railroad between certain points and carry coal at fixed rates. In return the corporation was to

The court held that by accepting the bonus the company became bound to carry coal at the stipulated rate, but that merely accepting the benefits of this contract which the plaintiff drew up did not bind it to pay for such legal services. The court says: "Now, when it is said that when a corporation accepts the benefits of a contract made by its promoters, it takes it cum onere, it is important to understand distinctly what is meant. 

There is, so far as this matter is concerned, a radical difference between a promise made on behalf of the future corporation in the contract itself, the benefits of which the corporation has accepted, and the promise in a previous contract to pay for services in procuring the latter to be made. This is well illustrated by the facts of the present case. Here a proposition was made on behalf of the company, by its promoters, that if a bonus should be subscribed and paid to it, it would build its road between certain points, and would carry coal at a certain stipulated rate. By accepting the bonus, the company became bound to fulfill the stipulation of that contract. That was the burden which it took with the benefit of the agreement. But it also appears that one of the promoters promised the plaintiff, that if he would assist in procuring subscribers to the bonus, the company would pay him for his services. This was no part of the contract the benefits of which were taken by the defendant. "The benefits of the contract are the advantages which result to either party from a performance by the other; and in like manner its burdens are such as its terms impose. A more accurate manner of stating the nature of the plaintiff's demand is to say, that the defendant has accepted the benefit of plaintiff's services and should pay for them. It is true, in one sense, that the company has had the benefit of the plaintiff's services, and it is equally true that it would have had that benefit if the serv- 243

§ Ch. 10 

ices had been rendered under an employment by the subscribers to the bonus; and yet in the latter case it could not be claimed the company would be liable for such services, unless payment for them by the company were made one of the terms of the contract between the company and the subscribers."

Ballantine in his work on corporations 33 criticizes the case. 

He says: "It is a serious question whether the distinction drawn by the court is sound, that the company did not take the benefit of the prior contract between the promoter and plaintiff by accepting and taking the benefit of the subscription contracts procured by the plaintiff. It is said that one may sometimes get the benefit of the work done by another without being liable to pay for it; but query whether this is true where you have notice of his expectation to be compensated by you when you accept the benefit." 34 

§ 427. Liability of Promoters on Contracts Made by Them 

The promoter may, by the form of the contract which he uses in contracting for the corporation, keep himself in any status which he chooses and to which the third party will agree. Special provisions exempting him from or fixing the nature of his liability on such contracts will be upheld by the courts.35 The parties may attach any condition to the liability of the promoter. 

Whether this is done or not is a question of fact. Under this theory the promoter may obtain offers from third parties to be accepted when the corporation is formed, and it may be agreed that he will be liable only until the corporation adopts the contract;36 or, having made a contract binding on himself, he may

suggests that practically all contracts with promoters may be construed as anticipating a novation, and so when adopted by the corporation, the promoter is thereby released.42 This idea is well expressed by him in Sec. 306 of his text on Contracts. In that section, he says: "Contracts are frequently made by promoters on behalf of corporations which it is expected will be organized. Often under the terms of these contracts if the corporation were already in existence, the contract would be that of the corporation and not of the promoter. But as it is impossible for the corporation to contract before it comes into existence, the contract is treated as that of the promoter even though the language of the contract is appropriate for a contract by the corporation. Not only is it impossible for the corporation to become liable before it comes into existence, but its mere incorporation will not of itself charge it with liability for contracts which prior thereto promoters purported to make in its behalf. The corporation, however, may enter into contracts based on agreements previously made; thus subscriptions to stock in a corporation thereafter to be formed, amount to offers to the corporation which subsequently may be accepted by it; though, until acceptance, the subscriber may withdraw. The principle governing other contracts intended to be made on behalf of the future corporation is the same. Though it can not when formed ratify the action of the promoter since it is an essential of ratification that the principal should have been in existence and capable of contracting at the same time the agent acted, the corporation either by formal action, or without such action if the contract is of a sort which requires no formality, may become bound as a party to the contract by adoption or novation. 

42. Williston, Contracts, § 306, p. 580.

"The cases generally speak of the obligation of the corporation as created by adoption, but novation seems the more accurate term. If the assent of the corporation to the bargain is merely an adoption of it, the promoter apparently must still remain liable. But it seems more nearly to correspond with the intentions of the parties to suppose that when the corporation assents to the contract, it assents to take the place of the promoter-a change of parties to which the other side of the contract assented in ad- There would then be a novation which would discharge the promoter at the same time the corporation assumed the obligation."

This way of solving the problem involved in these cases was partly followed in a recent Texas case.43 In that case, when

Weeks borrowed the money from the Bank, there was an express agreement that the bank would look only to the unborn corporation for the satisfaction of the obligation and not to Weeks personally. After the Company was incorporated, it "adopted" the contract, and the bank recognized the corporation as the debtor. In the opinion Judge McClendon, after quoting the above paragraph from Williston on Contracts, said: "We do not believe that what transpired subsequently to the incorporation was sufficient in itself, and independently of the alleged non liability agreement, to relieve Weeks of liability, if otherwise he would be held bound". In other words, Judge McClendon said that in a case where the bank knows that the promoter is borrowing for the unborn corporation, and the money is turned over to the corporation which uses it in its business, and after being incorporated it agrees to pay the obligation and does pay interest on the debt for several months and the bank considers the corporation the sole debtor until after the corporation becomes insolvent, the promoter is not released on the ground of novation unless there was an agreement when the obligation was created to look only to the corporation for the payment of the debt after it adopted the agreement. Surely without this specific agreement, the 

43. Weeks V. San Angelo Nat'l 

Bank, Tex.Civ.App., 65 S.W.2d 348. 247

§ 

Ch. 10

facts are sufficient to show a novation, and that should be the holding of the Texas court the next time the point is squarely presented to the court.44 In a true novation the release of the promoter is the consideration for the assumption of liability by the corporation.

Of course, if the facts show specifically that credit was given to the promoters and not to the unborn corporation, there is no basis for an implied novation. In such case the promoters would be liable in the absence of an express novation.45 The doctrine of an implied novation seems to be the more reasonable way of looking at the matter, and this view is gaining ground. It does not disappoint the reasonable expectation of business men, and, therefore, should be adopted by the courts. This theory was the real basis for the holding in Schwedtman v. Burns.40

It should not be substituted for consideration except in charitable gift cases. If it is substituted for consideration in the case of offers, many offers will become irrevocablethough the circumstances of the offeror have changed even though. 250

Ch. § 428 

A corporation is a collection of human beings to whom permission has been given to carry on a business as a legal unit without personal liability unless a statute of the state where the corporation was organized imposes some individual liability upon the stockholders. A corporation is no more a fiction than a partnership, a joint-stock company, or a Massachusetts trust. If the courts would realize this fact and quit trying to fit every problem of corporate law into the pattern of contracts, agency, and trusts, a large part of the reasons given for the existing rules of corporate law would soon disappear. Up to this time, the courts and text writers devote a large part of their discussion of corporate problems in an effort to show that their conclusions are consistent with the rules of law established in fields not very similar to the corporate organization. If they would realize that corporate problems are sui generis and should be decided on their own merits without laboring so earnestly to prove that their rules harmonize with the well settled rules of other fields of the law, their task would be very much simplified. For instance, if the promoters in selling stock before the company is organized perpetrated a fraud on the plaintiff, would the defrauded party have a right to rescind the contract for the reason stated in some of the opinions that "the promoters are the agents of the unborn corporation"? 54 The promoters associate themselves together for the purpose of forming the corporation. They agree to act jointly in doing what is reasonably necessary to bring about the formation of the corporation, or they delegate authority to one or more of their members to accomplish that purpose. They usually remain in control of the corporation for some time after when the offeror attempts to revoke the offer he does not know the offeree acted to his detriment.

Surely no court will change or lessen the liability or punishment of a guilty defendant merely because he changes the garb, subsequent to the wrongful conduct, in which he paraded when the wrong was accomplished. 

Again, if the courts would always discard fiction and say that a corporation is a collection of real persons, they would not hesitate to hold that the promoters have formed an organization to bring about the formation of the corporation; that the promoters, therefore, have authority to do what is reasonably necessary to accomplish that purpose. The promoters who are appointed to represent the promoter group would have authority to employ a lawyer to prepare a prospectus, the charter of the company and other instruments necessary to perfect the formation of the corporation; to solicit subscriptions of stock, and to perform all other things necessary to bring the corporation into being. If they spend part of the funds collected and abandon the enterprise before the corporation is formed, each promoter must bear his part of the legitimate expenses incurred.56 After the corporation is formed, the same human beings, as a general rule, still own the business and are conducting it under a different form. of organization. § 429. Obligation of Promoters to Corporation and Shareholders 

The promoters of a corporation stand in a fiduciary relation to the stockholders and to the company.62 This relation is partly an outgrowth of the power over the corporation which the promoters exercise. The relationship is comparable to that of trustee and cestui que trust, and principal and agent; yet it is different from both and not quite so strict as either.63 All courts hold that the promoters of a partnership stand in a fiduciary relation to each other from the time they begin to talk about the formation of the partnership. "In their dealings with each other, partners occupy positions of trust, and are required to exercise the most scrupulous good faith towards each other. Nor is this requirement confined to persons who are actually copartners, but it extends to those negotiating for a partnership not yet formed." 64 "In the purchase of the property for the partnership or association each one of the partners or associates is precluded from making any secret separate profit out of the transaction, and when one of them does make such a secret profit, it consti-

Surely the form of the business organization should be of no consequence. 

If there is a fiduciary relationship in the one case, the courts should hold that there is the same relationship in the case of the promoters of the corporation.

431.

When a Profit is Allowed the Promoters 

The prohibition against secret profits by the promoter only applies when at the time of the transaction he is trying to act in a dual capacity, as an individual and as the promoter of a corporation. He is in no way restricted from purchasing property, even for the sole purpose of selling to the company, and then after the company is fully organized and he no longer has any control over it, making any deal he can with an independent board of directors." But if the promoter still has any control over the corporation and purchases with the intent of selling to it, he is under a duty to make a full disclosure of all facts to an independent board of directors, or if he fails to do so, he must account for the profit which he gains from the transaction.75 

A distinction has been drawn between property purchased for the purpose of sale to the corporation and property owned by the promoter before he had any idea of forming a corporation. It is said in the former case that the promoter is under a duty to make a full disclosure as seen by the preceding paragraphs. In 

Densmore Oil Co. v. Densmore 76 it was held that where the promoters owned oil lands a long time before they decided to form a corporation, there was no duty on the part of these owners to disclose what they paid for the property. "They certainly stood in no confidential relation to the subscribers or purchasers of the stock in the future, when they acquired the property. A com-

§ 432. Assent of All Stockholders 

It is a disputed question as to whether there exists on the part of the corporation a right to sue the promoters for fraud in cases where the promoters own at that time all the issued stock of the corporation and sell the property to the corporation at an excessive price, intending as a part of their plan to issue further stock to subscribers who know nothing of the fraud. Although there is fraud on the individual subscriber, is there any reason or basis for a corporate right of action?

The English court in In re Seamless Paper Box Co." held that if there was no intention on the part of the promoters to bring in future subscribers, the corporation could not maintain an action when the stockholders were brought in at a later period. The 

United States Supreme Court, in the case of Old Dominion Copper Mining & Smelting Co. v. Lewisohn,78 has held that, despite the fraudulent intent, there was no corporate right to recover, even though part of the original scheme was to sell some of the stock to the public. The Massachusetts court on the same state of facts reached an opposite holding, allowing the corporation to recover.79

Ch. § 433 

In dealing with the fraud of promoters and the right of the corporation to sue, the cases have been subdivided into four groups. Each will be discussed separately. 

§ 433. The Effect of Promoters' Fraud Where Some of Stock holders do not Know of Fraud

The first type of case is where the promoters at the time of the sale to the corporation do not make disclosure to the other existing shareholders in the enterprise. It seems to be well settled that in such a case the corporation may sue and recover the secret profits.80

In the case of Davis v. Las Ovas Company 81 the promoters had secured an option on certain real estate at a price of $20,000. 

The corporation was organized and the promoters elected themselves directors of the company. Without disclosing the real purchase price to some of the subscribers, the company purchased the land for $35,000. The court allowed the corporation to sue and recover the $15,000 profit. The court distinguished this case from their previous decision in the Lewisohn Case on the ground that there were innocent shareholders when the sale was made to the company who had not acquiesced in the fraud. 

A case analogous to the Davis case arose in the state of Alabama. One Riles had an option on certain timber lands. He organized a corporation and conveyed the property to the corporation for stock valued at twice the price he paid for the property. 

The supreme court of Alabama held that the corporation could maintain an action against the promoter there being innocent

& Smelting Co. v. Bigelow,85 and Old Dominion Copper Mining and Smelting Co. v. Lewisohn.86 Both of these decisions involve the same state of facts. "The facts were that Bigelow and Lewisohn owned certain mining property for which they had paid $1,000,000. They proceeded to organize the corporation and with its control in their hands they turned over the mining properties for 13/15 of the stock, having a par value of $25.00 per share and a market value of $3,250,000. The profit was divided between Bigelow and Lewisohn. It was a part of their scheme to sell 20,000 shares having a par value of $500,000 by subscription to the public without disclosing the profit they had taken for themselves."

The question is, can the corporation sue and recover for these secret profits after the corporation stockholders at the time of sale ratified and assented to the transaction? Was there a wrong to the corporation? The Supreme Court of the United States, speaking through Mr. Justice Holmes, held there was no right of recovery because the stockholders of the corporation, who were the promoters, had assented to the transaction with full knowledge of the profits. He also stated "the plaintiff cannot recover without departing from the fundamental conception embodied in the law that created it; the conception that a corporation remains unchanged and unaffected in its identity by changes in its members." He was of the opinion that the wrong is not to the corporation but to the individual members.

The rule of the Lewisohn Case has been confined for the most part to the Federal Courts, and not many of the states have followed this holding. Some of the cases in the states which have adhered to this rule will now be considered.

The above case cannot be said to be a direct affirmance of the Lewisohn case as the court failed to show in its opinion whether the stock was transferred by the corporation, or was stock sold by the promoter which he had received from the corporation. 

As we shall see later, the courts do make a distinction between a case where part of the original stock is sold to the public and a case where the promoters take all the stock of the company and sell some of their own stock to innocent purchasers. 

The opposite line of decisions is headed by the case of Old Dominion Copper Mining & Smelting Co. v. Bigelow. "In that case suit was begun against Bigelow in Massachusetts as one of two joint wrongdoers, and he was held liable for secret profits amounting to over $2,000,000. The organization was controlled wholly by Bigelow and Lewisohn, and through themselves and their agents without providing the plaintiff corporation with an independent board of officers, they as the responsible and only managers of the plaintiff, acting in its name contracted with themselves as mine owners to sell to it the real estate of the Baltimore Company for $2,500,000 of the capital stock of the plaintiff at the par value without disclosing that they sold property costing them only $1,000,000 for three and a quarter times its cost.' The court held, contrary to the Federal ruling, that the corporation could maintain a suit since the fraud on the subsequent subscribers who purchased stock from the corporation as a part of the promotion scheme was to be regarded as an injury to the cor- 

265

§ 

Ch. 10

poration itself, representing their collective corporate interest. 

This recovery was allowed despite the nominal corporate assent. 

A California case goes further and holds that the fiduciary obligation of a promoter is owed as well to future stockholders who are to contribute the real capital, as to those making up the corporation at the time it takes over the property from the promoter. In that case, however, the defrauded parties were concerned in the enterprise throughout, and even though all the stock was originally issued to the promoter who made false representations to the innocent purchasers, it was intended from the beginning that some of this stock would be issued to innocent purchasers.90 In Pietsch v. Milbrath,91 which was decided before the Bigelow case, the promoters purposely restricted the issue of stock to anyone except themselves until they had completed the transfer of the property to a corporation at a large profit, and then the corporation sold the remainder to innocent purchasers. The court said that such an action was a direct injury to the corporation itself, saying: "Certainly the court did not intend to make the organization a mere secret conduit through which promoters can convert the money paid by future subscribers to their own gain the corporation being powerless to prevent it and yet the law furnish it no remedy for the wrong." 

The case of Lewis et al. v. Elk Hills 36 Oil Co.92 is analogous to the Bigelow case, although the latter was not cited. There the promoters, one of whom owned an option on certain mineral rights, organized a corporation and transferred these mineral rights to the corporation for 300,000 of the 500,000 shares of stock. The innocent purchasers of the other 200,000 shares from the corporation sued in the name of the corporation to cancel the stock issued to the promoters for property which was reasonably worth $20,000. The court here is merely following the common sense view that a corporation is a collection of individuals associated together to carry on a business and disregards the idea of legal entity as announced in the Federal cases.

99. Vernon's Ann. Civ.St. arts. 1538a-

The result reached by the Bigelow doctrine, "conceding that the injury is really to the individual subscribers no matter how small their number, and not to the corporation as an entity, the impracticability of numerous suits, the huge cost of litigation to the small stockholder, and the inaccessibility of evidence to the ordinary individual, especially where the corporate business is located in distant places, strongly suggest that some more feasible remedy should be found in that case to protect the shareholder." Such has been the view of the text writers as well as the courts.

The Bigelow doctrine has been criticized on the following grounds: (1) If the promoters had taken all the stock, and subsequently sold it themselves, they would have escaped liability to the corporation. (2) Many persons whom the promoters had not wronged profited at their expense. (3) The innocent subscribers are the only persons really injured by the wrongdoing of the promoters and they may no longer be stockholders. (4) 

Only 2/15 of the recovery could possibly reach the defrauded subscribers. (5) The doctrine takes away from the defrauded subscribers the remedy which belongs to them personally and gives it to the corporation.¹

In the states that follow the Bigelow case the rule of that case will not be followed where the unissued stock is not sold until long after the corporation started operations. The stock must be purchased "during the promotional stage." The reason for this limitation on the Bigelow holding is that, "In more than six years much water can be squeezed out of stock, and, we may assume that the corporate balance sheet during such a period may have materially changed." 2 From the time parties begin to contemplate the formation of a partnership a fiduciary relation exists between the parties. Therefore, when promoters organize a corporation and deliberately transfer property to it at an excessive valuation at the same time intending to invite others to come into their organization and share the hazards of the business, should the courts not hold that these parties are under a fiduciary duty to disclose to these invited stockholders exactly what they paid for the property? If they do not disclose all material facts to a disinterested board, should not the transaction be voidable at the mere instance of the injured parties the same as in the case of the partnership? When the promoter or agent of the corporation invites a member of the public to buy some of the unissued stock he usually expressly states that he wants the purchaser to come in "on the ground floor." Even though he does not expressly state that the purchaser is to come in on the same basis as the promoters, yet the reason for the majority holding of the states, as illustrated by the Bigelow case, is that there is a fiduciary relation between the promoter and those invited to share the hazards of the business the same as in the case of the partnership.*

This is the better holding. The doctrine of caveat emptor should not apply. In other words, when the promoter offers to sell some of the original unissued stock to the public during the organization of the company the purchasers should be allowed to assume that the promoter will not ask par or above for such stock when he has paid only fifty cents on the dollar for the stock that was issued to him. However, if the promoters take all the stock of the corporation and offer their individual stock to the public, according to the weight of authority, the parties deal with each other as strangers and in such a case the doctrine of caveat emptor applies.5 In this case the purchaser must investigate and determine for himself the condition of the company. This is a narrow distinction and has been criticised by many eminent writers. When one buys stock in a new corporation he does not know whether he is paying for unissued stock or stock that has already been issued to a promoter. From the authorities cited above it is evident that a majority of the state courts think that the promoters should not be allowed to purchase their shares of stock for less than the unissued stock is sold to the public, and this surely appeals to the sense of justice of most persons. Suppose we assume that the cases contra to the Old Dominion-Bigelow holding are correct; namely, that one offered even unissued stock, is forced to determine all the facts concerning the organization of the company. Is he in a position to ascertain the actual facts? Will promoters who have agreed among themselves to make a large profit out of the formation of the company freely disclose their plan of organization? The writer is firmly convinced that the rule of the Old Dominion- Bigelow case is more satisfactory than the holding of the Supreme Court of the United States in the Old Dominion-Lewisohn case, and is preferred.

Admitting then that the innocent purchaser has been injured and not the corporation, since every stockholder consented, what should be the remedy? Mr. Weston in 30 Harvard Law Review 

39 has shown very clearly that the payment of over $2,000,000.00 by Bigelow to the corporation did not recompense the innocent stockholders, for most or all of them had sold their stock, and where this was the case the purchasers of this stock got the benefit of the judgment rather than those who were injured. It is evident, therefore, that the injured parties should be permitted to recover enough to put them on the same basis as the promoters. Suppose the capital stock is $100,000.00 and that the promoters took $50,000.00 of stock for property that cost them $25,000.00 and the balance of the stock was sold to the public at par. The innocent stockholders should recover $12,500.00 from the promoters. If this were the remedy finally worked out by the courts, each set of parties paid the same for their stock. 

But in this case few suits could be instituted by the injured parties. Unless they can combine their efforts to right the wrong, only the wealthy stockholder could afford to run the risk of litigation. For this reason the court should apply the doctrine of the repentent trustee to this situation. Under the holding of 

Wetmore v. Porter and other cases a trustee who has connived with another to defraud the cestui que trust may repent and sue his joint tort feasor for the injury done the trust estate. Just so in the above case the corporation as the collecting agent of the injured parties should be permitted to sue for the innocent purchasers and recover enough to put them on a parity with the guilty parties. When the judgment is paid the proceeds should be given to the injured parties.³

This may seem at first unfair to some, but if it is remembered that the above judgment is in the nature of a penalty, and unless some penalty is imposed on the promoter for his wrong doing he will not be deterred, the injustice of the above result becomes negligible. 

§ 435. Sale of Promoter's Stock 

The third type of case with which the courts have dealt, is the situation in which the promoter sells property at a grossly overvalued sum to a corporation which he has organized, and instead of selling other stock on behalf of the corporation, he takes his own personal stock which he has received for the over-valued property in the original transaction, and sells to the innocent public. In most of these cases the promoters take all the stock of the corporation. Does the corporation have a right of action 

2 HILDEBRAND TEX.CORP. 

274

against the promoter for his fraud which he has perpetrated on the innocent assignees? The courts hold that no cause of action lies in favor of the corporation in this type of case, because all the original subscribers have assented to the transaction, and the injury is to the individual subscriber, and the cause of action lies with him.⁹

The reason for this rule has been stated thus: "Where one is not an original subscriber to stock but purchases shares from a broker or other vendor of stock, the corporation is not a party to the transaction. If any wrong is committed on the buyer, it is by the seller, not by the corporation. The buyer, under those circumstances, is not in a position to enforce rights of the corporation. Such a case bears some analogy to the rule that, where the act of an intelligent and responsible human being intervenes between an original cause and a resulting damage, the law will not look beyond the cause most recently operative. 

The buyer has gone into the market to make an investment. 

He knows that he is not an original subscriber. He becomes a holder of stock because of a direct relation not to the corporation but to his vendor." 10 

Ehrich in his discussion of the above proposition says: "The rule that the profit is lawful in the one case but unlawful in the other, makes the legal liability, as well as the honesty of the promoters, depend upon the form of the transaction rather than

The holding in the above cases is consistent with the Federal ruling, but on principle it seems to be inconsistent with the holding of a majority of the state courts, for the liability of the promoter is determined by the manner in which he manipulates the corporation, and, as stated before, the holding of the above cases has been criticised by eminent writers.13

Under our authorities the corporation is a legal entity, distinct from its stockholders. In this regard, strictly speaking, the ownership of the corporate assets is vested in the corporation itself and not in its stockholders. Also, strictly speaking, the ownership of the stock does not carry with it the equitable title to the corporate property. This simply means, however, that the stockholders have no right to require the corporation to convey to them the legal title to the corporate property. In a larger or real sense the stockholders of a corporation are the beneficial owners of its corporate properties. Yeaman v. Galveston City 

Co., 106 Tex. 389, 167 S.W. 710, Ann.Cas.1917E, 191. It follows that, under the record we have detailed, when this concern was chartered and the properties above described conveyed to it, it became the corporate owner thereof, but the real or beneficial owners of such property were the three stockholders in the proportion in which they held the stock of the corporation. There were no creditors. Under such a record, as between the stockholders themselves, certainly no one or more of them could have questioned the beneficial interest of any one of the others in the properties of the corporation. All this being true, we are unable to see how the corporation's rights could then rise higher than the rights of all of its beneficial owners, and in this regard there is nothing in this record that would change the status at this time from that which existed at the time it was originally organized and its capital stock originally issued. "Finally, as already shown, the three persons who subscribed for all of the capital stock of this corporation were fully cognizant of all that was done in its organization and in the issuance of its charter and capital stock. Also, the Secretary of State was fully apprised of what was being done and how each subscriber and stockholder was paying for his stock. As between the original parties, there was no concealment and no overreaching. Also, except as to the State, no person or party other 278

than the corporation and the three persons who subscribed for and received all of its capital stock had any interest in this corporation or its corporate affairs. Under such a record we think that, as between each other, neither the corporation itself nor any of its stockholders has any right to say that the issuance of the stock to McAlister was a void transaction in its incipiency.

If those facts had been established the case would have come squarely within a dictum by the Supreme Court of Massachusetts in the Old Dominion-Bigelow case; and according to its dictum that court would have permitted the plaintiff to recover for the overvaluation of the lease.17 For the above reasons it cannot be said that the McAlister case adopts any of the above theories, and, therefore, the courts of Texas are free to adopt the most reasonable theory that they can devise. The court held that the receiver of the corporation could recover from the promoters the profits they made from a sale of not only the bonds but also the stock of the Duquesne Corporation. The Court also intimated that a recovery by the receiver would not bar suits by individual bondholders against the promoters for the loss they sustained in the purchase of the bonds by reason of fraud perpetrated by the promoters in selling the bonds. Mr. Justice Cardozo wrote the opinion of the Court, but 

Justice Roberts filed a dissenting opinion with which Mr. Justice 

Sutherland, Mr. Justice McReynolds, and Mr. Justice Butler concurred.

Justice Cardozo based his decision mainly on two grounds. In the first place, he relied on the familiar principle that the promoters of a corporation occupy a fiduciary relation not only to the future corporation but also to its stockholders. In this case the promoters violated their duty when they pocketed all the proceeds of the sale of the stock and bonds of the corporation except the purchase price of the gas properties and a small working capital. It was their duty to give this balance to the company, especially as they stated in the prospectus that "These bonds are issued by the corporation in connection with the acquisition of properties, and to provide cash for developments, extensions and other corporate purposes." All through the opinion 

Justice Cardozo stresses the fact that the Duquesne Gas Company was insolvent when it began operations because the promoters had pocketed so much "illicit gains" which should have gone to the company instead of into the pockets of the "promoters and their confederates." Yet he makes it very plain that he would have reached the same conclusion even though the machinations of the promoters had not made the corporation insolvent at its outset, if a recovery of these "illicit gains" was needed to pay subsequent creditors. On this point Justice 

Cardozo said: "The shareholders were not at liberty, at all

events to the prejudice of creditors or other shareholders, present or prospective, to set that policy at naught. If the effect of what they did was to put illicit profits in the pockets of trustees, their consent will not avail to block pursuit and reclamation." 25 * * In the second place, Justice Cardozo held that the defendants were liable because they had violated the Constitution of Pennsylvania which provides: no corporation shall issue stocks or bonds except for money, labor done, or money or property actually received; and all fictitious increase of stock or indebtedness shall be void." 26 In discussing this point he said: "The prohibition is not escaped through the receipt of some property or money if the amount or value is inadequate. * True, the securities are valid in the hands of innocent purchasers, whatever the consideration 

(Guarantee Title & Trust Co. v. Dilworth Coal Co., 235 Pa. 594, 

84 A. 516), but the liability of the directors or other fiduciaries who have put them into circulation is not thereby released. 

Nowhere is it held that delinquent fiduciaries who have nullified the statute may keep the profits for themselves when creditors will be injured unless the profits are returned." 27

The Old Dominion-Lewisohn case held that promoters who sold property to their own corporation at an excessive valuation at a time when they owned all the stock of the company, even though at that time they intended to sell some of the unissued stock to the public at a much greater price than they actually paid for their stock, were not liable to the corporation for not permitting the innocent purchasers to come in "on the ground floor." Justice Holmes reaches this conclusion because of his reverence for the corporate fiction,—a feeling which caused him on one occasion to write: "Twice lately I have had to guard against the corporate entity becoming a nonconductor in the wrong place. U. S. Grain Corp. v. Phillips, 261 U.S. 106, 113, 43 S.Ct. 283, 67 L.Ed. 552, and U. S. v. Walter, 263 U.S. 15, 44 

S.Ct. 10, 68 L.Ed. 137, Oct. 22, 1923. But as I said when young, on the Massachusetts bench, the very meaning of the fiction is that you are to act as if it was true." 32 The Supreme Court took the position in the Old Dominion-Lewisohn case that the corporation could not recover because the parties to the transaction owned all of the issued stock, and that, therefore, the corporation was bound by their acts even though at that time they intended to sell some of the unissued stock to outsiders. A majority of the state courts that have considered this question refuse to follow the holding of the United States Supreme Court in the Old Dominion-Lewisohn case. In other words, those courts permit the corporation itself to recover from the promoters under the above facts.33

Some writers contend that under the Bigelow holding the promoters are unnecessarily penalized, since the Massachusetts court allowed the corporation to recover the difference between the cost of the properties to the promoters and the par value of the stock taken by them. It has been pointed out that in many of these cases the stockholders who were duped sell their stock before the judgment is paid, and hence that the parties who were injured receive no benefit from the recovery by the corporation, and that, if the guilty parties have not disposed of their stock, the ones who caused the injury benefit from the decree of the court.35 For this reason the theory of the state courts is criticized, and the contention is made that the injured stockholders should recover only enough to put them on a parity with the promoters, or that the corporation as a repentant trustee should recover that amount for the sole benefit of the injured stockholders.36

§ 436. Subsequent Plan and Sale to the Public 

The fourth type of case which has come before the courts is that in which the promoters organize a corporation and take all the stock themselves, not intending at the time of the organization to take in future subscribers, but after a lapse of time additional stock is sold, and the question is whether there can be corporate recovery for the secret profits made by the promoters.

The English courts have held that if at the time the corporation was organized the promoters were and intended to remain the sole proprietors of the stock of the company there could be no corporate right of action against the promoters for secret profits. The English court in handing down its opinion in In re 

British Seamless Paper Box Co. was careful to point out that there had been a long lapse of time between the organization of the company and the subsequent issuance of stock, and there were facts clearly going to show that there was no intent originally to issue further stock in the company.38 The Federal courts clearly would not allow a recovery by the corporation in such a case, for there could be no recovery in the Federal courts even though there was a fraudulent intent at the time the promoters organized the corporation to sell to future subscribers.39

A majority of the state courts follow the Old Dominion-Bigelow case and will not allow the corporation to recover where there

In this comment the author suggests the following remedy: "Some device is needed which will compenstate only those persons actually damaged by the promoters' fraud. Thus, if an innocent shareholder has sold without loss, the vendee holding when the fraud becomes known and the market price of stock falls, is the real loser and should be the distributee; conversely, if the shares were sold at a loss caused by the original fraud, the vendor alone should participate in the distribution. The main difficulty with the solution set forth in the last note and that of the repentant trustee suggested above, is that in most cases the directors of the corporation will not direct that the suit be brought in the name of the corporation, and thereby run the risk of paying the court costs and other incidental expenses of the litigation where they realize that even if the company is successful the entire amount of the recovery must be paid to the injured parties and not retained by the company. 

From the above discussion of the liability of promoters for fraud perpetrated on innocent shareholders it is evident that the courts have not as yet reached a satisfactory solution to many of the problems discussed in the above sections. This is one of the most troublesome problems in the law of private corporations. One court has said: "The question of secret profits has caused endless discussion in the courts, textbooks and legal periodicals, and the only safe statement that can be made is that hardly any two authorities have been in absolute accord." 43 

If the courts would realize that when they say that there is a fiduciary relation between the promoters and the future stockholders who are invited to contribute their property to the corporation, they are begging the question, and that they have adopted that technique merely to reach a desirable result, and look at the fact situation realistically, there would be less confusion in the opinions, and more desirable results would be attained. For instance, the holding of the Hays v. Georgian, Inc.44 case taught the promoter how to escape liability under the Old Dominion-Bigelow case. Instead of taking part of the stock and selling the balance to the innocent public, the promoters realized that if they took all of the stock and sold some of their own stock to parties who had no notice of the fraud even though such parties thought that they were subscribing for unissued stock, no wrong would be done the corporation, and, therefore, it could not recover.

Again, the result of the Piggly Wiggly-Delaware v. Bartlett case 45 shocks our sense of common justice and fair dealings. In that case the promoters were permitted to take 15,000 shares of common no-par value stock for a method of doing business for which they paid $1,000.00. The promoters then sold the preferred stock along with their common stock to innocent parties who thought that they were purchasing unissued stock of the corporation. They sold their common stock for $100,000.00, and, after paying the expenses of selling the stock, divided the balance among themselves. The facts of this case bring it squarely within the Old Dominion-Bigelow case since the promoters took. only part of the authorized stock and intended to sell the balance to the public. As we have already seen, New Jersey follows the Old Dominion-Bigelow case where the company is authorized to issue only par value stock.46 However, the court in the Piggly 

Wiggly-Bartlett case did not follow the Old Dominion-Bigelow case merely because the stock was no-par stock. Clearly in this, and the McCandless v. Furlaud case,47 the purchasers of the stock thought that the money they paid for their stock would become the property of the corporation. Most assuredly when a person subscribes to the capital stock of a corporation he has a right to assume that those who invited his subscription paid the same for their stock as they asked the subscriber to pay for his stock.48 If the promoters paid less than the innocent subscribers, the corporation itself is injured; for in most, if not all of these cases, the stock taken by the promoters could have been sold for the same price that the innocent subscribers paid for their stock. Besides, quite often it can be shown that the company failed, or was not as successful as it otherwise would have been, because the promoters crippled it financially by paying much less than par for their stock. If the courts should adopt this reasoning they would permit the corporation to recover from the guilty promoters the difference between the price paid by the innocent parties and that paid by the promoters. If the innocent parties paid par or above par for their stock, and the suggested remedy were adopted, two possible claims would be settled by one suit-(1) the suit of the corporation for the promoter's fraud and (2) that of the future creditor against the promoters for watering the stock. If the innocent parties paid less than par for their stock, or less than "the stated value" if the stock is no-par stock, the rights of future creditors would be the same against all of the stockholders. If the above rules were generally adopted by the courts there would be no more reason for the innocent parties to sell their stock at a loss as soon as they discovered the fraud, than if some of the assets of the corporation were destroyed by the negligence of a third party. In both cases the corporation could recoup its loss by enforcing its claim against the guilty party. Therefore, the argument that if the corporation is given a remedy those who are really injured by the fraud of the promoter are not benefited by the recovery, since most of them sell their stock at a loss as soon as they discover the fraud, would not be very convincing. 

At present the innocent parties sell their stock because of the uncertainty of the law. If their rights are definitely determined by court decisions, or a legislative enactment, the innocent parties will not become frightened at the first signal of the promoters' fraud.

The courts should make no distinction between a purchase of shares from the promoters on the one hand, and a purchase directly from the corporation on the other. The injury is the same in both cases, and there is no logical basis for such a distinction.51 In every case where the promoter paid less for his stock

The promoter takes the lead in launching the business, and, therefore, the responsibility of making a success of the enterprise should rest on his shoulders. Many contributors, outside of the promoter group, are reluctantly persuaded to invest in the new enterprise. 

These parties feel outraged when they realize that they paid more for their stock than the promoters. Such conduct on the part of the promoter shocks the conscience of any honest investor. The courts give relief to the innocent party because "there is a fiduciary relation" between the parties. That is the usual technique adopted by the courts to reach a desirable result. The real reason for the court's decision is that honestynot as that term is defined by a single judge but by the conscience of the entire community-demands fair treatment on the part of co-investors in a business, rather than that there is fiduciary relationship between the parties. In determining what the promoters paid for their stock, objective realities, rather than the subjective intent of the promoters, should be the primary consideration of the courts. Let us suppose that when A bought a tract of land two years before he spoke to B, C, and D about forming an irrigation company he subjectively intended to form such a corporation in the future, and that the land doubled in value during the two years. A corporation is merely a method of conducting a business. § 437. Remedies of the Corporation and Stockholders 

In those jurisdictions where the corporation is allowed to sue the promoters the following remedies are available. The cor- 'poration may rescind the transaction or sue to set the transaction aside and recover what it has parted with provided it offers to return to the promoters property it has received from them.58 

The corporation may sue in equity to compel an accounting for secret profits made by the promoter, or it may proceed in a court of law for damages.59 The courts treat the fraud of the promoters as a joint tort. For this reason the remedy is joint and several. Therefore, the plaintiff may recover the entire damages against one or more of the promoters.

In those jurisdictions where the corporation cannot sue, the stockholders have these remedies. If the promoter is guilty of false and fraudulent representations, a stockholder who has been

§ 438. Liability of the Promoter for Failure to Organize the Cor poration 

Promoters are liable to subscribers for failure to organize the corporation unless it specifically appears that there was an agreement to the contrary.62

Where the subscriber to the proposed corporation has paid money, or transferred property to the promoters, with the understanding that it might be used in an effort to perfect the organization of the company, there is no right of recovery from the promoters where the money or property was used in an effort to incorporate the enterprise.63 

§ 439. Liability for Torts before Incorporation 

Where the promoters begin operations for the corporation before its charter is approved by the Secretary of State, they become personally liable for torts committed by themselves or agents before the corporation comes into existence.64

§ 470. In General 

If the business of a corporation is successful, and profits are realized, the directors set apart from time to time, from these profits, a fund to be divided among its members in proportion to 299

DIVIDENDS 

Ch. 11 the amount of their shares. This fund is called a dividend. The term, as understood in the law of corporations and as applied to corporate stock, has a technical, but well-understood, meaning. 

It indicates "corporate funds derived from the business and earnings of the corporation, appropriated by a corporate act to the use of and to be divided among the stockholders."1 "Dividends" and "profits" are not synonymous terms. Dividends are paid out of the profits, but they can exist only where they have been declared or set apart by the directors. Profits are not dividends until, as expressed in the above quotation, they are "appropriated by a corporate act" to be divided among the shareholders. In Hyatt v. Allen,³ the plaintiff sold stock in a corporation to the defendant, reserving "all profits and dividends of and upon such stock" up to a certain time. A dividend having been partly earned before the time specified, but not declared until afterwards, it was held that the plaintiff was not entitled to any part of it under the reservation in the contract, for there was no dividend until it was declared. Until dividends are declared, the profits are part of the assets of the company, and do not belong to the stockholders individually, nor is there any debt from the corporation to them, even though the circumstances are such that a dividend ought to be declared. It follows that, where

a corporation becomes insolvent before its surplus fund has been set apart for the stockholders by declaring a dividend, the surplus, as well as the other assets of the corporation, must, if necessary, be applied to satisfy its debts to the exclusion of any claim by the stockholders. Until a dividend has been declared, the stockholders cannot maintain an action to recover from the corporation their proportion of a surplus. Their remedy is by suit in equity to compel the directors to declare and pay a dividend." 

It was said in an Alabama case that "dividends unpaid are assets of the company and liable for its debts," but this is not true if the dividend has been declared. It is only true of surplus profits not officially set aside for dividends. When the directors of a corporation have lawfully declared a dividend from profits earned and received, the right of the stockholders to payment becomes vested, and there is a debt due them from the corporation; or, if money or other property equal to the amount of the dividend is specifically set apart as payment of the dividend, the share of each stockholder therein is thereby severed from the common funds of the corporation, and the corporation thereby becomes a debtor to each stockholder to whom the dividend is payable.

Ch. 11 "Now, it is not essential to the right to receive a dividend that there should have been a formal declaration of a dividend, but where the corporation sets apart a fund for distribution to its stockholders to such extent as to become segregated from the property of the corporation, such property henceforth becomes, equitably, the stockholders' property. There has been in legal effect a declaration of a dividend, and of course if such fund is actually delivered to the stockholders, there has been a payment, and the fund is legally that of the stockholder. In other words, where there has been such a segregation of the corporate funds, and such a dedication to the stockholders, the assets thus segregated cease to belong to the corporation, but do belong to the stockholders individually." According to some authorities when a cash or property dividend is declared, the right of the stockholders thereto becomes vested, and the board of directors cannot afterwards, without their consent, revoke its action in declaring the dividend, and refuse to pay it.10 Nor will insolvency of the corporation arising after the dividend has been declared defeat the right of the stockholders to their shares as against creditors.11

DIVIDENDS § 471. When Dividends are Irrevocable 

To give shareholders a vested right therein, the dividend must have been fully declared. It has been held in Massachusetts that, where a dividend has been voted by the directors but their action not made public, nor communicated to the stockholders, and where no funds are set apart for payment, the vote may be rescinded.12 But the Missouri appellate court has recently expressly repudiated the Massachusetts holding, saying: "The decision of that case can only be sustained upon the theory that the declaration of the dividend did not create a debt to the stockholders, for if a debt was thereby created, it is preposterous to say that such debt can be canceled by the action of the debtor without the consent of the creditor. In fact, we understand the opinion, inasmuch as it is there asserted that 'the passage of the vote did not constitute an actual contract of the corporation with the stockholders,' as holding that the declaration of the dividend did not create a debt; and if this be its holding, it stands out boldly, single and alone in this country, against an unbroken line of cases."13 The Massachusetts and Missouri courts seem to understand the term "declaration" in quite different senses; the one requiring publication of the vote of the directors, whereas the other regards the vote per se of the directors as amounting to the declaration of the dividend, thereby creating a debt on the part of the corporation to the stockholders in the amount of their respective shares thereof. Resolutions passed by the directors are conditional and subject to change at any time before the meeting is adjourned.
