As a rule, it would be bad policy for a corporation to borrow money with which to pay dividends.28 One court in a rather old case has said that dividends cannot be declared out of borrowed money, for borrowed money is not profits "arising from the business of the company."29 However, in that case the company had no surplus or net profits and the court even held it had no authority to borrow money. But money may be borrowed temporarily for the purpose of paying dividends, if the corporation has used its current profits to make improvements or extensions of the plant or with it purchased other property provided it actually has an earned surplus.30 

Before there can be net profits a reserve for depreciation and obsolescence must be established. If part of the assets of the company consists of buildings or machinery, they will become obsolete in a certain number of years even though they may be kept in perfect repair. For instance, an office building becomes obsolete as a general rule within twenty-five to forty years. "The net income of a corporation for dividend purposes cannot be determined until all taxes, depreciation, maintenance and upkeep expenditures have been deducted. Otherwise the dividend is not paid from the earning but by a depreciation of the capital account."31

Provision should always be made for renewal of plant and machinery 32 and for future and contingent claims as well as for

all present indebtedness.33 In a recent publication it is said:34 "Only the interest, and not the principal, of debts not falling due but in the nature of permanent or bonded debts need be deducted from profits before dividends are payable." The meaning of this quotation is ambiguous. If it means that bonded indebtedness need not be put on the liability side of the balance sheet in determining whether there are any profits that may be distributed as dividends, it is an incorrect statement of the law, and is not supported by the cases cited in the notes to the above publication. 

Suppose the capital stock of a company is $100,000.00 and its assets are worth $90,000.00. It issues $40,000.00 of long term bonds and sells them at par. The assets would then be worth $130,000.00. It owes no debts other than the bonded indebtedness. Would anyone contend that the directors could declare a tihrty per cent dividend? Even if a sinking fund is set aside each year, all of the debts of the company minus the amount of the sinking fund should be listed as a liability of the company. The sinking fund will be reflected in the "assets" of the company.35 

The amount of the sinking fund is listed as a liability on the balance sheet in the form of a "reserve" or merely as a "sinking fund" to retire the bonds. The assets that represent the sinking funds are commingled with the other properties of the company unless a cash reserve is set up for this purpose. They are not earmarked and set aside for the bondholders except as a matter of bookkeeping. Therefore, if the corporation becomes insolvent, the assets that represent the sinking fund should be distributed among all the unsecured creditors and not set aside specifically for the bondholders. If the deed of trust has an "after acquired" property clause or some other provision that creates a lien on the property set aside as a sinking fund the property is impounded

The capital stock of an insurance company is not the primary fund for the payment of losses which may accrue upon existing risks, but premiums received for insurance and the interest on the capital stock constitute the primary and natural fund for the payment of the debts and losses of the company. 

Therefore, the unearned premiums received by an insurance company on which the risks are still running are not surplus profits of the company, out of which dividends can be legally declared, unless a sufficient surplus is left on hand to meet the probable losses upon risks then assumed and not yet terminated, independent of the capital stock of the company.48 

In deciding whether a dividend was rightfully or wrongfully made, the transaction must be viewed from the circumstances and conditions existing at that time, and not in the light of subsequent events. Notes or overdrafts, for instance, by persons then considered perfectly solvent, should not be considered as losses because they afterwards proved to be such.49

A most interesting problem arises in connection with the right of the directors to declare a dividend when the assets of a corporation increase in value but no cash or direct tangible pecuniary gain has been actually realized. For example, suppose a corporation has land valued at twenty thousand dollars, there is a boom, and the land increases in value to forty thousand dollars. Can a corporation declare a dividend on the strength of such increase alone? In the case of Dealers' Gran ite Corporation v. Faubion,50 the Texas Court of Civil Appeals denied the right of the corporation to declare a dividend solely on the strength of an increase in the value of its assets. The

* * As we have already seen in the previous part of this chapter, several courts have said that unrealized appreciation in the assets63 especially fixed assets should not be considered in determining whether the company is in a position to declare a dividend. The case most often cited for that rule is Foster v. New Trinidad Lake Asphalt Co. In that case the company invested its capital in assets a part of which was a note that was considered worthless. A few years later the note, amounting to over $100,000.00, was paid and the directors thought that this entire amount was "net profits," and determined to declare a dividend of that amount without determining whether the capital assets of the company were impaired. 

The court held that the directors should be injoined from declaring a dividend until a general accounting was had. In its opinion the court said: "It is clear, I think, that an appreciation in total value of capital assets, if duly realized by sale or getting in of some portion of such assets, may, in a proper case, be treated as available for purposes of dividend. 

If I rightly appreciate the true effect of the decisions, the question of what is profit available for dividend depends upon the result of the whole accounts fairly taken for the year, capital as well as profit and loss; and although dividends may be paid out of earned profits in proper cases, although there has been a depreciation of capital, I do not think that a realized accretion to the estimated value of one item of the capital assets can be deemed to be profit divisible amongst the shareholders without reference to the result of the whole accounts, fairly taken." It is evident that the above case held that realized appreciation of capital assets may be an item in the accounting when the directors decide to declare a dividend. However, it did not decide the negative of that proposition. In other words, it did not decide that unrealized appreciation cannot be considered in determining whether the company is in a position to declare a dividend although the case is often cited for that rule of law.

From this review of the cases usually cited for the rule that "circulating assets" should be valued "at cost or market, whichever is lower" and that "fixed assets," such as lands, machinery and other assets owned by the corporation which are to be used business judgment or financial policy or of proper accounting practice, or even what the law ought to be. My views of the business acumen or financial sagacity of these directors, as well as my views as to what the legislature ought to permit or prohibit, are entirely immaterial. The question I have to decide is whether or not an existing statute has been violated. The problem is one of statutory construction. 

"In summary, I think that it cannot be said that there is a single case in this State which actually decides that unrealized appreciation cannot be taken into consideration, or, stated in different words, that cost and not value must be used in determining whether or not there exists a surplus out of which dividends can be paid. I think, further, that such a holding would run directly counter to the meaning of the terms capital and capital stock as fixed by decisions of the Court of Appeals construing the earlier statutes, and that such construction of those terms must be deemed to have been adopted by the legislature in enacting the statute here involved. See 

Matter of Scheftel's Estate, 275 N.Y. 

135, 141, 9 N.E.2d 809. I thus obviously cannot follow decisions to the contrary in other States or any contrary views of economists or accountants. If the policy of the law be bad it is for the legislature to change it. "Throughout the period in question the company carried upon its books as assets its investments in and advances to its subsidiaries at their face value, i. e., at the cost thereof, and despite his insistence that unrealized appreciation of one asset cannot be taken into consideration, the plaintiff yet insists that these investments and advances must be written down to the value thereof as shown by the books of the subsidiaries, even though the subsidiaries are still carrying on business, and, further, that those books shall be what he calls 'properly adjusted,' so as to cause them to show the actual value of the stock of and claims against those subsidiaries. He thus, as it seems to me, takes the inconsistent position that while unrealized appreciation cannot be considered, unrealized depreciation nevertheless must be. Defendants, also, take the equally inconsistent position that while unrealized appreciation must be considered, unrealized depreciation need not be. I am of the opinion that the same reasons which show that unrealized appreciation must be considered are equally cogent in showing that unrealized depreciation likewise must be considered. In other words, the test being whether or not the value of the assets exceeds the debts and the liability to stockholders, all assets must be taken at their actual value. * * * The directors are the ones who should determine the figures by carefully considering values, and it was for the very purpose of compelling them to perform that duty that the statute imposes upon them a

De ins ake th ther t -TLE: et by it in making profits and not purchased for resale, should be inventoried at cost, it is evident that the above rules concerning circulating assets have not been established by the courts of America. The writer understands from his interviews with many business men that it is customary to inventory the propertiesboth real and personal-of Texas corporations at their market value at the time the inventory is prepared.69 The directors of personal responsibility for declaring and paying dividends when the value of the assets is not sufficient to justify them. What directors must do is to exercise an informed judgment of their own, and the amount of infor mation which they should obtain, and the sources from which they should obtain it, will of course depend upon the circumstances of each particular case. What is said in Bourne v. 

Bourne, 240 N.Y. 172, 148 N.E. 180, with respect to courts reviewing the discretion and judgment of directors was not said with reference to the legality of the declaration of a dividend, and, furthermore, the statements there made are predicated upon the assumption that directors realize that they are under a duty to exercise an informed judgment with respect to the assets of the company of which they are directors and have performed that duty. If directors have blindly or complacently accepted either cost or any other arbitrary figures as indicative of value, they have not exercised either discretion or judgment and no court is required to act as if they had. When directors have in fact exercised an informed judgment with respect to the value of the company's assets, the courts obviously will be exceedingly slow to override that judgment, and clear and convincing evidence will be required to justify a finding that such judgment was not in accordance with the facts. In the last analysis, however, the issue, in any case in which it is claimed that dividends have been paid out of capital, is the value of the assets and the amount of the lia- 'bilities to creditors and stockholders at the times the dividends were declared and paid."

They should limit the rule as to unrealized appreciation of fixed assets to property purchased and used as the location of the business of the company, and only so long as it is used for that purpose, and to other property, such as the machinery in a manufacturing plant, that is purchased, not to be sold but used by the company in making profits, if courts continue to make a distinction in this regard between circulating and fixed assets. If the balance sheet does not reflect the actual condition of the corporation, it will be misleading not only to the stockholders of the corporation but also to the investing public. If fixed assets are listed on the balance sheet at cost when their true value is much less, and on the other hand, if they are listed at cost when they are worth much more, the balance sheet does not reflect the company's condition and is of little value to any one. 

According to the rules of the Securities and Exchange Commission, even fixed assets must be listed at their reasonable market value in the statement of a corporation whose securities are presented for approval by the Commission. The rules of the Commission are discussed in detail in the 28 California Law Review, pages 369 to 378 inclusive. In this comment it is said: "In view of the many difficulties inherent even in the objective valuation of fixed assets at cost, there is reputable authority which insists that the proper presentation of fixed assets on the balance sheet is at market or reproduction value rather than cost."81 "The practice of carrying fixed assets at reproduction value would seem to merit serious consideration. Limited by the standards of proper appraisal methods assiduously followed as set forth by the Commission, the reflection of current values would have more significance to the average investor than past figures with little or no present meaning."

The actual point decided in that case was that a loss arising from a fire must be taken into account before a dividend could be declared.

In a recent New York case, the court held that the circulating assets of the corporation could not be valued at cost or market, whichever is lower, where the market price of the assets consisted of stocks of corporations, and the price was above the "intrinsic worth" of the stock because of manipulation of the market by the directors of the corporation. In several places in the opinion the courts stress the point that the property of the corporation must be valued at its intrinsic worth.88 

Some accountants seem to know little about law, although accounting is, in the main, the interpretation and expression of legal rules in figures. Many of their arguments, therefore, are of little value to the lawyer and very often are not germane to the question under consideration. For instance, Professor Hatfield seems to think that the rules which determine the rights of the individual should apply to the stockholders of a corporation. He gives as an illustration, the income of an individual derived from ten houses, each worth $10,000 and each yielding $1,000.00 net income every year. He says, "If two of these houses burn down, uninsured, the common sense view is that the proprietor's income is thereby cut down from $10,000.00 to $8,000.00 per annum, and that coincidentally there is a loss of capital of $20,000.00. 

It never occurs to him that he must consider his income as entirely cut off for two years until the principal can be restored. Similarly, it might be an act of cruelty to dependent stockholders to stop dividends entirely until an exceptional loss is reimbursed."89 

Based on such arguments, accountants advise that if a corporation sustains a similar loss the stockholders should vote either to reduce the capital stock or amortize the loss over a period from five to ten years. Even in Professor Hatfield's hypothetical case of the individual, if all ten houses were mortgaged and two of them burned without any insurance, the creditor would make the individual restore the full amount of security by giving a mortgage on other property or would sell the unburned houses under execution.

However, in the case of a corporation, the only property that is considered a safety fund for the benefit of creditors is "the capital" of the corporation. In consideration of the state's agreement to permit the stockholders to conduct a business with limited personal liability, it is understood that the stockholders will keep intact the above safety fund for the benefit of creditors. In the case of the individual all of his property is liable for the payment of his debts.

In one sense, the courts should consider that the capital of a corporation is mortgaged to secure the debts of the company. 

Let us apply Professor Hatfield's illustration to a corporation. 

In other words, suppose that a corporation has lost $20,000.00 of its $100,000.00 capital. In such case most accountants advise that the loss be amortized over a period of five years. By this method of bookkeeping, they permit the payment of dividends over the five-year period without first making up the entire $20,- 000.00 loss. If the company is thrown into the hands of a bankruptcy court at the end of the five-year period or soon thereafter and it is clearly shown that all of the dividends paid during that period were actually paid out of the capital of the company, the result is that funds which should have been kept intact for the payment of creditors were returned to the stockholders. Under such circumstances, the courts should not hesitate to hold the directors liable under the Texas statute.⁹⁰ The same holding should be followed in a case where a loss of the capital of the company was sustained when the company first began business because the directors used most of the capital of the company in purchasing property that was actually worth at the time of purchase only one-half of its purchase-price. 

Under the Texas Securities Act the promoters are authorized to take twenty per cent of the capital stock of the company for promoting and organizing the company. Even if this statute is constitutional, as is contended in this treatise in the chapter on "Payment for Capital Stock," the court should not permit the directors to pay a dividend until the capital is fully replenished. Very often the courts confuse the meaning of "capital” and "capital stock." In some statutes these terms are used interchangeably. The word "capital" should be used to designate that portion of the assets of a company which was acquired through the issuance of shares pursuant to subscription agreements, plus the property of the company that was capitalized by declaring a stock dividend.93 As we have seen in the chapter on "Payment for Capital Stock," if a Texas corporation issued par value stock, the property received from the subscribers should be reasonably worth the par value of the stock issued for the property. If the corporation issues non-par stock the consideration to be paid therefor must be prescribed in the charter, "or if no consideration is so prescribed, then for such consideration as may be fixed by the stockholders or by the board of directors."94

For this reason Texas corporations are not authorized to issue "true non-par stock," but what is known as "stated value nonpar stock." Therefore, if the directors receive property which

The "capital stock" of a corporation is a bookkeeping item and comprises the total amount of the par value of all of the stock that the company is authorized to issue plus the stated value of all non-par value stock provided for in the charter or amended charter of the company. If a corporation has not issued all of its authorized shares the aggregate amount of the issued capital stock should be put on the liability side of the balance sheet. 

Very often accountants advise that the entire amount of the authorized capital stock be shown on the balance sheet, but if some of the stock has not been issued the aggregate amount of such unissued stock is subtracted from the authorized capital stock in determining whether the company has a surplus or undivided profits. Soon after most corporations begin operations the property of the company which is its "capital" becomes commingled with the other assets of the corporation, and thus loses its identity. As a matter of fact, what lawyers, accountants and judges are concerned with is the amount of the issued capital stock of the company, because the directors should always keep, as a safety fund for the benefit of creditors, assets reasonably worth the aggregate amount of the issued "capital stock" of the company, and sufficient in addition to meet the other liabilities of the corporation. Take, for instance, a mercantile corporation with a capital stock of $100,000.00. Suppose $10,000.00 are invested in the store building, $80,000.00 in goods, wares and merchandise, $1,- 

000.00 for furniture and $9,000.00 is put in the bank to pay operating expenses for the first few months. Additions are made to the store building, and a more expensive location is later purchased and new furniture is installed after selling the old for onetenth of its purchase price. Of course, part or all of the loss due to the depreciation is shown on the books as a "reserve for depreciation." But how is it possible to identify the original "capital" of the company many years later?

For this reason statutes should not provide that the "capital of the company shall not be impaired," or that the directors are liable "if they knowingly pay a dividend out of the capital of the company." The courts should demand that property equal to the issued "capital stock" should be kept intact for creditors and compel accountants to put on the liability side of the balance sheet an item equal to the issued "capital stock."96 When our judges and attorneys become better acquainted with the rules of accounting, the courts will not conclude that a corporation is solvent when its assets exceed its liabilities, "excluding its capital stock as a liability." On this basis of solvency many courts permit innocent stockholders to keep dividends paid out of "the capital" of the company," and some courts on the same hypothesis permit corporations to repurchase their own stock out of the same fund.98

A corporation may agree to pay interest on certificates of stock paid in, if it is paid out of the surplus profits,99 but such an agreement cannot be enforced where the corporation has no means or resources except its "capital" from which such payments can be made.¹ It would seem clear that if the capital of a corporation is invested in land, and any or all of such land is taken under the power of eminent domain, the money received as compensation therefor must become part of the capital, and cannot be distributed as dividends without taking into account the condition of the other assets and liabilities of the corporation. A sum paid in on capital stock does not become profit, and liable to distribution as profits, when stock is forfeited for nonpayment of the balance due thereon.³ 96. 97.

In the case of a mining corporation, according to the weight of authority, the profits subject to distribution are the net proceeds of its mining operations, without any deduction for decrease in value of the mine by reason of the ore being taken out. The same principle applies to all corporations organized for the purpose of utilizing a wasting property-a property that can be used only by consuming it-as a mine, a lease, or a patent. Such a corporation is not to be considered as having distributed its capital merely because it has distributed the net proceeds of its operations, though the value of the property constituting its capital is necessarily thereby decreased. Except in such cases, however, before profits can lawfully be set apart and paid out as a dividend, a proper sum must be set aside to represent the wear and tear upon the plant and property of the corporation, so that a fund will be created for the purpose of repairing and renewing the property when it shall become necessary.5

All issued capital stock should always be listed at its par value on the liability side of the ledger in determining whether there are "profits" that may be distributed as dividends among the stockholders. In the Branch-Kaiser case 23 the court held that a corporation should not declare a dividend where its capital was depleted. In this case the company had lost heavily due to post-war depression. 

The facts do not show what was paid for the stock when the corporation was first organized. The case does not directly hold that where the stock was originally sold for less than par it is unlawful for the company to pay a dividend until its assets exceed the amount of its capital stock. However, the case is very persuasive on that point, as the court held that the capital stock must be placed on the liability side of the balance sheet in determining whether a dividend can be declared. If the corporation actually began to do business with a depleted capital and the court meant to follow those cases which hold that a corporation may declare dividends out of "net annual profits," the court would have determined and stated whether the corporation sold its stock at the beginning for less than par. The dividends that were condemned by the court were actually declared out of net profits earned during the years in which the dividends were declared. Yet, all through the opinion the court says that "surplus or profits denote an excess in the aggregate value of all assets of a corporation over the sum of its entire liabilities, including capital stock." This case seems clearly to hold that before a dividend can be declared, a corporation must replenish its depleted capital regardless of what caused the depletion. Although the case is cited for various other rules of law, the exact point decided by the above case is that the directors of a corporation are personally liable for the payment of a dividend in violation of the Act of the Pennsylvania legislature passed May 23, 1913, 15 P.S. § 631, which provides that dividends paid out of profits "shall in no case exceed the amount of the net profits acquired by the company so that the capital stock shall never be impaired thereby."

DIVIDENDS § 474. Deferred Charges and Prepaid Expenses 

There is a dearth of authority on the question as to whether prepaid insurance or rent may be listed on the asset side of the balance sheet in determining whether a dividend may be declared. 

For instance, if both rent and insurance on the store building of the mercantile corporation has been paid for five years in advance it would seem reasonable to say that one-fifth of those payments may be listed as expense for the current year and fourfifths put on the asset side of the balance sheet. Authority upholds that position.24 But one case held that prepaid taxes could not be listed as an asset for the reason that they could not be recovered.25 Most accountants include organization expenses on the asset side of the balance sheet on the theory that the corporation is benefited therefrom during the fifty years of its existence, though incurred only once. Yet those accountants who make the above assumption advise that "this asset" be written off within five to ten years.

To a lawyer, it seems absurd to contend that such "expense" can be "an asset." Under the present Securities Act in Texas, Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 600a, twenty percent of the stock of the company may be absorbed in organization expenses. If twenty percent of the stock is given to the promoters for organizing a company with a $100,000.00 as its capital stock and the balance of the stock is sold at par the company begins operations with a deficit of $20,000.00. If at the end of the first year it made a net profit of $10,000.00 it should not declare a dividend as its "capital stock" is still impaired to the extent of $10,000.00. Yet some accountants would contend that it could declare a dividend since their bookkeeping would list the $20,000.00 "organization expense" on the assets side. This would make the statement show an earned surplus or net profits of $10,000.00 at the end of the first year, if they did not begin to amortize the "expense" during that year. Even if they began to amortize this expense that year

What case law there is on this question does not favor putting organization expenses as an asset.26 The same is true with reference to development costs after incorporation.27 In the case of Kingston v. Home Life Ins. Co.28 the court permitted expenses that would bring in profitable business in the future to be listed as an asset. Other courts reached the same conclusion with reference to development and experimental expenses.29 But in all these cases where the business is merely increased, and not the value of the tangible assets of the corporation, the value to the corporation will be reflected in increased profits. Such expenses, therefore, should not be listed as an asset, but should be considered as expense and listed as such on the balance sheet. But where the expenditure adds to the value of tangible assets of the corporation or is a prepayment of a right to be enjoyed in the future, it is an asset and should be inventoried at its present actual value instead of at cost, as is claimed by many accountants. 

If, for instance, a ranch corporation should buy yearlings and keep them until they are four years old and feed them cake costing ten dollars a head ninety days before they are shipped to the market, the cost of keeping the steers three years and the feed bill should not be listed as "assets." The value of the land is based on judgment, not guessing. Arriving at a sound judgment is often difficult. But no more difficult than hundreds of questions that confront a judge or even a lawyer in half of the matters that he must determine. Judging the value of land is not more difficult than judging whether a defendant in an ordinary damage suit was guilty of negligence. Lawyers are often forced to determine even the value of land. In condemnation proceedings, determining the profit that the vendor of land must account for on his income tax return, where he acquired title to the land before March 1, 1913, involves judgment of land values. Many other such instances are constantly facing lawyers in actual practice. It is evidently much easier for an honest board of directors to determine each year the reasonable market value of the assets of the corporation than it is for an attorney to ascertain the value on March 1, 1913 of a tract of land inherited by his client in 1900. 

Yet most lawyers are faced with that problem every 15th of March. "The Uniform Business Corporation Act apparently recognizes deferred assets and prepaid expenses as asset items.32 It is submitted that prepaid expenses, and deferred charges, generally, should be considered as assets to the extent that they increase the worth of a going business.

§ 475. Payment of Dividends from Paid-In Surplus 

When par value stock is sold above par the excess is sometimes called a premium. In recent years this excess is usually designated "paid in surplus." If the stock is non-par stock the statutes of some states provide that the directors or stockholders may determine what part of the money from the sale of stock is capital and what part is "paid in surplus." In Texas the non-par stock statute provides that the stockholders, charter or the directors when authorized by the charter or shareholders, may fix the sale price of the stock.35 It does not specifically provide that the directors may determine what part of the amount contributed by the subscribers is capital and what part is "paid in surplus."36 In recent years it has become fairly customary for the directors to pay dividends out of "paid in surplus," whether the stock is par value or non-par stock. From a technical legal standpoint there is no objection to this prac-

§ 477. The Discretion of the Directors as to Declaring Dividends 

When a shareholder becomes a member of a corporation, he expects to share in the profits of the business except as limited by the provisions of his contract with the corporation and contingent on the discretionary powers of the directors to declare a dividend. By statute it is provided that the board of directors shall manage the affairs of the corporation, and this includes the power, which is vested in the board of directors, to determine whether the surplus or profits of the corporation should be distributed as dividends or retained to be used for improvements in the business.

Unlike a partnership or unincorporated association, the shareholders do not own the corporate property; title is vested in the corporation. Therefore, the shareholders have no immediate right to the corporate profits as the profits earned by the corporation remain the property of the corporation until distributed among the shareholders in the form of dividends.45 The corporation may treat it and deal with it either as profits of the business or as an addition to its capital. Until a dividend of the profits of the corporation has been declared by its board of directors, a stockholder has no legal title to any interest in them.46 Therefore, it is by action on the part of the board in declaring dividends that profits of the corporation become prop-

The stockholders of a corporation are not entitled, as a matter of absolute right, to the payment of a dividend whether the earnings of the corporation in any year exceed its liabilities. 

Although there may be a large surplus, the board of directors may, if, in their opinion, the interest of the corporation makes it necessary or advisable, expend the same in improvements, or in a lawful extension of the business of the corporation. Under some circumstances, the board of directors may retain profits of the business as a surplus fund instead of dividing it among the stockholders. Whether they do so is generally a question within their discretion to determine.49 They should, however, look to the future, and "bear in mind that the only sure benefit to the stockholders to be derived from the successful prosecution of the corporate business must come from the distribution of the dividends in cash and that a piling up of a surplus which remains undistributed may in the end go wholly to future creditors of the corporation."50 This warning is especially true

§ 478. Can the Shareholders Compel the Board of Directors to De clare a Dividend

An action cannot be maintained against a corporation by a stockholder for a dividend, as for a debt due, until the dividend has been declared, though there may be funds from which it is the duty of the directors to declare a dividend. "A right to a dividend from the profits of a corporation is no debt until the dividend is declared. Until that time, the dividend is only something that may possibly come into existence, but the obligation on the part of the corporation to declare it, cannot be treated as the dividend itself."51 If the directors unreasonably and wrongfully refuse or neglect to declare dividends when there are profits out of which dividends may be declared, and there is no apparent good reason for withholding them, a stockholder may maintain a suit in equity to compel them to declare and pay dividends.52 But, the mere existence of a large amount of "sur-

66* * * A further contention is that the residuary beneficiaries of income were entitled to receive income as cash dividends from the corporation to an amount substantially greater than actually paid. There are also instances where the court refused to aid a stockholder of a corporation in an attempt to prevent it from selling its products for less than cost, where it appeared that the reduction in price was necessary to enable it to meet competition. The reported cases on this subject show an increasing tendency toward judicial willingness to allow the directors of a corporation a wide range of discretion as to what policies will best promote the interests of the stockholders. 62 The main issue involved in the Dodge-Ford Motor Company case was whether the directors, in withholding a large portion of the surplus profits for the expansion of the business, were acting for the best interests of the corporation. Although it is not unlawful for a corporation to reduce prices to promote humanitarian motives and to expand the business within the scope of its authority, the court said in giving its decision for the minority shareholders, "It is not within the lawful discretionary powers of a board of directors to shape and conduct the affairs of a corporation for the mere incidental benefit of the shareholders, and for the primary purpose of benefiting others, and no one will contend, that if the avowed purpose of the directors was to sacrifice the interest of the shareholders, it would not be the duty of the court to interfere." 63

The court emphasized the view that, primarily, a business corporation is organized and carried on for the benefit of the stockholders and the powers of the directors are to be employed to that end. Therefore, the discretion of the directors is to be exercised in the choice of means to attain that end, and does not extend to a change in the end itself. The reduction of profits, or the nondistribution of profits among stockholders is not to be done in order to devote them to other purposes. The court went

The present tendency is to treat the directors as fiduciaries for the stockholders as well as for the corporation, and allow the stockholders to compel a declaration of dividends, where it appears that the directors have ceased loyally to serve the shareholders of the corporation. 

This case has been criticized by writers 64 who say that public opinion has changed the view toward large business corporations, and that as economic institutions such corporations have a social service duty as well as a profit making function to perform. It will be a long time before this criticism will apply to small Texas corporations. According to Professor Dodd large corporations are affected with a public interest. There are three groups that are interested in business corporations: the investors, stockholders and bondholders, the employees, and the customers. 

This writer 65 questions whether the sole function of a large business corporation is to make a profit for its stockholders. He contends that the managers should take into consideration the interests of the other two groups of interested parties.

§ 479. 

Who are Entitled to Dividends

The profits of a corporation are to be distributed pro rata among those who are its stockholders at the time when the dividend is declared, no matter when the profits may have been earned, and without regard to the length of time particular members may have been stockholders.69 It is also settled that the directors in declaring dividends have no right to discriminate between stockholders, unless the contract under which particular shares were issued gives them the right." The right to payment of the proportional part of the dividend attributable to the shares of stock then owned attaches immediately. The right of the stockholder becomes fixed by the declaration. Other cases hold that under either of the above resolutions there is no intent on the part of the directors to determine who is legally entitled to the stock, and the sole purpose of the resolution is for the protection of the corporation. These authorities do not make an exception to the general rule, and, therefore, hold that the dividend belongs to the owner at the date the dividend was declared unless the contract of sale specifically provides that the dividend belongs to the purchaser.86 These often are declared by savings banks payable to the depositors of record on a fixed date. This form of vote in declaring dividends doubtless has been adopted because of its convenience and because it avoids confusion and misunderstandings. Such vote relates to a detail touching the internal management of the corporation. It belongs to a class of affairs which the corporation has a right ordinarily to settle and thereby bind its stockholders so long as the action taken is in good faith and without fraud or collusion. It is in substance a declaration that the vote for the payment of the dividend shall be operative and take effect as to stockholders on that date and not earlier. There is no inflexible rule of law which prevents such vote of those responsible for the management of the corporation from having its natural effect. Persons by becoming stockholders in a corporation impliedly agree to be bound by the reasonable rules and practices adopted for the management of corporate affairs. Business policies adopted by business men for the management of business transactions ought not to be frustrated unless contrary either to some rule of law or to fundamental ethical rules of right and wrong. 

Votes as to the time and method for ascertainment of the stockholders entitled to dividends, such as here are 370 in question, do not offend against either of these tests. It is but the logical result of general principles of corporation law to hold that a vote of that nature passed in good faith and reasonable in its operation is binding upon the stockholders. 

It was so held in a well-reasoned judgment in Richter & Co. v. Light, 97 Conn. 364, 116 A. 600. "All the dividends of this class had been voted during the life of the beneficiary for life but payable to stockholders of record as of a date after her death and payable at a still later date. We think that the rights of her estate should be determined by the effect of the vote to the same extent as if she had been herself a stockholder of record, and that the dividends should be paid to the residuary legatee and not to the estate of the life tenant."

) latter cases seem to be based on the better reasoning. evident that in passing the resolution the primary purpose of the directors is to protect the corporation, and they do not intend to do an ultra vires act or determine to whom the dividend really belongs by merely declaring that the books shall be closed at a specified date. If the stock is transferred after the dividend is declared and the resolution states that the books of the company will be closed thirty days before the dividend is payable, the mere closing of the books is not sufficient evidence to show that the seller intended to transfer his chose in action against the company to the vendee. The same is true if the resolution goes no further than to provide that the dividend "will be payable or paid to the record owner" at a certain date. If, however, the resolution provides that "the dividend will be paid to and owned by the shareholders of record" on a certain date, as the vendor knows that his vendee can easily have the transfer of the certificate made on the books of the company, this is at least some evidence that the vendor intended to transfer his debt against the company to the vendee if he had actual knowledge of the resolution before he sold his stock.

But suppose he has no notice of the above resolution when he sold his stock, or does not know that a dividend has been declared, would anyone contend that the above facts show that the vendor intended to transfer his claim against the company to the vendee of the certificate? It seems to the writer that the courts should not be so much concerned with the power of the directors to determine to whom the dividend belongs as to the intent of the vendor. By some authorities it is said that the normal rule is not followed in the case of stock dividends. Even though the stock is sold after the stock dividend is declared, the dividend belongs to the vendee if the stock is not issued before the sale. The rea- son for this exception to the usual rule is that in case of cash or property dividends the assets of the corporation are reduced to the extent of the dividend, while in the case of a stock dividend some of the surplus of the company is capitalized and not distributed among the shareholders.88 But in all of the cases cited for the above rule, the courts relied on some specific provision of the contract for the decision. The above rules are subject to change by specific provisions in the contract of sale. The contract may provide that the vendee is entitled to the dividend that was declared before the sale but payable thereafter, or the contract may give dividends declared after the sale to the vendor until a specified date,⁹⁰ or the contract of sale may contain any other lawful provision that the parties see fit to insert therein. 

Until an offer is accepted there is no contract between the parties. Therefore, where an option to purchase stock, whether revocable or paid for, is given, and a dividend is declared before the option is exercised, the offeror is entitled to the dividend. The reason for this rule is self evident.91 And even if there is an executory contract of sale, if the passage of the title to the stock is conditional, the dividend belongs to the vendor if declared before the condition is performed.92 But if the contract of sale is unconditional so that the title of the stock passes to the purchaser upon the making of the contract, although the contract is not to be performed until a later date, dividends declared after the making of the contract belong to the purchaser. 93

The pledgee of stock, whose name appears on the books of the corporation, or whose rights are known to the corporation, is entitled to dividends subsequently declared.  § 481. 

Cumulative and Non-Cumulative Dividends 

Where it is expressly stipulated that the preference accorded is cumulative or non-cumulative, effect will be given thereto.2 

In the absence of any specification of intention on this point the preferred stockholder is entitled to priority over the common stockholder from one dividend period to another until payment has been made in full to which the preferred had a right.³ 

Whether the dividends are cumulative or non-cumulative depends upon the provisions in the agreement with the corporation which is usually evidenced by the certificate of stock. 

If the certificate specifically provides that the dividend is cumulative, the conclusion is evident. But very often the certificate provides that the corporation guarantees a preferred dividend of a certain per cent each year, or that a preferred dividend is payable at specified dates each year, and in such cases the court must determine whether the dividend is cumulative or non-cumulative. The better holding is that unless it is expressly provided that the dividend is non-cumulative, the presumption is that the parties intended to make it cumulative.¹ 

This presumption prevails where the meaning of the certificate or charter provision is doubtful, whether this question arises when the corporation is a going concern or is in process of liquidation.5

"On final dissolution of a corporation, the common shareholders have at times contended that the right to accrued back dividends on cumulative preferred shares is gone, either on the theory that the right is a right to dividends and that dividends can be paid only by a going concern and not by one in the process of liquidation, or that there is no surplus and the right is merely to receive a preference in the distribution of profits. "Some of the cases referred to in the preceding paragraph reflect a strange notion that crops up from time to time even with respect to corporations that are active, going concerns, viz. that increases in the amount of the net assets, not resulting from payment for shares, may be realized and yet not be available for dividend purposes, despite the absence of any previous capital impairment. This delusion may result from familiarity with certain phases of English corporation law. There the term 'capital' is by some used not to refer to a figure indicating the amount (loosely speaking) which the shareholders have subscribed for their shares, but to the land or other property which the corporation acquires with such sum; Ammonia 

Soda Co. v. Chamberlain [1918] 1 Ch. 

266; Verner v. General & Common'l

Hence, in England, it makes some sense to indicate that a share, preferred as to capital, may be either limited to the amount of the preference or entitled to further participation in capital distributions.

If the dividend is non-cumulative, a serious controversy has arisen as to the rights of the owner thereof where profits have been made in previous years, and the directors did not declare a dividend of the earned profits, but used them in expanding the business or for some other purpose, and yet there were no legal grounds under the preceding rules for forcing the directors to declare a dividend. Under such circumstances does a "dividend credit" accrue to the holders of the non-cumulative preferred stock where profits are made but no dividend was declared? Before the decision of the Supreme Court in the caseof Wabash Ry. Co. v. Barclay,12 the New Jersey Court had decided that the preferred non-cumulative shareholders were entitled to a "dividend credit" for profits earned any year, though the directors elected not to declare any dividends of such profits.13 The Kansas Supreme Court also seems to favor this holding. But in the Kansas case the certificate, though non-cumulative, provided that the holder was entitled to a six percent "noncumulative dividend, payable semi-annually out of the net profit of the preceding fiscal year."14 The Court said: "The fair interpretation of the contract between the corporation and holder of this stock is that if in any year net profits are earned, a dividend is to be declared."

"'18 While some writers have criticised the opinion of Justice Holmes in the Barclay case,19 in a recent article Professor Berle says: "Wherever the corporate charter includes in its financial structure non-cumulative stock or its equivalent (participating preferred stocks form such equivalent in a great majority of instances) it is possible, by timing the dividend declarations properly, to withhold earnings, and to use these for the purpose of building up surplus which subsequently falls to junior stock. 

A New Jersey court and two federal courts came to the conclusion that where dividends were earned, they must be either declared or set aside as a dividend credit to the stock which would have been entitled to such dividends had they been declared annually or periodically. This doctrine must be regarded as shaken if not completely overset by the recent Supreme 

Court ruling in Barclay v. Wabash R. R. "That decision does not go as far as is currently supposed, since the only ratio decidendi is that although non-cumulative dividends, earned but unpaid, have not been paid out to the non-cumulative preferred shareholders, dividends may, nevertheless, be paid to the common stock provided the non-cumulative dividend for the year in question has been declared and paid. 

The facts are worth a glance. The Wabash Railroad had issued non-cumulative preferred stock. Over a period of years the unpaid dividends on this stock amounted to some $16,000,000. 

Year by year the railroad had earned sufficient profits to pay these dividends had the directors elected to declare them. The directors did not do so, but converted the earnings into surplus. 

Finally, having paid the dividends on the non-cumulative stock in one year, they then undertook to inaugurate dividends on the common. A bill for an injunction was brought by a preferred shareholder; and the Supreme Court reversed a decision of the

Until recently the federal courts did not follow the state decisions on questions of general commercial law. The rule of

While there is strength to these arguments, the self evident meaning of "non-cumulative" is that the profits are not cumulative, whereas if a "dividend credit" is established at least the stock becomes quasi cumulative. If sufficient profits are made every year to pay the non-cumulative stockholders their agreed per cent, it would in fact be the same as "cumulative preferred stock." Most of the writers who favor the New Jersey holding contend that a "dividend credit" accrues to the stockholder where a profit is made even though it is not sufficient to pay the non-cumulative preferred stockholder the per cent specified in the certificate. For instance, if in any year the corporation makes one per cent profit above the claims of all senior stockholders, a "dividend credit" to that extent is established, even though the stock certificate provides for six per cent. In other words, under the minority holding the corporation would be compelled to keep an absolutely correct set of books-more accurate than under the numerous tax statutes-and make a book entry of the credit due the non-cumulative shareholders even though the very next year a large loss may be sustained by the company. Such a rule may be satisfactory to the public accountant, but surely not to the lawyer who wishes to simplify rather than complicate business relations and who does not want to encourage a constant potential conflict between the directors and the non-cumulative shareholders. For these reasons is not Judge Holmes' idea based on common sense and does it not reflect the intent of the parties, where non-cumulative stock is issued?

Many instances could be cited to illustrate how difficult, if not impossible, it is to determine what dividend credit the stockholder is entitled to for any one year, where the courts hold that the non-cumulative preferred stockholder is entitled in subsequent years to a dividend credit. For instance, suppose that for several years the amount set aside for depreciation of machinery or

Right to Participate with Common Stock 

Where a corporation has a large surplus and has paid the preferred stockholders the per cent specified in the stock certificate and an equal amount to the common stockholders, some authorities say that the preferred stockholders are not limited to the per cent specified in their stock agreement but that they can participate in the remaining surplus with the common stockholders.28 On the other hand, there are other cases which hold that preferred stockholders are limited to their stipulated percentage only, unless the certificate specifically provides that they will participate in the balance of the dividend.29 The contract of preferred stockholders sometimes provides for participation.30 

§ 483. 

Rights of Preferred Stockholders in General 

Preferred shares are those which give the holder some priority over another class of shareholder, and there may be as many different forms as the ingenuity of the lawyer may devise to meet the necessities of the corporation and shareholders. The priority to which the holder of the preferred shares is entitled should be clearly set out by the terms of the contract between the corporation and the class of shareholders to which he belongs. The priority may be as to dividends or principal upon dissolution, or both, all depending on the terms of the contract.31 

The certificate may provide that the holder is entitled to 6% preferred dividends each year over the common stockholders. 

Such dividends may be cumulative or non-cumulative. In absence of agreement, express or implied, that the dividends shall be cumulative, unpaid dividends in the past can not be claimed.

§ 484. 

Cumulative Preferred Shares 

When a shareholder is entitled to "cumulative" or "guaranteed" dividends each year, it is meant that his claim to dividends is not lost for the year in which no dividends are declared but will accumulate. There may be years when there are no surplus profits out of which a dividend can be declared; or the directors, in their discretion in managing the affairs of the corporation, may decide to withhold the dividend even though there are sufficient funds available for the legitimate payment of a dividend. If there is no legal fund, surplus or profits, in the corporation from which the preferred dividend can be paid, and the stock is cumulative, it can be made up in subsequent years out of net earnings.37 As against the common stockholder, the cumulative preferred stockholders have the right to the dividend, although payment must be postponed until there exists a fund from which payment can be legally made. The dividend becomes fixed and vested even though payment is deferred. The dividend cannot be paid, but the claim exists and the dividend accrues, and the amount accumulates awaiting the existence of a legal fund for its payment.38 Where the dividends are cumulative, the relationship between the stockholder and the corporation is not strictly that of debtor and creditor until the dividends are declared, even for the amounts that accrued during the lean years when no dividends were declared. But the claim of the stockholder in that case is a property right that cannot be impaired by amending the charter and tendering the stockholder

Co.,42 by the provisions of an incorporating act of 1850, the holders of preferred stock (not "guaranteed") were entitled to a preference of ten per cent per annum and that the holders of all the other stock of the company should not be entitled to participate in any future dividends of the profits of the company until the holders of the preferred stock had first been paid from the funds applicable to a dividend of ten per cent per annum. The statute did not declare what dividend the common stockholders should be entitled to. During some of the years the preferred shareholders were paid more than ten per cent, sharing an extra dividend with the common shareholders but there were eleven years in which no dividends were declared. When the company became more prosperous and was able to declare a dividend, the preferred stockholders were paid ten per cent and the common shareholders one per cent. The court held that the preferred shareholders were entitled to cumulative dividends before the common shareholders could be paid. Since the dividends were cumulative, the preferred stockholders were entitled to arrears of dividend for the "lean" years without any deduction on account of extra payments received during the prosperous years. 

In the absence of a statute as involved in this early case, courts do not agree on the interpretation of the term "cumulative dividends". Difficulties are encountered when the holder's rights depend solely upon the use of the word "cumulative". Two different situations arise with respect to payment of cumulative dividends: first, in a going concern with an existing surplus profit out of which dividends can be paid; and, second, upon dissolution when the preferred shareholders make a claim to accumulated dividends.

In connection with the first problem, whenever a going concern has a surplus or a fund out of which the directors may legally declare dividends, the holders of the cumulative preferred shares

In other words, is this surplus of capital the same as surplus profits? If it constitutes surplus profits then the cumulative preferred shareholders will be given priority when it is converted into cash and paid out in the form of dividends. On the other hand, if it constitutes capital stock of a corporation it belongs to all of its stockholders in proportion to their holdings. Upon dissolution or in liquidation, shareholders are entitled to share out of capital ratably in the absence of an agreement giving some of the shareholders preferences.44 Where the certificate of incorporation provided that, "out of the surplus profits arising from the business of the corporation the holders and owners of the preferred stock shall be first entitled to, and be paid each year, a dividend equal to six per cent, before any dividend shall be paid on the common stock; such dividend shall be cumulative. * All the remaining surplus profits of such corporation shall belong to the common stock, and be divided among the holders and owners thereof, as the board of directors shall direct. In all other respects the preferred and common stock shall be alike," it was held that the capital left on hand after the reduction of the capital stock was not surplus profit out of which the preferred shareholders could be paid for the arrears of unpaid dividend.45 The common and preferred shareholders are alike in all respects except as to dividends, unless a preference is given to one or the other by a special provision in the certificates. If the directors are empowered, and in their discretionary management decide, to distribute this surplus capital, the preferred shareholders have no legal or equitable claim upon it in satisfaction of past due and unpaid dividends. In the case cited above the court said: "But, assuming that the directors in their discretionary management of the company's affairs, concluded, and were empowered, to distribute this surplus of capital, the preferred stockholders would have no legal or equitable, claim upon it in satisfaction of past due and unpaid dividends. Courts are in conflict on the second situation where the cumulative preferred shareholders make claim to dividends when the corporation is in the process of dissolution. The Supreme Court of Delaware in upholding the claims of preferred shareholders said that there is no legal barrier to a contract whereby the preferred shareholders are to be paid, not only the principal of their stock, but also, the unpaid cumulative dividends upon dissolution and before the common shareholders are to take anything. This is held valid even though upon dissolution no surplus or profit exists or had existed. Generally, this is conceded, although it may seem that dividends are to be paid out of capital which cannot be done while the corporation is a going concern. Upon dissolution the nonexistence of a surplus does not prevent a contract giving a preference of dividends as well as of principal to the preferred shareholders.40

This question is solely one of contract between the sharehold- The court in taking this view made a distinction between the provisions of the certificate of incorporation whereby the corporation as a going concern was obligated to pay seven percent preferred dividends each year out of the surplus or net profits, and the provision relating to liquidation on dissolution which entitled the preferred stockholders to par value plus all unpaid dividends accrued thereon, before assets were distributed to the holders of the common shares. A going concern must protect the rights of its creditors as well as that of its shareholders; so it is a well known rule that dividends can not be paid when the capital of the corporation is impaired or will be by the payment of a dividend. In the process of dissolution, after the rights of creditors have been taken care of, and only the relation of stockholders inter sese is involved, the court in this case finds no obstacle to a contract dividing the remaining assets in any manner specified in the agreement of the parties. Payment is merely postponed until there exists a fund from which it can legally be made. Should such fund exist when the company goes into the hands of a receiver, preferred stockholders should receive par value of their stock plus "unpaid dividends accrued thereon." 

Such action by the receiver only gives effect to the provisions in the certificate of incorporation relative to preferred shareholders. The effect of the provision for cumulative dividends was held by the court to mean that no dividend, cumulative or otherwise, can be paid unless there is a surplus or profits available. Therefore, for the years showing a loss or no profits made, there is no accrual of cumulative dividends for those years, since no dividends could have been declared. In other words, a provision for cumulative dividends is a charge only upon surplus or profits when made and is available as a fund for payment of dividends. 

This case follows an early English case 51 holding that the dividends were payable on dissolution only to the extent that profits had been made. It is based on the theory that dividends are not in arrears unless they could have been declared. A later English case, however, removed this limitation 52 and several United States' decisions have similarly held.53 

It seems that in the Michael Cayey-Caguas Tobacco Company case the New York court was illogical in holding that the incorporation agreement, in effect, was a violation of the corporation law of the state, which says that dividends may only be paid out of surplus profits. The purpose of the statute is primarily for the protection of creditors of a corporation while doing business. 

The necessity of carefully wording the provisions which are intended to assure preferred stockholders of a claim superior to the rights of common stockholders to the repayment of their capital, and the ultimate payment of cumulative dividends there-

§ 485. 

Rights of Common and Preferred Shareholders to Participate in Surplus Profits

The shareholder's contract with the corporation upon which the holder of preferred shares has a right to share in the surplus profits should be, as a matter of good business, explicit and clear. When it is not clear as to whether the holder of preferred shares is limited to the stipulated dividend, or is entitled to participate with the holders of common shares in the surplus profits that remain after the amount of the stipulated dividend has been paid to both classes of shareholders, the courts must determine the rights of the parties. If the intention of the contracting parties can not be ascertained, the courts must devise a rule which can be applied. For example, suppose, the statute or contract provides that the preferred shareholder is entitled to a specified preferential dividend before anything is paid to the common stock but there is no provision whatever respecting their rights to share in any surplus profits in excess of the stipulated dividend. Will the contract respecting the preferred shareholder's rights be said to limit their right to the stipulated dividends or only to define in what way the preferred shares differ from common shares and in all other respects imply equality of the shareholder's rights?

This problem can be solved in one of three ways. First, after the payment of the agreed preferential dividend to the preferred 

54. Penington V. Commonwealth

Hotel Const. Corporation, 155 A. 

514, 17 Del.Ch. 394, 75 A.L.R. 1136. 398

Ch. § 485 

DIVIDENDS 

stockholders, any balance of profits will be divided pari passu among both the preferred and common shares. Second, upon payment of the designated preferred dividend a like amount will be paid to the common stock and any profits remaining will be divided equally among both the preferred and common stockholders. Third, when the preference dividend has been fully paid the entire residue of the profits will go exclusively to the common stock.

There seems to be no court that has adopted the first view giving the preferred shareholder so favorable a position in the absence of an express provision for participation in the surplus. 

Logically, if the shareholders stand on an equal basis, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, then it can be argued that the contract giving the preference changes the relation of the shareholders in that respect and in no other. In other words, the contract is not one of limitation on the rights of the preferred shareholders but only differentiates their rights as above those of the common shareholders. Although this may seem the most logical theory there is a conflict of authority on the question, some courts adopt the second view while others give preference to the third view.

In Pennsylvania, the second view is followed and the Supreme Court of that state has held that it is the right of the preferred shareholder to share pro rata with the common shareholder in the distribution of the surplus profits remaining after payment of the stipulated preference dividend, and a like annual dividend upon the common stock.55

This decision proceeds on the theory that all the shareholders are on a par except as otherwise expressly provided in the agree-

A railroad company issued preferred stock which entitled the holder to an annual non-cumulative dividend "up to, but not exceeding four percent before any dividend shall be set apart or paid upon the common stock." A preferred stockholder who had received his stipulated dividend sought to participate upon an equal basis with the common stockholders in the division of the remaining annual profits. By the end of 1914, the generally accepted business view of the situation induced many courts to reject the Pennsylvania holding, and since that time the decision by the Maine Supreme Court is the weight of authority.62 This view has been adopted [in lieu of] the general principle of equality of shareholders in sharing extra dividends. Words in contracts should ordinarily be construed according to the common meaning of the language. Contracting parties must be presumed to intend what is reasonable under the circumstances; and, if it is now understood by business men that preferred stock is limited to the preference stated in the bylaws or certificate, the courts are justified in concluding that they are not entitled to share with common stockholders in the balance of profits left after the preferred shareholders are paid the dividends specified in the agreement. But if the court reasons, as many courts have done, from the premise that all persons who become stockholders in a corporation are equal except as otherwise provided in their agreement, it is difficult to find any flaws in the reasoning of the Pennsylvania Courts. 

In this day of high finance, when all kinds of highly preferred shares are issued, it is often difficult to determine whether the certificate of stock evidences a share of stock or a bond.64 

In such case it may be true that the purchaser understands that as to dividends he is limited to the preference of a six percent cumulative dividend, and enjoys no preference upon dissolution. 

The question is would it be more reasonable to say that the preferred shareholder is a part owner of the assets of the corporation to the same extent as the common shareholder, and, therefore, should share equally with him in the balance of the dividend left after the common shareholder is paid an amount equal to what was paid to the preferred shareholder? The Texas Supreme Court is free to select the more reasonable of the above two holdings, as the point has not as yet been decided by that Court. The so-called commercial view is not as prevalent in

Where the stock is sold at different dates, the question arises as to the relative rights of the shareholders in declared dividends. 

Since 1907 all the stock of most Texas corporations must be subscribed before the charter is approved by the Secretary of State. 

But even in such corporations the corporation may forfeit some of the subscribed stock for nonpayment of the balance due, or may repurchase some of its own stock. In the case of the nonpar stock corporation, only ten percent of its stock must be initially subscribed. For these reasons a shareholder may have purchased or fully paid for his stock only a few months before the declaration of a dividend. If the corporation has been successful and has accumulated a surplus, he will pay a premium for the stock so as to equalize the rights of the parties.84 For this reason all shareholders at the date of the declaration of the dividend should be treated alike and, therefore, should share ratably in the dividend. The same rule applies to bonds convertible into stock, although the convertible privilege is not exercised until a short time before the declaration of the dividend.85

§ 488. Stock Dividends 

Where a corporation has the power to increase its capital stock, and has the assets from which it may legally declare a dividend, it may, if its interests so require, retain such assets, and issue stock therefor, instead of distributing the assets among the stockholders by declaring a dividend payable in money.88 This is called a stock dividend. It is not in the ordinary sense a dividend, a "dividend" being a distribution of the profits to stockholders as the income from their investment, while a "stock dividend" is merely an increase in the number of shares, such increase representing the same property that was represented by the smaller number of shares.89 If stock is issued to the extent of the surplus profits, and the amount paid in as the capital stock of the corporation remains intact, such dividends are not a violation of the prohibition against reducing or withdrawing the capital stock by

A stock dividend effects a transfer of the surplus profits to the capital stock of the corporation. When such a transaction takes place the surplus is "capitalized." As the number of shares of the stockholders is increased, and cash or property is not given to the stockholder, the declaration of a stock dividend is not an actual distribution of the profits of the corporation. For this reason, the Supreme Court of the United States held that a stock dividend cannot be taxed as income.92 However, in a recent case the court held that the stock dividend may be taxed as income where common stock is distributed to preferred stockholders.93 The court also held that the stock dividend could be taxed as income where a certain class of preferred stock, some of which had already been issued, was distributed to the holders of common stock.94 A dividend declared out of the surplus, payable in shares of the capital stock of another corporation, is not a stock dividend; since the mere fact that a dividend may take the shape of certificates of stock does not necessarily make it a "stock dividend."95 But a stock dividend need not be paid in the shares of

$489. Set-Off Against Debt Due to Corporation 

A corporation may retain dividends, and apply them upon debts due to it from stockholders at the time the dividend is declared.⁹7 This right does not rest upon any idea that the corporation has a lien, but it is the right of set-off, for the dividend is a debt owing by the corporation to the stockholder.98 If shares are assigned and notice of the assignment is given to the corporation before the dividend is declared, the right to the dividend passes to the assignee, and the corporation cannot set-off a debt to it from the assignor, incurred before the assignment.99 But the right of set-off prevails up to the time notice of the assignment of the stock is given to the corporation.¹

Suppose there are ten equal shareholders in the company, and the directors, without any negligence, honestly believe the company owns a clear surplus of ten thousand dollars. A dividend is declared, and the secretary hands to each stockholder a bag which supposedly contains one thousand dollars in gold money. Every piece of the coins in plaintiff's bag was counterfeit. As the directors acted honestly and not negligently, in other words, made an honest mistake, they would not be personally liable to the plaintiff, but under the rules of quasi-contract the other stockholders who received one-ninth more than they were entitled to are liable to the plaintiff for his share of the dividend. Where A owes B $100.00 and pays that amount to C thinking that he paid the money to his creditor B, the latter can recover against C.13 

Section 10 of the Restatement of Restitution and Unjust En richment provides: "If a person, intending thereby to pay a debt, has paid money to another in the mistaken belief that such other is the creditor, the person who in fact was the creditor is entitled to obtain the money from the payee, unless the payee is a bona fide purchaser or unless the payor reclaims."

Section 126 of the Restatement provides: 

"Where a person pays money or transfers property to another in the erroneous belief, induced by a mistake of fact, that he owed a duty to the other so to do, whereas such duty was owed to a third person, the transferee, unless a bona fide purchaser, is under a duty of restitution to the third person."

When the stockholder would lose his right to sue the other shareholders is also determined. In the comments to Section 126 of the Restatement it is said: "Where a person pays money to satisfy a debt or transfers property in the performance of a contract and by mistake makes a transfer to a person not entitled thereto, ordinarily he remains liable to the creditor or the other contracting party. 

If, however, the mistake was one of fact, the payor is entitled to rescind the transaction and to recover back what he has given to the transferee, thus restoring the original position of the parties. * * * This right to rescission exists as long as he is solvent, unless the third person has obtained the property from the transferee or has elected to hold the transferor solely liable. * * * 66 *** Although the transaction is one which, aside from the existence of the interests of the third person, can be rescinded, the transferor's right to rescission is subordinate to the right of the third person to obtain restitution from the transferee. 

The right of the transferor to rescind is terminated if, before he acts, the transferee makes a settlement with the real creditor or if the latter accepts the transferee's sole liability. If the transferor becomes insolvent and the payment was not a voidable preference his right to rescind the transaction is terminated, and if he makes a settlement with the transferee, the proceeds of this settlement are held on a constructive trust for the benefit of the person intended to be paid. If the transferee reconveys to the transferor without notice of the latter's insolvency, the liability of the transferee is terminated."

These rules apply to the suppositious case stated above. An action cannot be maintained against a corporation by a stockholder for a dividend, as for a debt, due, until the dividend has been declared, though there may be funds from which it is the duty of the directors to declare a dividend. "A right to a dividend from the profits of a corporation is no debt until the dividend is declared.
