It must be borne in mind in this connection that it is only in a clear and extreme case that the equity court will interfere with the discretionary powers of the directors by compelling them to declare a dividend. When a dividend has been declared payable at a definite future time, but no fund has been set apart by the directors for the payment of the dividend, and the corporation meanwhile becomes insolvent, the stockholders, to the extent of their proportions of the dividend, share ratably with the creditors of the corporation in its property.28 If a specific fund to pay a dividend, however, has been set apart, it has been held that a preferential lien exists upon it, which the stockholders can enforce to the exclusion of the general creditors of the corporation.24 As to such fund, "the stockholders are not required to go in pro rata with the general creditors for such unpaid dividends, but may proceed as against a trustee on account of such trust fund and recover the whole of their pro rata thereof."25

In this case the court said: "Is there a sound distinction between a case where a corporation disposes of its capital by issuing bonus stock, or stock partly paid for, and one where it disposes of its capital by paying dividends out of it? Both are dispositions of the corporate assets, just as transfers of the tangible assets of the corporation are. As said in the Hospes case, they are all forms of one and the same thing, all reaching the same result, a disposition of corporate assets. Indeed 

Justice Mitchell expressly includes paying dividends out of capital in his enumeration of such disposition of assets. We see no distinction.

In each case the right of a creditor to question the transaction depends wholly on whether he dealt with the corporation on the faith that its capital was as represented, and not impaired by gifts to stockholders or to others. In the case at bar it is not shown that the creditors knew of the payment of these illegal dividends when they trusted the corporation. It is not shown that they did not rely on the capital being intact. Under the Hospes and Randall Printing Co. [120 Minn. 268, 139 

N.W. 606, 43 L.R.A.,N.S., 706] cases, it is presumed that they extended credit to the corporation in reliance upon its capital being as represented. "The argument is made that defendant should not be liable because he believed the dividends were earned. This does not seem to us a feature of any importance. Defendant received assets of the corporation to which he was not entitled. 

Subsequent creditors who trusted the corporation in ignorance that its capital had been impaired by the payment of these dividends are entitled to recover on the ground of fraud, not actual fraud, but constructive fraud, fraud in law. It is surely no defense that the beneficiary of a voluntary conveyance which is fraudulent as to creditors, is himself innocent of any wrong. 

Knatvold v. Wilkinson, 83 Minn. 265, 86 N.W. 99." See 55 A.L.R. 8; 76

Assuming that the payment of the dividend is made when the corporation is insolvent, or such action renders it insolvent, when does the statute of limitations begin to run against the creditors cause of action against the stockholders? Generally the statute of limitations begins to run against causes of action sounding in fraud from the time that the fraud was discovered or, by the exercise of reasonable diligence, should have been discovered. If the stockholder has accepted the dividend in good faith, the creditor and the shareholder are free from fraudulent conduct. A majority of the courts have said that the statute of limitations begins to run as against the good faith stockholder from the date the dividend was paid.53 It has been said, however, that the same rules which are applied to the stockholder who has not fully paid for his stock should apply when an innocent stockholder received a dividend out of the capital stock.54

Ch. § 492 DIVIDENDS § 492. Apportionment of Dividends Between Life Tenants and Re maindermen-In General

Where the stock of a corporation is held by one for life with remainders over, the respective rights of the life tenants and of the remaindermen with reference to dividends has given rise to prolific litigation resulting in a mass of conflicting decisions.61 All American Courts substantially agree that the question, whether a distribution made by a corporation during the continuance of a life estate is to be regarded as income or capital, is one primarily of construction, i. e., a question of interpretation of the intention of the maker of the will or other instrument. The difficulty arises when the provisions of the instrument directing payment of dividends are not explicit enough to direct the apportionment of the dividends.62 Before launching into this veritable sea of conflicts, it would be well to sum up the instances in which the courts agree.

a. The Massachusetts Rule- 

Under the Massachusetts rule, the rights of the life tenant and the remainderman depend on the character of the dividend. In other words, all cash dividends are awarded to the life tenant, and all stock dividends go to the remainderman.68

The Massachusetts rule is essentially one of convenience, the theory being a saving of expense, even though it is admitted that under this rule the intention of the testator is not always carried out.69 The Massachusetts rule has been applied by the Supreme 

Court of the United States, and has been followed by the following state courts: Connecticut, Georgia, Illinois, Maine, North 

Carolina, Rhode Island, Ohio, Virginia, and West Virginia.70

b. The Pennsylvania Rule 

Under the Pennsylvania or American rule, the rights of the life tenant and remainderman to an extraordinary cash or stock dividend declared during the life tenancy are determined by a division of the dividend between the claimants so as to preserve intact the book value of the corpus as it existed at the testator's death. In other words, the court exacts an accounting of the estate at the time of the commencement of the life estate, and takes into account the accumulation of the earnings from which the extraordinary dividend was made; if it ascertains that the entire dividend was earned before the commencement of the life interest, the court awards the entire dividend whether stock or cash, to the remainderman. If it finds that the entire dividend was earned after the commencement and during the continuance of the life interest, the court awards such dividends to income and gives it to the life tenant, provided "the intact value of the estate" is not impaired. If accumulated partly before and partly afterwards, the court apportions the dividend, whether stock or cash, between the life tenant and remainderman." The Pennsylvania rule, subject to minor local modifications, has been adopted by the majority of the American Courts, i. e., the general idea of apportionment as set out by

c. The Kentucky Rule- 

Under the Kentucky rule, a dividend, whether of stock or cash goes to the person entitled to receive the income at the time the dividend is declared, without regard to the time when it was earned.73 Under either of the three rules, if the directions of the testator are specific, they should be enforced. Ch. § 493 

DIVIDENDS 

(a) ordinary dividends declared during the period out of earnings of the corporation are income unless the dividends are payable to those who are shareholders of record on a designated date which is not within the period; if such dividends are payable to shareholders of record on a date within the period, they are income although declared prior to the period; (b) extraordinary dividends declared during the period, whether in cash or in shares of the corporation or in other property, are income to the extent and only to the extent that they are declared out of earnings of the corporation which accrued subsequent to the creation of the trust or the acquisition of the shares by the trustee; (c) rights to subscribe to the shares or other securities of the corporation and rights to subscribe to the shares or other securities of another corporation than that whose shares are held in trust are principal whether exercised or sold by the trustee; (d) upon the total or partial liquidation of the corporation during the period, such part of the proceeds received by the trustee as represents earnings of the corporation which accrued during the period is income and the remainder is principal; (e) the earnings of a corporation not distributed by the corporation during the designated period either as dividends or on partial or total liquidation of the corporation are not income; (f) a distribution by a corporation which is a return of capital and not a distribution of earnings is principal."

§ 497. Where Two Parties Claim Stock-Bill of Interpleader 

Where two parties claim title to the stock of a corporation and the corporation is made a party to the suit brought to determine which party owns the stock, the company should not pay declared dividends to either party until the ownership of the stock is determined. It should file a bill of interpleader, if no suit has been filed. If the corporation pays the dividend to the wrong party, it can be forced to pay the amount of the dividend with interest to the rightful owner of the stock. § 531. Stockholders' Meetings-In General 

In order that the acts of a majority of the stockholders may be binding on the corporation, they must be done at a meeting of the stockholders.¹ It is only at a meeting duly held and regularly conducted that the stockholders represent the corporation. Thus, according to many cases, the assent of a majority of the stockholders to the appointment of an agent to execute a mortgage on behalf of the corporation, if expressed elsewhere than at a meeting, as where the assent of each is given separately, and at different times, to a person who goes to them privately, is invalid, and a mortgage given in pursuance thereof is uninforceable.³

§ 532. Calling Meetings 

It is generally expressly provided by the charter or by-laws who shall call stockholders' meetings, and no meeting can be legally called except in compliance therewith. If the charter and by-laws are silent on the subject, a meeting may be called by the directors or the general agent to whom is intrusted the management and control of its affairs, whenever, in their or his opinion, the condition and affairs of the corporation are such as to render a meeting necessary. If all the stockholders are present at a meeting, the fact that it was called by one not authorized will not render the proceedings invalid. If the proper officers refuse to perform their duty, positively imposed by law, to call a meeting of the stockholders for an election of directors, a stockholder may compel such performance by mandamus." how they are to vote, whether per capita or according to the amount of shares held by each. In these respects their proceedings and the validity of their acts, must be judged of according to the principles of law, applicable to corporations in general. If the two minority meetings be laid out of view as void, the whole rests upon the assent expressed by a majority of the stockholders not in a meeting of stockholders, but by each one separately and at different times, and evidenced, not by the minutes of their corporate proceedings, but by a separate paper in the possession of a committee. We cannot see in this any legal evidence of the consent of the corporation, either according to its charter or the general principles of law."

STOCKHOLDERS MEETINGS-RIGHTS § 533. Notice of Meetings 

It is essential to the validity of a stockholders' meeting, and of the acts and votes of the majority thereat, that due notice of the day, hour, and place of the meeting shall have been given personally to each stockholder, unless the stockholders were in fact all present, in person, or by proxy, or unless the time and place of the meeting were definitely fixed by statute, or by the charter or by-laws of the company, or by usage. 8 It is not enough to give notice of the day, but the notice must also specify the hour. If the meeting is a stated one-that is, if the time and place of holding the same are fixed by the charter or bylaws, or by the statute or usage-no notice is required of the time and place of holding it.10 It is immaterial in what way the time and place of a general meeting are fixed. If they have been fixed by usage, a tacit understanding of the members, or in any other way, it is enough.11 The fact that a by-law fixed the day and place for an annual meeting does not dispense with the necessity for notice, for the stockholders are entitled to notice of the hour. 12

If the meeting is a special one, notice must be given to each stockholder, not only of the time and place of meeting, but also of the business which will be transacted, and there is no power to transact any other business.13 But if the meeting is a general one-that is, for the transaction of all business within the powers of the corporation-such notice of the business is not necessary, 14 unless the business to be transacted is a fundamental change in the organization of the company." 15

But even though the meeting is a general or stated meeting, and, therefore, any ordinary business incident to the chartered powers of the corporation may be transacted without special notice to each stockholder of the purpose of the meeting, the common and better practice of many corporations is to give notice of unusual business to be acted on at such meetings.16 Stated meetings are to be regarded as general ones, unless restricted by statute, by the charter, or by-laws.17

§ 534. Time and Place of Meeting 

24 Meetings cannot be held at an unreasonable or inconvenient time or place. If a particular time or place is fixed by the charter, by-laws, or by statute, the provisions must be observed. 

As a corporation has no legal existence beyond the limits of the state by which it was created,25 at common law the stockholders cannot hold a meeting, and do strictly corporate acts, outside the state. This proposition has been laid down broadly and without qualification. The leading case on this point is Miller v. Ewer.26 In this case, under a charter granted by the state of Maine, the corporators met in the State of New York, and there organized and accepted the charter and elected officers

and directors. The directors then met in the city of New York and authorized the president and secretary to execute a mortgage on the corporate property, which was done accordingly. It was held that the action of the corporators in meeting and electing directors was a corporate act and could not be performed outside of the state of Maine; that the directors were not legally chosen; and that the mortgage, therefore, was invalid. The corporators, it was said, as natural persons, have no power to bring the corporation, the artificial being, into life and active operation unless the initial meeting is held in the state where the company was incorporated. "The charter confers upon them a new faculty for this purpose-a faculty which they can have only by virtue of the law which confers it. That law is inoperative beyond the bounds of the legislative power by which it is enacted. As the corporate faculty cannot accompany the natural persons beyond the bounds of the sovereignty which confers it, and they cannot possess or exercise it there, (they) can have no more power there to make the artificial being act, than other persons not named or associated as corporators. Any attempt to exercise such a faculty there is merely a usurpation of authority by persons destitute of it, and acting without any legal capacity to act in that manner. It follows that all votes and proceedings of persons professing to act in the capacity of corporators, when assembled without the bounds of the sovereignty granting the charter, are wholly void."""

It will be noticed that in this case the corporators named in the charter met and organized outside the state granting the charter. They did not meet and organize in the state, and then hold a meeting outside the state for the election of the directors. 27.

The decision, therefore, might well have been based on the ground that the corporation had not been legally organized, leaving untouched the question whether the stockholders of a corporation which has been duly and legally organized within the state may hold meetings and transact corporate business in another state. And this view has been taken in Missouri. In 

Ohio & M. R. Co. v. McPherson,28 the stockholders of an Illinois corporation, which had been organized in that state, held meetings and transacted corporate business in Missouri. The subscribers sought to defeat an action on their subscriptions on the ground that the calls for stock assessments were made in Missouri, and it was therefore urged that the votes and proceedings of the stockholders and directors in that state were void. 

It was held that the defense could not be sustained. The Court said: "After the corporation had become full-fledged," it was said, "I see nothing in reason or principle why the stockholders could not as well elect directors, as the directors elect a treasurer, on the Missouri side of the line. The most that could be said, under such circumstances, is that the election was irregular. The corporation having once been put into existence, if the members of the board of directors, whether charter members, or their appointees, or those elected by the stockholders in St. 

Louis, accepted their office, and acted under their appointment or election, as the evidence shows was the case, they became de facto directors, and their authority to act on behalf of the corporation could not be questioned by the appellants in this collateral suit, without showing a judgment of ouster against them in a direct proceeding by the government for that purpose. held their annual meeting in Paris, France, and elected directors for the ensuing year. In holding a by-law enacted by this board of directors to be void, the court said: "A private corporation, whose charter has been granted by one state, cannot hold meetings or pass votes, or have any legal existence in another state. It must dwell in the place of its creation, and cannot migrate to another sovereignty. "This prohibition as to the performance of acts, outside of the state where chartered, refers to acts of a strictly corporate character, such as must be discharged by the corporators themselves, such as the original organization, the election of directors, etc. 

The better opinion is, that the mere transaction of such business as is usually done by the directors or other agents of the body may be done by the directors or other agents of the body as well without the state as within it. 66 * The directors were elected at a meeting of the stockholders held in France, which election was absolutely null and void, and which was subject to collateral attack, and gave the persons elected no more power than if there had been no election whatever. The proceedings of such a meeting no court of justice could respect, no matter in what manner it might be questioned."

The Supreme Court of Texas subsequently held that the Woodmen of the World could exercise strictly corporate acts outside the state of its creation. 535. Conduct of the Meeting

The meeting of the stockholders must be conducted regularly and fairly, and regulations contained in the charter or by-laws must be observed.37 But it is not every slight and immaterial irregularity that will vitiate the proceedings. Thus, the fact that the inspectors at a stockholders' meeting are not sworn, or are not sworn in the proper manner, will not invalidate an election, if no objection is interposed at the time of the election. It is enough that they are duly appointed and enter on the discharge of their duties, and are therefore inspectors de facto.38 If the inspectors recognize a proxy where its genuineness is not assailed and enough appears from it "to give it the appearance of prima facie authenticity" the election of directors cannot subsequently be declared void because of some irregularity of the proxy.3 

It is not necessary, in the absence of some express requirement, that the clerk, moderator, inspector, or chairman chosen to preside over a stockholders' meeting shall be a stockholder or member. He acts merely as an agent of the corporation to preside and see that the proceedings are conducted in a legal and orderly by-laws providing that it shall be held at a specified place in the state, is illegal; and, as against the officers thus elected, those previously in office have the right to retain control of the affairs of the corporation. 536. Quorum and Majority

By the term "quorum" is meant the number of members of a corporation, board, committee or other body who must be present in order to take action for the party represented. Generally, by statute, or by particular charters or by-laws, persons owning a majority of the shares must be present or represented at a stockholders' meeting to constitute a quorum, and, unless there is a quorum present, no action can be taken.43 Less than a quorum should adjourn until a quorum is obtained. Since the corporation has no right to vote its treasury stock, that stock cannot be counted in determining whether a quorum is present at the stock-

It means, in the absence of a provision to the contrary, the major part of those who are present at a regular corporate meeting. "There is a distinction taken between a corporate act to be done by a select and definite body, as by a board of directors, and one to be performed by the constituent members. In the latter case a majority of those who appear may act, but in the former a majority of the definite body must be present, and then a majority of the quorum may decide. This is the general rule on the subject, and, if any corporation has a different modification of the expression of the binding will of the corporation, it arises from the special provisions of the act or charter of incorporation." 49

At a valid stockholders' meeting, the charter and by-laws being silent on the subject, a majority of the votes cast, though but a minority of the stock represented, prevails. Those having an opportunity to vote, and not voting, are held to acquiesce in the result of the votes actually cast. Therefore, if some of the members become dissatisfied, and fail or refuse to vote, a majority of the legal votes actually cast, though less than a majority of all the votes represented at the meeting, will elect.50

§ 537. Disability of Individual Stockholders 

If all of the stockholders are present, or have been duly notified, the meetings and proceedings are not rendered illegal by the fact that one of them is non compos mentis, or otherwise under legal disability. The law does not look into the capacity of the stockholders to transact business, but only regards the capacity of the aggregate body when duly assembled. "If it were otherwise," said Bigelow, J., "the legal incapacity of a stockholder, such as coverture, infancy, or insanity, would operate as an effectual obstacle to a valid assembly of any aggregate corporation. 

The law confers the attribute of individuality on the entire body constituting a corporation, and in which the individuals composing it are merged. When duly assembled, the corporation itself becomes the individual or person whose acts and proceedings the law can alone regard. If, therefore, it is legally called together, the law presumes that the individual members are competent for the transaction of business."57 

§ 538.

§ Ch. 12 STOCKHOLDERS MEETINGS-RIGHTS 540. Presumption of Regularity. 

Every reasonable intendment is to be made in favor of the regularity of stockholders' meetings, and the burden is upon the one who claims that they are invalid to show the circumstances rendering them so. In the absence of evidence to the contrary, their legality will be presumed. "The maxim of law in such cases is, 'Omnia rite acta praesumuntur.' "70 Thus, it has been held that, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, it will be presumed that due notice was given to all the stockholders." Where the by-laws of a corporation required the meetings to be held at the counting room of the company, and it appeared from the records that a meeting was held at the dwelling house of the general agent, without stating that it was at the counting room, it was presumed that the counting room was, for the time being, at such place. It will be presumed that a quorum of members was present, unless the contrary clearly appears.73 

§ 541. Adjourned Meetings 

A corporation may transact any business at an adjourned meeting that could have been transacted at the original meeting, for it is but a continuation of the same meeting. § 542. Equity Jurisdiction 

A court of equity has jurisdiction to supervise and control an election of directors, and to appoint a master for that purpose, when it appears that through fraud, violence, or other unlawful conduct on the part of a portion of the corporators, a fair and honest election cannot be held without the court's intervention.""

It has been held that, if an election is held illegally, a court of equity has jurisdiction to set it aside at the suit of a dissenting stockholder. But, by the better opinion, some other ground for equitable relief must exist, for otherwise the remedy at law by quo warranto would be adequate. A court of equity will not primarily take jurisdiction to determine the legality of an election of directors, or to remove a director who is in possession of the office. It will inquire into the regularity of the election, or the right of the person to the office, only when the question arises incidentally and collaterally in a suit of which the court has right-

§ 543. Expulsion of Members 

Joint-stock companies and corporations organized for gain have no power to remove or expel their stockholders, unless the power to do so is expressly conferred upon them by charter or by agreement with their members.81 In the case of other corporations, however, they have the power to remove members for good cause, provided the charter or statutory provisions are not thereby violated. This power need not be expressly conferred by the charter. It is an incident to every corporation other than a corporation for gain.82 It is, in its nature, really consequential upon the powers expressly granted.83 Questions as to the nature and extent of this power have frequently arisen in connection with incorporated clubs, literary and medical societies, benevolent societies, boards of trade, and labor unions. 

The power can only be exercised for good cause, and it must be for some offense that has an immediate relation to the duties of the party as a member, or for an offense of an infamous character, indictable at law, and of which the party has been convicted. And a by-law or rule authorizing expulsion for a less cause is void.8+ "It appears to be well settled that when the

In upholding the expulsion of the member the court said, "When, therefore, persons enter into organizations for purposes of social intercourse or pleasure or amusement, and lay down rules for their government, these must form the measure of their rights in the premises, and it is vain to appeal to the Bill of Rights against their own agreements." The court by way of dictum said: "When membership in certain societies confers upon the individual important benefits or peculiar advantages in trade or business-such rights are protected by the law of the land, and are generally secured in some way by the charter."

This dictum was employed by the court in Cotton Jammers' & Longshoremen's Ass'n No. Two v. Taylor,89 to require notice to the member about to be expelled. The court in this case said: "The case before us is one involving valuable rights. In such cases the weight of authority tends to support the doctrine that a by-law providing for expulsion without notice or trial will be held invalid.-A by-law to be valid, must be reasonable.-An unreasonable by-law has been held binding as a contract when assented to by a member,-and this rule enables us more clearly to distinguish the Manning Case,-from the case under consideration. In the absence of any by-law, there could be no such assent. The contention of appellant that the acts of expulsion were binding upon appellee is not tenable." 

It seems that the courts will not interfere in favor of a person expelled without notice or trial unless it be to protect "some 'distinct, individual property right under a contract or other obligation of the association' with its member as such, and that if the right is only incidental to membership it is not such a distinct and individual right as will authorize the assumption of jurisdiction on the part of the courts and the granting of such relief." However, the constitution or by-laws usually provide that notice must be given to the affected member and that he shall be given an opportunity to be heard, and in such case the by-law is effective.90

544. Remedies of Members Wrongfully Expelled 

It is the general rule that the courts will not interfere with such societies by directing or controlling them as to questions of internal policy, except to protect pecuniary or property rights of their members.93 In Screwmen's Benevolent Association v.

Benson⁹ the court said: "By uniting with the society, the member assents to and accepts the constitution, and impliedly binds himself to abide by the decision of such boards as that instrument may provide, for the determination of disputes arising within the association. The decisions of these tribunals, when organized under the constitution, and lawfully exercising these powers, though they involve the expulsion of a member, are no more subject to collateral attack for mere error than are the judgments of a court of law. But if the tribunal act illegally; if it declare a sentence of expulsion for an offense for which that penalty is not provided by the constitution and laws of the association; and if there be no right of appeal, within the association, reserved for the redress of the injury,-the courts will review the proceedings, and, if found illegal, will treat them as null, and restore the member to his privileges as such."

The right to vote the stock is suspended while it is so held.2 27 It has been held that a corporation which has purchased shares in another corporation may not vote them.28 But, on principle, when the laws of the state in which a corporation is organized authorize the holding by it of stock in other corporations, a corporation holding stock in another corporation may vote the stock to the same extent as any individual stockholder could do.29 In many states this result is fortified by express statutory provisions conferring upon corporate stockholders all the rights, powers and privileges of individual stockholders.30 $549.

However, if two or more persons are merely joint owners of stock in their own right it would not seem unreasonable for the courts to permit the majority of the co-owners to vote the stock. The cases cited above are all of the cases that discuss this question, and while they are not entirely satisfactory, yet they certainly hold that the rule with reference to co-trustees, applies to individual joint owners.

If one trustee dies, may the other trustee or trustees vote the stock at the stockholders' meetings? Vernon's Ann.Civ.St. art. 

2580, provides that "where two or more persons hold an estate, real, personal or mixed, jointly, and one joint owner dies before severance, his interest in said joint estate shall not survive to the remaining joint owner or joint owners, but shall descend to, and be vested in, the heirs or legal representatives of such deceased joint owner in the same manner as if his interest had been severed and ascertained." The Texas courts have not decided the above question. The Supreme Court of 

Alabama, under a statute that is identical with the above Texas statute, held that the survivor could vote the stock. If stock is owned by a partnership the surviving partner has the right to vote the stock.40 Executors, administrators, and trustees may give a proxy to a third party where they expressly direct how the votes shall be cast, but cannot give a proxy which permits the agent to vote as he pleases.41 The reason for this rule is that fiduciaries cannot delegate authority that contemplates the exercise of judgment, discretion or skill. But executors, administrators and even co-trustees may appoint a joint fiduciary as proxy to vote stock held jointly by them even in the absence of a statute, by-law or charter provision which declares that when two or more persons shall hold an estate, real or personal, jointly, and one joint tenant dies before severance, his interest in the joint estate shall not survive to the remaining joint tenant or joint tenants, but shall descend to, and be vested in, his heirs or other legal representatives, in the same manner as if his interest had been severed and ascertained: 

Clay's Di 169. This act, however, only applies to such joint tenants as hold the absolute property in their own right, and not to those who hold as trustees merely, or in autre droit. The evil that our statute intended to remedy was, to cut off the jus accrescendi, or right of survivorship, which existed at the common law, and to give to the heirs at law of joint tenants the interest of their ancestors, in the same manner as if they had held as tenants in common, and not as joint tenants. 

It was thought unreasonable that the death of one joint tenant should give the entire estate to the survivor for his own use, to the exclusion of the heirs or next of kin of the deceased tenant. But when the tenants hold as trustees for particular purposes, or in autre droit, and can gain no advantage to themselves by the right of survivorship, then they are not within the reason of the statute, nor does the evil exist which it intended to remedy, for no profit or benefit will result to the survivor, and although he take, by the death of his co-tenant, the entire legal title, yet he will hold it as trustee, or in the right of another, and for his use and benefit.

Joint trustees are not within the reason of the statute, nor the evil intended to be remedied by it, and to hold that their joint title is affected by the act, could be productive of no good; it could avoid no evil, but, on the contrary, might often lead to protracted litigation, and serious injury to the trust estate. It is a well settled principle of law, that if a power, coupled with a trust, be given to two or more, it may be executed by one who has survived the others."

Restrictions in Charter or Statute 

The right to vote may be restricted by the charter or by statute. Sometimes it is expressly provided, for instance, that nonresident stockholders of particular corporations shall not be allowed to vote at meetings of the stockholders. The object of such a provision is to prevent corporations from being controlled by nonresidents. Often the number of votes which a single stockholder shall be allowed to cast is limited. The object is to prevent the corporation from being controlled by a single person unless he owns all its stock.45 551. 

- Evasion of Statutory or Charter Prohibition 

Where, by statute or by the charter, particular stockholders are prohibited from voting, the prohibition cannot be evaded by transferring the stock to others merely for the purpose of enabling them to vote the stock. Thus, where the charter of a corporation provided that no stockholder should be entitled to cast more than one-fourth of all the votes at an election of directors, it was held that a stockholder who owned more than one-fourth of the shares could not gratuitously transfer part of the stock for the purpose of enabling the transferee to vote it. Indeed, it has been said that the custom of giving the shareholders in corporations a vote for each share has become so well established that an intention to follow the custom may be implied, in the absence of any indication to the contrary.54 And it has 

53. Fletcher, Cyc.Corps. Vol. V. § 

2045 (Per.Ed.). In this section 

Fletcher says: "At common law, since the members of a corporation were entitled to equal rights, each member was entitled to one vote and no more, and this is still the rule in the case of nonstock or membership corporations. In the absence of express provisions, it has been held that the rule still applies to corporations having a capital stock divided into shares, and that a stockholder has only one vote, however many shares he may own, and not a vote for each share. The soundness of this is at least doubtful. The common-law rule was adopted with respect to public corporations and private corporations not having a capital stock, and at a time when joint stock corporations were unknown, and was based upon the ground that all the members of a corporation, since they were equally interested, were entitled to an equal voice in its affairs. The rules of the common-law change as conditions change, and, by the application of common-law principles to new conditions, new common-law rules arise. It follows that a commonlaw rule, adopted with reference to nonstock corporations, in which all the members were equally interested, giving each member a single vote, cannot properly be applied to a new kind of corporation, not known at the time the rule was adopted, in which some members have a greater interest than others. Cessante ratione, cessat et ipsa lex. On the contrary, the principle of the common law that each member of a corporation in which each has an equal interest is entitled to an equal vote, if logically applied to the new kind of corporations-joint stock corporations-will give to stockholders a vote for each share. Even aside from this view, the common usage in giving a vote for each share would seem to be sufficient ground for implying an intention on the part of the legislature, in the absence of express provision to give each share a vote."

 554. Cumulative Voting 

1158

In some states, in order to allow the minority of the stockholders to secure representation on the board of directors, there are statutory or constitutional provisions allowing cumulative voting. Thus, it is provided in West Virginia that, "in all elections for directors or managers of corporations, every stockholder shall have the right to vote the number of shares of stock owned by him for as many persons as there are directors or managers to be elected, or to cumulate said shares, and give one candidate as many votes as the number of directors multiplied by the number of his shares of stock shall equal, or to distribute them, on the same principle, among as many candidates as he shall think fit." 

The above statute is typical of the statutes of the other states. 

Where cumulative voting is given by a statute each stockholder may cast all of his voting strength to one director, or may distribute his votes among two or more of the candidates for the directorate. If the stockholders are permitted to vote cumulatively, to determine the number of votes each may cast, the number of shares owned by a stockholder is multiplied by the number of the directors to be elected. By this method of voting in many cases a rather small minority is enabled to elect one or more of the directors.59 By some authorities the right to cumulative voting does not exist unless expressly given by a statute or a constitutional provision of the incorporating state.60 One court said:

According to the authorities discussed in previous paragraphs of this treatise, the common law rule could be changed by a charter or by-law provision, even in the absence of a statute or constitutional provision authorizing the shareholders to vote by shares. In other words, even at common law the shareholders had the right to vote at all shareholders' meetings, and, therefore, such right is inherent in every corporation and exists in the absence of a statute or constitutional provision in the state where the corporation was chartered. How the shareholders shall vote, and the number of votes each shareholder is entitled to, are matters that affect the shareholders only and not the public, or creditors of the company. It would therefore seem that, as an original question, the shareholders should be permitted to determine by a by-law or a charter provision whether the shareholders can cumulate their votes. In the latest edition of Fletcher 65 it is said: "In the absence of express provision therefor, a stockholder has no right thus to cumulate his votes; but the right is frequently given by the charter or by-laws of a corporation, or by a general statute, and in some jurisdictions it is given by a constitutional provision." The author has examined all the cases cited by Fletcher for his statement of the law, but none of them holds directly that the right to cumulate their votes may be given to the stockholders by a by-law or charter provision in the absence of a statute or constitutional provision authorizing such voting. This is an important question in Texas and the Supreme 

Court is free to adopt either view, especially as the cases cited for the rule that the right must be given by a statute or constitutional provision, are very unsatisfactory and what is said in the opinions on this question is dictum since in most states statutes have been passed authorizing the stockholders to cumulate their votes.66

556. Voting Trusts and Pooling Agreements 

How far it is possible to tie up a majority of the stock of a corporation by a surrender on the part of the stockholders of the voting power so that the control may be secured for the support of a continuous policy of management, is a question on which the authorities are not in agreement. Such a result has been attempted in various ways: sometimes by an agreement between stockholders to vote together, sometimes by an agreement by which proxies are given to trustees with power to vote as they may be directed or may determine, sometimes by an agreement by which the stock is transferred to trustees with power to vote.93 A voting trust might be defined as an arrangement whereby the stockholders, or a portion of them, transfer their shares of stock to trustees, who thereby acquire the right to vote said stock, and in return trust certificates are given to the shareholders, these certificates being transferable, like stock certificates are, subject, however, to the trust agreement.94 Some

Ch. § 557 

STOCKHOLDERS-MEETINGS RIGHTS § 557. Effect of Illegal Reception or Rejection of Votes 

When illegal votes are offered, an objection must be raised at the time. If they are not challenged, their acceptance will trust to be contrary to public policy, and six dissented. Swayze, J., dissenting, however, said: "If the only object to the voting trust is to secure permanency of management, with a view to what the stockholders honestly consider to be the best interests of the corporation, I see no objection to the adoption of any necessary means authorized by the statute to secure that end. When it is said that the stockholder of a corporation is entitled to the benefit of the judgment of every other stockholder in the management of the affairs of the corporation, it cannot be meant that he is entitled to hamper in any way the free and honest exercise of his fellow stockholders' judgment. He may on each occasion act as he chooses, and, as Chief 

Justice Holmes intimated in Brightman v. Bates, 175 Mass. 105, 55 N.

E. 809, the question is whether it is unlawful to contract to do what it is perfectly lawful to do. The legality of the purpose must depend upon the good faith of the stockholder, and upon whether his purpose is the general welfare of the corporation. 

If it is, I cannot believe that purpose is made illegal merely because he may think that the general welfare of the corporation will be promoted by securing permanency of management for a long series of years. The fact that the voting power is surrendered for a long series of years may be an important, or even a controlling, fact in determining the question of good faith of the stockholder. A case may readily be conceived where such action would indicate bad faith, and a desire to secure an advantage of a fellow 

2 HILDEBRAND TEX.CORP.-32 

497 stockholder, rather than the good of the corporation. But can it be contended that, if a corporation finds it necessary to borrow money upon bonds issued for a long term of years, the stockholders cannot, consistently with public policy, in order to secure the loan, vest the management of the corporation in hands satisfactory to the lenders and for a term commensurate with the loan? 

Nor do I think that it can be said to be contrary to public policy for stockholders to combine for a long term of years, because such a combination may enable a minority to control the corporation. Practically the only way in which holders of small amounts of stock can protect themselves at all is by means of a combination by which they act together. If this is not permitted to them, large stockholders, even though they may not hold a majority of the stock, will possess a great advantage in the management of the corporate affairs, and I cannot see how public policy is violated by allowing small stockholders to make their union effective by making it endure for more than three years."

afford no ground for setting the election aside.10 Before a stockholder can complain that his vote was not taken at a stockholders' meeting, he must show that he offered to vote, or that he properly presented his claim of right to vote, and that it was excluded.11

A stockholder may by mandamus compel inspectors of an election to receive votes entitled to be cast.12 If the charter and by-laws prescribe no different rule, and the meeting appoints no tellers or inspectors for the purpose, it is for the meeting to determine, in the first instance, who can vote. The president of the corporation or chairman of the meeting has no right to determine that issue. One who, upon an adverse opinion expressed by the proper officer, refrains from offering his vote, and does not present his claim of right to the members for their decision, cannot be heard afterwards to complain.13

It is not a valid objection to an election that illegal votes were received, or legal votes rejected, unless the majority is thereby changed.14 To set aside an election on such a ground, it must be made to appear affirmatively that the majority would be changed if only legal votes had been cast. Such a result will not be presumed.15

Powers of Stockholders 

By statute in Texas the general management and control of the corporation is vested in the board of directors.18 The above statute does not attempt to vest all corporate powers in the board of directors. The directors' powers extend to purchase, encumbrance, or alienation of corporate property, the making of bonds, contracts, and other obligations of the corporation, and to every other corporate power relating to the business affairs of the corporation. These powers as a general rule cannot be exercised by the stockholders. Extraordinary and unusual powers not relating to the ordinary business transactions of corporations remain in the stockholders as a body. § 

559. Power of the Majority

When shares in a corporation are acquired by a person, no matter what the manner of acquisition, he impliedly agrees to be bound by the will of the majority, so long as they act bona fide and for the best interest of the corporation. The theoretical justification for this yielding to the will of the majority is found in the terms of the contract stated to exist between the stockholders and the corporation as embodied in the charter, by-laws and statutes. The practical justification is found in the need for efficiency in and the expedition of business. The corporation must function. It is better to reach an erroneous decision than for the business to come to a halt by reason of inaction.

To this general rule there are certain exceptions or limitations. 

Machen 25 has summed up these restrictions in the following language: "(1) The action of the majority, to be valid, must be within the powers of the corporations—that is to say, not ultra vires of the company. (2) The majority may be expressly restrained by statute or by a valid regulation of the company from exercising some power which is conferred upon the corporation, the assent of two-thirds or three-fourths of the shareholders, or some other proportion greater than a mere majority being required. (3) The majority must act honestly and not fraudulently; for while the majority, however mistaken they may be in respect to the course dictated by the interests of the company, cannot be controlled so long as they confine themselves within the powers of the corporation and their own power (which with the exception just mentioned are coextensive with the powers of the corporation), yet if they are actuated by fraudulent motives, the courts will treat their action as in excess of their powers." 

In Texas, the general management of corporate affairs is vested in the board of directors.26 Since this is true, no cases have been found where the majority of the stockholders, as such, have attempted to perform an ultra vires act. Similarly, situations where a majority of stockholders, as such, have attempted to deal fraudulently with the corporation's affairs have not arisen.28 

That they would be required to act honestly and fairly is recognized.29 25.

"The breach of duty or conduct of officers and directors which would authorize in a proper case the court's interference in suits of this character (by a single stockholder) is that which is characterized by ultra vires, fraudulent, and injurious practice, abuse of power, and oppression on the part of the company or its controlling agencies, clearly subversive of the rights of the minority or of a shareholder, and which, without such interference, would leave the latter remediless."

By giving the directors the general management of the corporation, the legislature did not deprive the stockholders of their inherent power over fundamental alterations of the corporate purpose or structure.31 The statutes do prescribe the procedure that the stockholders are to follow in the exercise of certain powers, and these statutes may not be abrogated by either the charter or the by-laws.32

The majority may ratify and validate the acts of the directors even though the directors were personally interested in the transaction, if the act of the directors was not prohibited by a statute or the common law nor against public policy, and provided their act was not induced by fraud. The resulting effect of their act must not be oppressive nor a hard bargain for the corporation,33 but fair.

The majority cannot use their superior strength to control the corporation for their own benefit and profit where they act fraudulently. If the majority attempts to do this, they may be enjoined or compelled to answer in damages to the corporation, and this is true notwithstanding the particular act done, or contemplated, may not be beyond the powers conferred on the corporation by its charter.34

What expenditures the directors may make to acquaint the stockholders of the policies for which the directors stand, is a question that has not been raised very often. In a recent Delaware case it was said: "I quite agree with the proposition that if all that is at stake is the ambition of the 'ins' to stay in, the corporation should not be called upon to pay for the expense of their campaign to persuade the voting stockholders to rally to their support. "But if the so-called 'ins' are engaged in answering attacks against their re-election because of a position they have taken upon some matter of important concern to the corporation, I am unable to see why they should not be permitted to make the same sort of expenditure from the corporate funds in defense of their offices as they would if their policy were under attack in a manner entirely disassociated from individuals."35 In this case the court held that the directors may send literature to the stockholders setting forth the policies of the directors and enclose blank proxies to be used at the next meeting of the stockholders and charge such expense to the operation of the business.

In the case of St. Regis Candies, Inc. v. Hovas 44 the Supreme

Court held that a corporation could issue stock without the voting privilege except where the statute of incorporation expressly or impliedly gives the stockholder the voting right. In a dictum the court intimated that in at least three instances of fundamental changes all the stockholders had a right to vote. The reason given for this dictum was that in old article 1330 and articles 1332 and 1387 providing for the increase and decrease of the stock of a corporation and its dissolution, the statute provided for a certain percent vote "of all its stock" or "all its outstanding stock."

In the opinion the Court said: "The fact that the Legislature, in execution of the command given, made specific provision for voting rights in what we have called the exceptional situations and omitted provision therefor in other cases is not without cogency. 

With the exact subject of voting-rights present in the minds of the lawmakers, a specific enactment for named conditions and silence in respect to other conditions would seem to indicate a purposed omission in deference to liberty of contract." writer doubts that the Legislature intended to give shareholders without voting rights the voting privilege even in the above instances and all other cases where the statute provided for a vote of a certain per cent of "all the stock". When the above three articles were enacted in Texas the lawyers and legislators were not familiar with stock without the voting privilege, and wherever the statutes have been amended in recent years the Legislature has substituted for "all stock" the phrase "stock entitled to vote" or some similar expression.45 If the legislators knew nothing about shares without the voting privilege when the above articles were enacted surely they did not intend to give the voting right to stock issued in the future without the voting privilege. Men cannot intend to do what they do not know exists. They may do such a thing, but certainly there is no instant intention to accomplish an end they have never thought of.

The by-laws of a corporation may be altered, changed, or amended by a majority vote of the stockholders at any election or special meeting ordered for that purpose by the directors, on a written application of a majority of the stockholders.40 46 

§ 561. Majority Stockholders as Fiduciaries 

The general rule is well settled that a stockholder may vote to ratify a contract in which he is interested,47 even though it is a voidable contract.48 But if the directors are guilty of fraud, the majority stockholders cannot ratify the fraud. It takes the unanimous vote of all the stockholders to ratify a fraudulent transaction.49 Of course, if the transaction be only voidable for some reason such as by reason of irregularities in the make up of the board or otherwise, or by reason of the directors or some of them being personally interested in the subject matter of the contract or act, or for some other similar reason, the majority may ratify the transaction.50 In many cases it is said that the majority sustains a fiduciary relation to the corporation and to the minority in their dealings with the corporation and the exercise of their controlling power.51 And if the majority stockholders take

While there are conflicting statements in the decisions as to whether the majority stockholders are under fiduciary obligations to the minority, a survey of the decided cases leads one to the undoubted conclusion that the fiduciary relation is invoked against the majority stockholders who in fact direct the affairs of the corporation as distinguished from those who merely have the power to elect controlling directors. This distinction was made in Robotham v. Prudential Insurance Company 54 where the .court said: "Authorities have been cited to support the proposition that an individual or a corporation holding a majority of the capital stock of another corporation sustains, by reason of such holding, a fiduciary relation to the minority stockholders, But these authorities only hold, in effect, that the fiduciary relation arises when the majority stockholder assumes control of the corporation and dictates the action of the directors. The majority stockholder is not made a trustee for the minority stockholder in that they shall not dishonestly exercise the legal power which they have, to secure an advantage to themselves over the minority. § 563. Right to Inspect Books and Papers of the Corporation- At Common Law 

Stockholders, as owners of the corporation, are entitled to reliable information as to its condition and affairs and the manner of conducting its business. To secure such information they are, as a general rule, entitled at common law to inspect the books and records of the corporation containing such information. Usually this right will be enforced in favor of the stockholder by mandamus, the inspection to be had at reasonable times.67 However, the * * a

common-law right is not unlimited or absolute in any sense of the word. The old English rule, supported by very little American authority, withheld the right unless the petitioner showed some particular matter in dispute.co 

The majority rule in the United States, in the absence of statutory regulation, gives the stockholder the right of inspection of the books if he demands an inspection at a reasonable time and place, for a proper purpose, and does not want the information through idle curiosity or to injure the company. There is no requirement that he show some dispute. But if the corporation proves that he requests an inspection of the books for a purpose in no way connected with the business of the corporation, through idle curiosity, or for the purpose of using the information for a competing company, the request will be denied.6⁹ 

§ 564.

The corporation cannot defeat the stockholders' right of inspection by showing that the stockholders were furnished full information as to the financial condition of the company through its annual financial statement and copies of annual audits made at its instance." Nor is the fact that the stockholder hopes to find something alarming in the affairs of the company, which he intends to communicate to other stockholders, any reason for denying him his right of inspection.78 In fact, the stockholder may examine the books in order to secure the names and addresses of the other stockholders and notify them of conditions in the corporate management which he regards as prejudicial to the best interest of the corporation and its stockholders.79

In a recent case the Court of Civil Appeals held that a shareholder in a holding company had a right to inspect the books of both the parent and subsidiary corporations where the subsidiary corporation was an agent of the holding company. The plaintiff brought the suit against both corporations, and served the subsidiary as party defendant and as agent for the holding company. The court held that the service was valid, and that plaintiff was entitled to inspect the books of both companies.83

In section 308, High's Extraordinary Legal Remedies (1874) it is said: "Mandamus is the appropriate remedy to enforce the rights of corporate stockholders and members to an inspection of the books and records of the incorporation, and the writ will issue for this purpose upon a proper showing of the relator's right and a refusal on the part of the corporate authorities to allow the inspection. Thus, the writ will be granted to compel the cashier of a bank to submit the books of the bank to the inspection of one of the directors. Nor is it sufficient ground for refusing the mandamus, that the book which it is sought to inspect is a book of accounts between the company and its shareholders, and therefore regarded as confidential, or that the information which it contains might be used for improper purposes." 1 Sup- a stockholder had an absolute right to inspect the books. pose the Legislature by statute gives equity jurisdiction in this matter, as has been done in many states-will the Supreme Court of Texas hold, as it did in the Moore case with reference to mandamus, that the plaintiff must come into the equity court with clean hands before a mandatory injunction will be granted? Besides, if the Texas statutes give a stockholder an absolute right to inspect the books, why could the stockholder not resort to the doctrine of self help? The stockholders are the "ultimate owners" of the property of the corporation.90 If they have the absolute right to inspect their own property, why can they not use all force necessary to accomplish that result? It seems to the author that the Legislature never intended to allow the blackmailer, or a stockholder who wishes to sell the information acquired, the privilege or “right” of inspecting the books, and, therefore, the Supreme Court should follow the cases cited above which hold that even under a statute the stockholder's right is not absolute. All so-called absolute rights have an ending. In the American Mortgage Company-Rosenbaum caseº¹ the court said: "The principle involved in this case is not new, but, on the contrary, is very old, very simple, and very fully in accord with good sense and common honesty; that is to say, one may possess a legal right, unconditional in character, with respect to the enforcement of which he may avail himself of all legal remedies applicable thereto, and, still, if the results which must attend and follow the enforcement are such as will shock the conscience of a court of equity, that court, if asked to issue its mandatory injunction as an aid to such enforcement, should, in the exercise of a sound discretion, deny the application and leave the party to pursue his legal remedies. Extraordinary writs are issued by courts of equity to prevent and correct wrongs, but are not employed to promote wrongs." By the bet-

§ 570.

By-Laws 

The office of a by-law is to regulate the conduct and define the duties of the members of the corporation to the corporation and between themselves.⁹ A by-law has been defined as "a permanent and continuing rule for the government of the corporation and its officers." 10 The proper office of by-laws is to regulate the transaction of the incidental business of the corporation." Every private business corporation has the implied power to make by-laws. The power is often expressly conferred by the charter or by statute, but this is not at all necessary, for the power is always implied.12 Primarily, the power to make by-laws is in the majority of the stockholders.13 But a statute or charter may authorize the board of directors to make them.14 The stockholders may also through passing a by-law

The by-laws of corporations, and especially fraternal benefit associations, clubs, literary societies and religious corporations, may prescribe the qualifications requisite for membership.23 gain. By uniting with the society the member assents to and accepts the constitution and impliedly binds himself to abide by the decision of such boards as that instrument may provide for the determination of disputes arising within the association. 

The decisions of these tribunals, when organized under the constitution and lawfully exercising their powers, though they involve the expulsion of a member, are no more subject to collateral attack for mere error than are the judgments of a court of law. But if the tribunal act illegally-if it declare a sentence of expulsion for an offense for which that penalty is not provided by the constitution and laws of the association, and if there be no right of appeal within the association reserved for the redress of the injury, the courts will review the proceedings, and if found illegal will treat them as null, and restore the member to his privileges as such. But if there be a right of appeal, should a mandamus be awarded before that remedy has been exhausted? We think not."

law.28 A by-law cannot affect the jurisdiction of courts, as fixed by law, nor impair the right to sue.29 But if the by-law does not completely bar the member from resorting to the courts, it will be upheld. For instance, if it forces the member to appeal to the governing body before resorting to the courts for relief, especially if such body is resorted to merely as a fact-finding body, the by-law is valid and must be complied with where the remedies provided are reasonable.30 Nor can it give the corporation the power to declare shares forfeited for nonpayment of calls.31

To be reasonable, and therefore to be valid, by-laws must be general; that is, they must not be directed against particular individuals, nor in favor of particular individuals, but must operate equally upon all to whom they apply. In Budd v. Multnomah St. Ry. Co.,32 the directors of a corporation passed a resolution to forfeit and sell the shares of a particular individual for nonpayment of assessments. The sale was sought to be upheld under a statute requiring a by-law to authorize such sales.

Nor can a by-law impose upon a stockholder, without his consent, any new liability. Thus where neither the charter of a corporation, nor any general statute, imposes on the individual members a liability to pay its debts, such liability cannot be imposed by a by-law to which he does not consent.46 A person becoming a member of a corporation after a by-law has been adopted, prohibiting members from doing certain things, is bound thereby. It is a part of his contract, and he cannot object to it on the ground that it deprives him of vested rights.¹ 

A by-law which consists of several distinct and independent parts may be valid as to one part, though void as to the others. 

Thus, where a by-law of a mutual insurance company provided that in case of loss, if the assured should not acquiesce in the determination by the directors of the amount thereof, any action for the loss claimed must be brought within four months after such determination, in a proper court in the county in which the office of the company was established, it was held valid as to the limitation of time for suing, though void in so far as it affected the jurisdiction of courts.48

Adoption

Article 1326,56 provides that the directors may adopt by-laws for the government of the corporation, and that the by-laws may be amended, changed, or altered by a majority vote of the stockholders. The inquiry arises, whether article 1326 precludes stockholders from initiating by-laws. Is article 1326 such as to exclude stockholders altogether from taking the initiative or is it merely cumulative? It would seem that article 1326 is merely cumulative of the common law. Effect as to Third Persons 

In so far as a by-law of a corporation is in the nature of a contract, the parties thereto are the corporation, upon the one side, and the individual members, upon the other. The right of any third person to establish a legal claim through a by-law depends upon whether he contracted with reference to it. If he did not, then it does not enter into his contract, and he cannot claim the benefit of it. Thus, where the members of a corporation signed a by-law by which they pledged themselves, in their individual as well as their collective capacity, for all moneys that might be loaned to the company, it was held that a person who loaned money to the company could not hold a member individually liable by virtue of the by-law, where there was no evidence that the loan was made on the credit of it.70

Nor, on the other hand, can a by-law impose liabilities on third persons who contract with the corporation without reference to it, or deprive third persons of their legal rights against the corporation." Thus, a by-law of a bank cannot take from a depositor the right to money deposited by him, but which, by mistake

court in denying relief said: "There are two reasons why the defendant corporation cannot be held: 1. Because plaintiff knew at the time that the corporation did not own the property; 

2. Because the secretary was not authorized to bind the corporation in a contract of sale." The court said further that, "the by-laws contained a provision that no purchase or sale of realty shall be consummated without consent of the board of directors. * * * A corporation, being a creature of the law, must act and be bound as the law provides. Parties dealing with it are charged with the duty of knowing this. They must know that whatever power the agent has is derived from the board of directors." The court did not say that the plaintiff was charged with notice of the by-laws, only that the plaintiff was charged with knowledge of the fact that the management of the corporate affairs were in the hands of a board of directors. The law gives the directors control of corporate affairs, and there is nothing singular in charging even the public at large with knowledge of the law.

In the Denton Milling case,83 no mention whatsoever was made relative to charging third persons with notice of the by-laws. 

In that case plaintiff, a former manager, sued defendant corporation for breach of a contract of employment and for recovery on certain notes which the secretary had given him in payment of his salary. The contract of employment was for five years, but the by-laws provided that the directors were to be elected annually. The court held that since the statute requires corporations to be managed by a board of directors, manifestly a board of directors who hold office for one year, do not have authority to control future directors in their employment of a manager. 

In the Cleburne case,84 the Court of Civil Appeals reversed and remanded a judgment for plaintiff where the trial court had refused to allow in evidence the by-laws of the corporation which would show whether the president had authority to make the

The First National Bank case,85 has absolutely no connection with the proposition for which it was cited by Texas Jurisprudence. In that case a Hotel Company was organized and doing business. Its secretary gave a note to plaintiff as accommodation indorser; defendant took with notice that it was accommodation paper. The court held the corporation not liable, saying, "The Hotel Company was not a trading or manufacturing corporation," and there had been no holding out by the corporation, of the maker of the note, or at least not to the plaintiff's knowledge. The only reference to a by-law in this case was made when the court threw it in as a further reason for its judgment saying, "besides the by-laws of appellee require both the president and secretary to sign." This was simply a case where the plaintiff relied on agency by estoppel and failed to prove it. The reader should note particularly, the last paragraph of the court's opinion.

It is believed that Texas will, when the proper case presents itself, follow the better reasoned cases and the great weight of authority, that third persons are not charged with knowledge of these rules passed for the internal management of the corporation's affairs. In line with this view, the Commission of Appeals said, "The by-laws of the average corporation are not usually open for public inspection; hence, the public trading with it can have no notice of their contents." 86 § 575. 

Repeal and Amendment 

A corporation generally has the power to repeal by-laws and enact new ones at pleasure, especially when it reserves that 

85. First Nat. Bank v. Abilene Ho- 86. Sealy Oil Mill & Mfg. Co. v.

The power to alter by-laws has the same limits as the power to make them in the first instance. These limitations have just been pointed out. The power to make by-laws, as we have seen, is to make such only as are not inconsistent with the charter of the corporation and the law. And a by-law cannot impair vested rights of a stockholder. The alteration of a bylaw is invalid if it contravenes these rules. Thus, where a bylaw divided the stock of a corporation into equal shares, giving equal rights to the shareholders, and the stock was thus issued, a new by-law providing for the surrender of shares, and the issuance of preferred stock instead, on payment of a certain additional sum, was held void, as against dissenting stockholders, because it impaired their vested rights under the contract with the corporation under which they took their shares.88 

Where the question is whether an amendment of the by-laws had been properly adopted and the facts are not disputed, the court should decide the question as it is a question of law and not fact.89 The adoption of a new set of by-laws necessarily annuls those previously adopted.90 A corporation has an inherent right to amend its by-laws though they contain no provision for their amendment.91 Though, as we have seen, the directors may, by a by-law, be given the power to enact and to alter and amend

Waiver The by-laws may be repealed by the body that adopted them.

§ 577. Authority of Stockholder to Take Acknowledgment 

An acknowledgment taken by a notary public who is a stockholder in the corporation to an instrument in which the corporation is directly interested is a nullity. However, if the corporation had no interest in the instrument when the acknowledgment was taken, the fact that the acknowledgment was taken by a stockholder notary has no effect on the validity of the instrument, even though the corporation subsequently acquires an interest in the instrument.¹

§ 631. In General 

In most jurisdictions where general incorporation statutes have been passed, the management of the corporation is vested in a board of directors. In Texas, Vernon's Ann. Civ.St. art. 1327, provides that, "The directors shall have the general management of the affairs of the corporation, and may dispose of the residue of the capital stock at any time remaining unsubscribed, in such manner as the by-laws may prescribe." Where the general man- 544

Ch. § 631 

agement of corporate affairs is vested by statute¹ or charter 2 in the board of directors all ordinary corporate powers are to be exercised by the board of directors and by no others,³ unless by agents expressly or impliedly authorized by the board. The Texas statutes do not authorize the stockholders to appoint an agent to act with the directors. Such person cannot dictate to the directors and his acts are not binding on the corporation in the absence of authorization or ratification by the directors.5 The

In this case Justice Walthall said: "It is not denied that Coursen was president of the Atlas Corporation, nor that he as such executed the written lease for it, but it is insisted that in doing so he was without authority, and therefore his act in executing the written lease was not binding on appellant. Under article 1322, R.C.S.1925, appellant could act in the matter through its president. Our Supreme Court, in 

Ballard v. Carmichael, 18 S.W. 734, 83 Tex. 355, held that when a corporation so acted, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, it would be presumed that the instrument was executed by authority, citing Smith v. Smith, 62 Ill. 493, holding that an act pertaining to the business of the company is performed by him, it will be presumed the act was legally done and binding upon the company. Without quoting appellant's pleading at length, it is alleged that while Coursen was president of the corporation, Eli Howell was 'managing director and superintendent,' and as agent and attorney in fact for and holding the proxies of the owners of all stock of said corporation and as such and on behalf of said stockholders, and under the direction of said stockholders, was vested with the management, superintendency, and absolute control of said corporation,' and for that reason Coursen had no authority to act for appellant save and except such authority as was from time to time specially conferred by said stockholders through said 

546 

Howell, and that Coursen's authority to act was so limited. "It will be observed from the pleading that Eli Howell was acting for and on behalf of the stockholders of the corporation, and under the direction of the stockholders, and not the official board of directors or trustees of the corporation. 

"The Atlas Corporation could le gally act only through its directors and its chosen officers; a managing trustee and superintendent, and agent and attorney in fact of the stockholders, could not, we think, though assuming to act for the corporation, divest the board of directors and its chosen officers of the powers and authority vested in them by the law."

" 15 In an English case the directors are said to be "managing part- It has always seemed strange to the writer why the courts, in determining the position of directors of a corporation, felt called upon to reason from analogy. They should realize that the position of the directors is sui generis, and should determine the many problems that have arisen concerning the rights, duties and powers of directors without saying that the directors are "agents," "principals" or in the nature of "managing partners." The courts should realize that in the organization of the corporation a legal personality is created, the exact counterpart of which is not found elsewhere in the legal world. The directors of an insolvent corporation may petition to throw the company into bankruptcy, however. The reason for this rule is stated as follows in the Kenwood Ice Case: "A board of directors ought to have the power to put the company into bankruptcy. They have care of the general business of the corporation. They are the persons who know whether the corporation is able to go on or not. It might very well happen that under the articles and by-laws of the corporation it would be impossible to hold a meeting of the stockholders for months. Under these circumstances the bankruptcy of the corporation might be delayed so long that in many cases the purposes of the bankrupt law would be defeated and preferences given. I am satisfied that the board of directors at a duly called meeting has the power to put the corporation into bankruptcy." As dissolution usually follows bankruptcy, it could be argued that the filing of a petition in bankruptcy is more in the nature of a fundamental change than of an ordinary transaction of the corporation. The same could be said of an assignment for the benefit of creditors. 

In both of these cases the courts have reasoned that when the company has become financially embarrassed the directors should have the power to determine whether they or the trustee in bankruptcy or an assignee, should attempt to re-establish the corporation financially. Since it is much easier now than formerly to reorganize a corporation under the liberal provision of 77B of the present Bankrupt Statute, 11 U.S.C.A. § 207, and later amendments of the Bankruptcy Act, taking bankruptcy is an ordinary affair that falls within the jurisdiction of the directors. It is not a fundamental change.45 The Supreme Court of the United 2
