Guffey Petroleum Co.50 the court held that "the terms, 'otherwise convey' in the statute embraces the power to lease the land which belonged to the corporation." The court held that an oil company has the right to lease its land on a royalty basis and that such lease is not an abandonment of the purposes for which the corporation was organized. The statute provides that "every private corporation" has the powers enumerated in the statute. It does not specifically provide that those powers are vested in the directors. But in the Starke-Guffey Petroleum Case the Supreme Court of Texas held that these powers were vested in the directors. In the opinion the court said: "The law authorized the corporation to lease its property and each stockholder entered into the corporation, with the understanding that in doing so he empowered the directors to lease the property." Where there is any prospect of oil, it is very customary for the owner of real estate to lease it on a royalty basis. Therefore, one should not conclude from the above holding that in Texas the directors of all private corporations have power "to sell" all of the property of the corporation with the intent to quit business. That would be a fundamental change not authorized by the Texas statute. In the above case the Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Civil Appeals. Judge Gill for the Court of Civil Appeals said: "If the concern had purchased mining machinery and equipment for the conduct of the business, it would doubtless be beyond the power of the directory to sell or lease the plant, and permanently cease business, though they could unquestionably sell it and buy different and more suitable machinery; the principle being that the directory is confined to acts in furtherance of the corporate ends, and cannot put the corporation out of business."51

§ 633. Rights of Stockholders with Respect to Acts within the 

Directors' Powers

In the preceding section it was pointed out that authority to effectuate fundamental changes is lodged in the stockholders. To carry out some of those changes the directors are required to do the acts authorized by the stockholders.56 The present discussion is limited to situations where (1) the stockholders have attempted to exercise powers that normally belong to the directors or (2) one or more stockholders seeks to interfere with the directors' management and control of the ordinary affairs of the corporation.

To justify the interposition of the courts there must exist as a foundation for such suit some action or threatened action of such board or officers which is beyond the power conferred by its charter, or such fraudulent transaction, completed or contemplated among themselves or with others, as will result in serious injury to the shareholder suing.

By an instrument in writing a number of stockholders assented and agreed that Nichols, a director and officer, should have authority to make improvements on the land of the corporation at his own expense and be reimbursed by the corporation. This instrument was signed individually and not at a meeting of the directors, though Nichols and the stockholders who signed the instrument owned about 60,000 shares which included all of the shares except about 100. Those signing included all the directors and most of an executive committee of which Nichols was chairman, which committee was created by the by-laws to investigate and recommend improvements to the board of directors. The court held that such instrument imparted no authority to Nichols to bind the corporation. In the opinion the court said: "Superior to any such consideration is the proposition that neither the individual directors, nor a majority, however great, of the stockholders, acting separately, could thus bind the corporation. Action, in itself binding on the corporation, could only be taken by them as a body at a properly constituted meeting, for the reason that it is only thus that all interests are represented and heard." 

From the italicized portions, we may take it that the case in dictum at least stands in substantial accord with Ballantine's observation; that is, that if the stockholders had assented by a vote at a meeting regular and proper, the corporation would have been bound, since the interest of all would have been given due regard. Of course, the court in its language makes no distinction between the directors acting as a body and the stockholders acting as a body. According to the opinion of the court either could have bound the corporation. Its language is suggestive of the proposition that the minority stockholders who dissent or who are not consulted have a right to insist that corporate significance will be given to the acts of the directors only when they are acting as a body. In Aransas Pass Harbor Co. v. Manning, the Supreme Court held that the consent of the directors individually and that of the stockholders unanimously to a conveyance by the president of the corporation of its property was authority for such conveyance without any action by the directors as a board. It was said: "In its last analysis, the stockholders are the beneficial owners of the assets of the corporation. * * * The directors must ordinarily make disposition of the corporate property, because its creditors have rights which it is their duty to protect. A majority of the stockholders, even all save one, cannot authorize a sale of the corporate assets, for the reason that every stockholder has the right to require the action of the legally constituted agencythe board of directors-in the management of its business. But when all assent, there being no creditors to complain, they should not be permitted to complain. When every one who has an interest in the property, although that interest may, as long as the corporation exists, be indirect, consents that the officer appointed by the law to convey the assets of the corporation, when duly authorized so to do, shall convey, and it is accordingly so conveyed, we are of opinion that the conveyance should be held good."

In a case that has often been cited by many writers, the Supreme Court of Texas held that the directors can not delegate their entire power to an agent or committee and thus relinquish to an agent their own supervision, general control, and discretion as to matters of corporate policy. The celebrated case of 

Tempel v. Dodge is authority for this proposition. In that case it was held that the board of directors could not confer upon an executive committee created under a by-law, the entire management of the corporate affairs, which the charter authorized the board to do. This executive committee was to be appointed not by the board of directors, but by the president. The court said: "Undoubtedly the board of directors can appoint agents, whether in the form of committees or as single agents, to transact the ordinary business of the corporation; but we believe that the rule is well settled by authority and sustained by sound principle that a board of directors cannot confer upon others the power to discharge duties imposed upon them which involve the exercise of judgment and discretion, except in the transaction of the ordinary business of the corporation, unless authorized to do so by the charter. * * The by-laws in express terms substituted the executive committee to be appointed by the president, for the board of directors, and attempted to confer upon that committee all of the powers given by the charter to the board of directors. The directors of many Texas corporations do not meet oftener than once a month, and many do not meet that often. 637. Notice of Meeting

To constitute a valid directors' meeting, all the directors must have notice of the time and place of the meeting, unless the meeting is a stated one so that each director is chargeable with notice of the meeting; and hence is privileged to be present if he so desires. It is immaterial in what way the day of the regular meetings of the directors is fixed. If it has been fixed by usage, by a tacit understanding of the members, by the by-laws, or in any other way, it is sufficient.89

Therefore, it is not practical to notify the directors what matters will be considered at their next meeting. The general statement in notices of meetings that "any other matter that any member wishes to submit to the meeting will be considered," is meaningless.

There is a line of Texas cases holding that in view of Article 1322,19 providing for the form of a corporation's conveyance of real estate, a conveyance with the statutory requisites carries with it a prima facie presumption of authority to execute the conveyance even though there is no recitation of the authority in the deed.20

Therefore, it seems that in Texas it is fairly well settled that informal action on the part of the directors will not bind the corporation. For instance, if the action of the president is based on authority given him by the directors at a street corner meeting or over the telephone, it is not binding on the corporation. 

But if the directors knowingly ratify what the president has done without authority, the corporation is bound although silence alone is the only evidence of ratification. Again, if the directors sit silently by, even in their separated offices, and do not object to unauthorized action on the part of an officer, under many circumstances, the corporation is liable on the transaction under the doctrine of ratification. themselves if these latter rules

This method of holding the principal liable should be called "impliedly granted authority." In the third place, an agent is impliedly authorized to do what is usually and customarily done by an agent in the same or similar employments. The cashiers of banks have from time immemorial exercised the power of certifying checks drawn by depositors of the bank. Therefore, anyone can rely upon this custom unless one has actual knowledge that this authority has been denied to the cashier in the transaction before the court. Express authority may be shown not only by an explicit resolution of the board of directors, but by their conduct. If by acquiescence, the directors virtually abdicate and permit the manager or president to dominate and conduct the business of the corporation without interference on their part, such officer has express authority co-extensive with the authority of the directors to bind the corporation. As the agent has express authority, a third party dealing with such an agent need not show that he had notice of such conduct on the part of the directors before he dealt with the agent of the company. 324-325. Many courts confuse "apparent authority" and "implied au 589

§ 

Ch. 13

ways made the above classifications when stating how the principal may be bound by the acts of his agents. But the author firmly believes that if the above classifications or the ones de veloped by Professor Seavey in the Restatement of the Law of Agency, are adopted by the courts, much of the confusion that now appears in many of the opinions will disappear. 

Of course, classifications or criteria for determining when the principal is liable for the acts of his agents, or other parties who purport to act for him, in themselves are not useful in determining the principal's liability. But for our courts to give definite meanings to words and phrases used by them is most important. For instance, the same court will state that the liability of the principal on "implied authority" of the agent, or "apparent authority," or "ostensible authority," is the same as liability "by estoppel." As long as the courts refuse to adopt a definite classification for determining the liability of the principal and assign a definite meaning to the terms used by them, nothing but confusion will result. The American Law Institute was organized to clarify the law. It is the duty of all courts. to become well acquainted with the Restatement of the law by the Institute. These Restatements were prepared by the best lawyers of America, and the Institute has tried diligently to assign definite meanings to words and phrases used in the Restatements. If the Texas Courts would adopt the classification of the Restatement of Agency for determining the principal's liability a great deal of the confusion in the Texas opinions would disappear. The pertinent sections of the Restatement of Agen cy are referred to in the last note. 

These rules will be illustrated and discussed in subsequent sections in this chapter as they apply to the acts of the agents of corporate principals as well as to individual principals.

A typical statement of the rule as announced in the cases cited in the last note is found in the Joseph Steel Co.-Pecos Valley 

Gas case. In that case the court said: "The control over the company's business and property is vested in the Board of Directors, but subject to this control certain powers are delegated by implication to certain officers. Corporations have assumed and acquired such a position in the business world that the office of President carries with it certain implied powers of an agency. 

He is usually either expressly or by implied consent made the chief executive officer, without special authority or explicitly delegated powers he may perform all acts of an ordinary nature which by usage or necessity are incidents to his office and by virtue of his office he may enter into a contract and bind his corporation in matters arising from and concerning the usual course of the corporation's business. These are the implied powers of the President of the corporation and they inhere in him by virtue of the position itself. Beyond these powers-beyond the carrying out of the usual and proper functions of the corporation necessary for the proper and convenient management of the business of the corporation, the President remains as any other director of the company, and other and further powers must be specifically conferred."

From the above review of the Texas cases it is evident that they are confusing. Some assert that the president has no inherent powers, others say that he has some implied powers, and still other Texas cases say that he is presumed to have certain powers. It is true that most of these cases were decided by Courts of Civil Appeals, but writs of error were denied in many of them. It remains for the Supreme Court to determine the implied powers of the president. In some of the above cases the courts hold that if the magic word "manager" is added to

Of course, if the directors permit the president to carry on the routine business of the office, a person who knows of previous acts of the president would ordinarily be protected under the doctrine of estoppel or ratification. 

However, to the writer it has always seemed legalistic and theoretical for a court to hold that a company can escape liability, where the plaintiff cannot show estoppel or ratification, although the directors put the president in charge of the general office of the company and the plaintiff honestly believed that the president had the authority he purported to exercise. Proof of the above facts should suffice to show that the directors gave to the president authority to conduct the ordinary business affairs of the company. In such cases the courts should at least attribute to the president as much implied authority as to the “general manager" for he is in fact, if not in name, the general manager. But some of the courts shut their eyes to the actual facts and unduly limit the powers of the president.34 The innocent third party should not be forced virtually to insult the president by demanding an exhibit of his authority. The Supreme Court is free to follow this position when this question is finally decided in Texas.

It shocks one's sense of justice when one reads the above Texas cases to realize how often innocent third parties are in-

In Ballard v. Carmichael 36 the court said: "We may safely assume to know judicially that a vice president in the common acceptation of that term is an officer designated for the purpose of performing the functions of the president when for any reason the latter can not act. In case of the absence of the president or of his inability for any reason to perform the functions of his place, as a very general rule, at least, the vice president becomes invested with his powers and responsibilities. In such contingencies the vice president is in fact and in law the president in all except name. He certainly becomes 'the presiding member' of the corporation. When, therefore, a deed is produced signed by the vice president of the corporation and sealed with its seal, we think in the absence of evidence to the contrary it should be presumed that the contingency has arisen which authorized the vice president to act, and that he is to be deemed 'pro hac vice' the presiding member of the corporation. 

The only cases we have found bearing upon the question are in consonance with these views. Colman v. Oil Company, 25 W. 

Va. 148, 172; Smith v. Smith, 62 Ill. 493. In the latter case the

Supreme Court of Illinois, in speaking of the President of the corporation, say: 'when an act pertaining to the business of the corporation is performed by him, it will be presumed the act was legally done and binding upon the company; and as a general rule, in the absence of the President the Vice President may act in his stead and perform the duties which devolve upon the 

President.' And we think the like presumption in absence of direct evidence to the contrary should be indulged in favor of the validity of his acts, especially when such acts are authenticated by the seal of the corporation."

The board of directors cannot supervise the details of the business of the corporation. Therefore, when they appoint a president, or manager, and put him in charge of the company's affairs do they not impliedly, if not expressly, authorize him to conduct the business of the company until the next meeting of the directors? A more evident implication cannot be found even in the field of contract law, if the courts will visualize the actual method of conducting the business of the corporation between meetings of the directors.38 In many cases, after the directors have permitted the officer to represent them in business transactions, the doctrine of estoppel will be sufficient protection to the innocent party. But should not the first person who is misled by the appearance of authority be protected, and should the innocent party be forced to rely either on estoppel or ratification? When the third party is protected under the rules of estoppel and ratification is explained in previous and subsequent sections in this chapter.

Cable Co. v. Southern Independent Tel. Co.,40 the court held that the president had no authority to buy personal property needed by the company. Most of the opinions of the Courts of 

Civil Appeals are based on the Supreme Court decisions in Fitz hugh v. Franco-Texan Land Co.41 and Franco-Texan Land Co. v. 

McCormick.42 It would be difficult to find in the Texas reports two decisions that meted out more injustice to the innocent third party than those two cases. In them most of the directors lived in Paris, France. The president was put in charge of the company's business in Texas and agreed to sell several sections of land for part cash, a note of a third party, and a note of the vendee payable in horses. The note of the vendee was not secured by a vendor's lien. As this was not the customary method of selling land on credit, the court held that the company could recover the land from a remote vendee, since he had notice of the lack of power of the president as the company's deed recited the actual considerations paid by the original vendee. 

In the recent case of Helms v. Home Owners' Loan Corporation 43 the Supreme Court held that the general manager of a foreign corporation doing business in Texas has power to conduct the ordinary routine business of the corporation. In other words, the Court stated that the powers of the general manager of a foreign corporation "are co-extensive with the powers of the corporation he represents". In the Franco-Texan Land cases the president was actually the "general manager" in Texas. If the Court really meant what it said in the Helms' case it virtually overruled the Franco-Texan Land cases; for surely the manager of a Texas corporation, where all the other directors live in Paris, France, has as much power as the manager

§ 642. 

Secretary

The secretary of a corporation keeps the minutes of the meetings of the directors, is custodian of the corporate seal and records, and generally acts as transfer agent for the shares of stock. 

The secretary is an officer of the corporation as much as any other officer, and while his powers are very limited, he is more than a mere servant of the corporation. But he has no inherent power to bind the corporation by contracts made by him.68 A secretary-treasurer of a corporation is not clothed with implied authority to execute a chattel mortgage.69 He cannot bind the corporation by a contract to sell its realty,70 nor by the execution of accommodation paper. He is without authority to execute a release of a mortgage held by the corporation. He cannot lease the property of the corporation.73 

The secretary is without authority to make statements respecting the record title to lots which had been owned by the

Treasurer

To the treasurer is entrusted the duty of receiving and disbursing the moneys of the corporation in accordance with his directions from the directors. He has no authority to bind the corporation solely by virtue of his position. He has no authority to borrow money for the corporation, and in the absence of a holding out or acquiescence, the corporation will not be bound upon a note executed by him.80 The corporation is not bound when the treasurer, with general authority to issue negotiable paper, signs the corporation's name to a note, forges the general manager's signature, and negotiates it for his own use, where a resolution was passed requiring all such paper to be executed by the general manager.81 He has authority to check against a deposit of the corporate funds deposited in his name as treasurer, and if the bank has notice that the treasurer is misusing the money belonging to the corporation, as, for instance, paying a private debt with corporate funds, the bank is liable to the extent of this misappropriation.82 The Commission of Appeals held that persons dealing with the treasurer of a corporation are charged with notice that the treasurer cannot indorse checks of the corporation for the purpose of transferring the funds to him- Common- viously stated, appear in the minute book. Since the furnishing of such a certificate was within the authority of the secretary, the trust company was justified in relying upon it, and the corporation is estopped to assert that such resolution was not in fact passed by the board of directors."

1 self individually.83 But the Supreme Court overruled this opinion, after having approved it, and held that the bank was an innocent purchaser of the bills indorsed by the treasurer of the railroad company in his official capacity and deposited to his individual credit for the reason that, "Although the bank knows that the funds deposited are trust funds, and the deposit is made in the name of the trustee personally, the bank is not bound to make inquiry whether the trustee is committing a breach of trust in making the deposit; and although the deposit is made in a breach of trust, the bank in receiving the deposit is not liable for participation in the breach of trust, in the absence of further circumstances known to the bank indicating that the trustee is committing a breach of trust. "Thus, if a trustee indorses a check payable to him as trustee and deposits it in a bank to the credit of his personal account, the bank is not bound to make inquiry whether the trustee is committing a breach of trust in making the deposit; and although the trustee in fact commits a breach of trust in making the deposit, the bank is not liable for participation in the breach of trust in the absence of further circumstances known to the bank indicating that the trustee is committing a breach of trust.' 84 As a general rule the secretary-treasurer of a corporation has power to endorse checks payable to the company. As incidental to this power, the officer who has power to endorse checks has implied power to cash the checks at the bank since the corporation very often needs cash in the conduct of its business. If the check is endorsed in blank, the bank is protected in paying the money to the person who presents the check for payment. However, if it is endorsed specially, or to "any bank, banker or trust company," it cannot be cashed by anyone except the agent of

General Manager

The directors of the corporation may employ a general manager even though the charter does not provide for such an office.86 

No matter what name he may be given, the managing agent is a mere employee of the board of directors, subject to the contract of employment.87 The governing principle with respect to the power of a general manager is that the corporation will be bound by his acts and contracts which are necessary or incident to the conduct of the business, without other evidence of authority.88 

In general, the admissions of the general manager made in the scope of his authority are admissible against the company.89 

As a general rule, he has authority to do anything which is ordinarily necessary to the conduct of the business of the corporation, and is not in excess of its powers,90 such as agreeing to lease

Branch or District Manager

A branch manager and a general manager are not synonymous terms, and the implied powers of a branch manager are limited to the usual and customary incidents of the business of the branch over which he is manager, and he has no implied powers as to other branches of the same business.35

The cashier has implied authority to accept money in payment of a debt due the bank, but he has no implied power to accept a renewal note in payment of the original note where some of the parties on the original note are released.46 Under our statute giving the control of the bank to the directors, the cashier is without power to permit the use of leased premises for a purpose which is prohibited by the lease.47 He is not authorized to employ an architect to draw plans and specifications for a proposed building for the bank.48 The cashier of a national bank is not authorized to purchase land for the bank, although taken in satisfaction of a debt due the bank,49 nor assume the payment of outstanding liens thereon.50 He can make a contract

Since the statutes provide for the election of directors annually and endow that body with the general management of the business, a general manager may not be employed for a longer period than one year.80

Where the transaction is between the corporation and the general public, limitations in the by-laws will not restrict the apparent authority of the corporate agent. "The by-laws of the average corporation are not usually open for public inspection; hence the public trading with it can have no notice of their contents. If it should be taken that the by-laws were a limitation upon the authority of the general manager, this is met by proof that the contents of the by-laws were not made known to plaintiff. It is a well settled rule of law that the principal is bound by the act of the agent, done within the scope of his apparent authority in dealing with innocent third persons although such act may be in direct violation of his private instructions." 81

However, it has been held that where one seeks an important position with the corporation, he is charged with notice contained in the by-laws of the method required to elect such official.82 Thus where he secures employment from an official authorized by the by-laws to employ him, the contract is subject to the conditions and limitations expressed in the by-law conferring this authority.83 This is a harsh rule as it charges

Should the court in the Faulkner case not have held that the vice-president with the consent of the president had authority to employ the plaintiff and the provision of the by-laws that "officers appointed by him may be removed by him at pleasure" is a secret instruction which would not be binding on the plaintiff unless he had knowledge of its contents? The by-law gave the vice-president specific authority to employ the plaintiff and then provided that such officers "may be removed by him." The by-law did not provide that every contract of employment must be on the condition that the vice-president could discharge the officer at any time. The corporation surely never intended that the vicepresident represent to the prospective employee that he had no authority to employ anyone, except subject to discharge at the wish of himself, the vice-president. Few persons could have been induced to accept such precarious employment. Therefore, the latter part of the above by-law was a secret instruction to the vice-president, not intended to be disclosed to the third party; just as where the principal instructs his agent to buy his neighbor's horse, but "do not pay more than one hundred dollars for the horse." The same notion was pushed too far in a later case where the court charged the head physician with notice of the by-laws of the corporation before he was employed. If the court had said that the president and vice-president did not have authority to employ the plaintiff, and no ratification or estoppel was shown, the decision would not have been so absurd. That was what the court really meant to say in the Faulkner case cited in the last note. But in the recent case the court charged the plaintiff with notice of the by-laws before he was employed.84

§ 649. Ratification 

The Texas courts apparently use the terms estoppel and ratification interchangeably. Technically, the former implies a representation of an existing fact by one party, and a reliance thereon by the other party to his detriment. The latter signifies the validating of a contract otherwise unenforceable, because the agent in making the contract exceeded his authority by the principal, who must have had capacity to make the contract in the first instance. A corporation may ratify any contract made in its behalf that it could have made in the first instance.89 The

Civ.App., 188 S.W. 38. This case seems to hold that the corporation can escape liability by tendering back the consideration received on the ultra vires contract when it was not ratified by the director or all the stockholders. See further discussion of this case in the chapter "Rights & Liabilities Arising out of 

Ultra Vires Transactions." The law has not as yet been definitely decided in Texas. 644

Ch. § 649 

The directors do not have authority to enter into an ultra vires contract. But as is shown in the chapter on "Right and Liabilities Arising out of Ultra Vires Transactions" in Texas the corporation is liable when it receives a direct benefit from the ultra vires contract. Therefore, mere ratification even by the directors of an executory ultra vires contract would not be enforceable against the corporation. But if it is executed on one side, and the corporation receives a direct benefit from the contract, it could be ratified by the corporation. 

An individual principal can ratify a contract made by a purported agent without authority, although the principal receives no benefit from the transaction. As a corporation has no authority to enter into an ultra vires contract, as a general rule the directors cannot ratify such a contract. In Texas under the Bond-Terrell doctrine, the corporation is liable on such contracts, however, where a benefit is received by the corporation; and it could, therefore, ratify an ultra vires contract by receiving benefits therefrom. A corporation ratifies an unauthorized contract of employment of an attorney by receiving benefits from his services. Where one renders services for the corporation with the knowledge and without the objection of the officers, though the contract of employment was made by an agent without authority, the contract is thereby ratified." Acquiescence with knowledge of all material facts is evidence of ratification.8

notice of a fact in a matter that does not come before the directors, such knowledge is not imputed to the corporation. On the other hand, knowledge of one director is imputed to the corporation if the transaction comes before the directors and is determined by them. This rule is well stated by Judge Pleasants as follows: "The general rule that notice to an agent is notice to his principal can only be applied when the matter with reference to which notice is given is within the scope of the agent's authority, or has some direct connection with his agency. Corporations can only act through agents, and frequently have numerous agents whose duties are entirely separate and distinct; and it goes without saying that notice to an agent of a corporation with reference to a matter entirely beyond the scope of his agency would not be notice to the corporation. 

Knowledge possessed by a director of a corporation would not be notice to the corporation, unless the matter with reference to which notice is sought to be charged was one with which the board of directors, or the director receiving such notice, dealt directly. If one of the eleven directors of appellant corporation had incidentally acquired knowledge of the fact that appellee had sold the engine to Gohmert and that only one half of the purchase money therefor was paid, and that appellee held a lien on the engine for the balance, we do not think it would have been his duty to have disclosed these facts to the officers of the company who had charge of the construction of the miil and making payments to Gohmert as they became due under the contract. Unless notice of such fact was given to him officially for the purpose of notifying the appellant, such director could reasonably presume that appellee would give proper notice of his lien, either by having it recorded, or by giving active notice to some general officer of the company, or to the officers or agents of the company in charge of the construction of the mill. If such director, however, was present and took part in any settlement made by the board of directors with Gohmert, by which he was paid any money, after such director had notice of the appellee's lien, such notice might be imputed to the corporation. All we mean to hold is that a director of a corporation is not such an officer or general agent of the corpora- 652

tion that the corporation should be charged as a matter of law with notice of facts within the knowledge of the director, without regard to the nature of the transaction with reference to which notice is sought to be charged against the corporation, or the connection the board of directors, or the director having such notice, might have with such transaction."40 

If the director or agent is adversely interested in the transaction his knowledge is not imputed to the corporation,¹¹ unless the agent is the "sole representative" of the corporation in the transaction involved in the controversy,42 or has a controlling influence over the board of directors.43

If courts shut their eyes to actual realities and look upon the corporation as an ideal nebulous person, absolutely separate from its stockholders, they would hold notice to the officers and stockholders of one company is not notice to another company although the officers and stockholders of the latter company are identical with those of the former company. But if a realistic view is taken of the corporation and it is considered a group of individuals to whom a franchise has been given to carry on a business as a legal unit, the courts will impute knowledge acquired while acting for the former company to the latter. In such case, and also where a new corporation is formed upon the expiration of the charter of the old company, the better holding is that knowledge by the officers and stockholders of the first company is imputed to the other corporation.44 If the promoters became officers in the subsequently formed corporation, notice to the promoters is notice to the company as to transaction equally important and decisive, that is, in cases in which the agent when committing the fraud was the sole representative of the principal.

When this appears, the general rule of imputed notice to his principal applies."

Lowndes v. City Nat'l Bank, 72 A. 

150, 82 Conn. 8, 22 L.R.A.,N.S., 408. 66 In the Goldstein-Union Nat'l Bank case the Supreme Court said: * * the true test, as to notice, in cases of this character, is, we think, not whether there is some slight adverse interest existing in the agent, although, to much greater extent his individual interests in the transaction are entirely consistent with the interests of his principal, but whether, in the premises, and under all the circumstances of the particular case, the agent's interests are so incompatible with the interests of his principal as practically to destroy the agency or to render it reasonably probable that an ordinary person, in the agent's position, under such circumstances, will neither act, in behalf of his principal, upon his so acquired knowledge, nor disclose that knowledge to his principal, but, because of such incompatibility in interests, will withhold such knowledge from the principal."

In another case involving a principle somewhat similar to the above rule a Texas Court of Civil Appeals considered the corporation as composed of living human beings. In this case the plaintiff leased his hotel to a Texas corporation most of the stock of which belonged to the McCoys. The latter parties sold their stock to Hilton. The plaintiff instituted a suit in equity to reform the lease contract. He claimed that it was understood by him and the lessee that the lease should contain a provision that the McCoys "should be the executive officers of the corporation (lessee), vested with the exclusive control and management of the hotel during the entire life of the lease." When 

Hilton bought the stock of the McCoys he had no knowledge of the alleged agreement. The court held that since Hilton was an innocent purchaser of the stock of the lessee-corporation, the plaintiff was not entitled to a reformation of the lease.40 As the 

McCoys were officers of the corporation, their knowledge would be imputed to the corporation, and if the traditional view is followed, the plaintiff would have the right to reform the lease. since the corporation was the defendant and it never changes according to Blackstone, though its stockholders may change from day to day. But the court virtually said that a business corporation is composed of human beings-they are the corporation, and, therefore, held as all the stockholders had sold to innocent purchasers the corporation no longer had notice of the mistake. That was the just way of determining the problem before the court.

court permitted the state to recover 59,281 acres of land from the company that built the State Capitol for 3,000,000 acres of land on the ground that the grant contained 59,281 acres in excess of what the State had agreed to give for building the Capitol, although there had been a substantial change in the stockholders of the corporation. The directors of a corporation are charged with knowledge of the terms of the contracts that they make for the company. 

Therefore, where they purchase property for the corporation and the vendor retains a lien on the property for part of the purchase price, they are charged with notice of such lien.49 The directors are presumed to know that which it is their duty to know, and which they have the means of knowing.50 Where a a third person notified three directors and officers that he repudiated an alleged contract with the corporation the latter was charged with notice of the repudiation of the contract.51 The rule that notice to an officer while acting in the scope of his authority is imputed to the corporation applies generally to the agents of the corporation. There is no imputation when the agent has a personal interest in the transaction adverse to that of the corporation.52 A stockholder-officer's interest in the assumption of his purchase money notes by the corporation in buying land prevented his knowledge of a defect in the title from

some of the Texas cases it is stated that notice acquired by an agent before he represented the principal involved in the transaction before the court would not be imputed to the principal except in a very few cases, and that the Texas courts have not adopted as broad a rule as that stated in Section 276 of the Restatement of the law of Agency. From a recent case by the 

Supreme Court it is evident that the section from the Restatement will soon be followed in Texas, if it has not already been adopted. In Wellington Oil Co. v. Maffi62 Judge Hickman said: "This brings us to a consideration of the question upon which the application for writ of error was granted, that is, whether Wellington was charged with knowledge acquired by O'Neil in his transactions with Maffi when he, O'Neil, was representing Santa Clara, and at a time before he became the president and representative of Wellington. Upon this question there cannot be said to be a uniformity of decisions. The rule recognized in most jurisdictions appears to be that announced in Section 276 of the American Law Institute's Restatement of the law of Agency, as follows: (a) Relevant knowledge may have been acquired by the agent before the time of his employment or after he becomes agent, either while acting for himself or for the principal. In any case except where the knowledge is acquired confidentially (see sec. 281), the important matter is not how the agent acquired it, but whether or not he has the knowledge at the time when it becomes relevant in his work for the principal. 

If he has the information in mind, the principal is bound, under the rule stated in this Section, equally where it was not acquired because he was acting as an agent, as where he obtained it as such agent. "This court has not adopted so broad a statement of the rule. 

The rule has been announced by this court that a principal, whether a corporation or a natural person, is not affected by notice which comes to the agent or officer unless such knowledge came to him while he was transacting the business of his principal.63 While this court has announced that as the gener-

That exception is that where the agent is the actor (sometimes designated sole actor), representing his principal in the transaction to which his knowledge relates, the principal will not be permitted to avail himself of the benefits of his agent's services without being charged with his knowledge.64 "In the case of American Surety Co. v. The case is distinctly in point here. "A rule which would permit a principal to profit by a transaction of his agent without at the same time charging him with relevant knowledge possessed by his agent at the very time he carried on the negotiations would be, to our minds, indefensible. 

In the instant case if the testimony of Maffi is to be believed, O'Neil has acquired for his principal, Wellington, a valuable piece of property. He could not have acquired same but for the services of Maffi. In negotiating the transaction under which the property was acquired, O'Neil was the sole actor for Wellington and knew at that time that Maffi had rendered services which made it possible for him to acquire this property for his principal, and that Maffi rendered such services under an agreement for compensation. Upon reason and the above-cited authorities, we hold that Wellington must be charged with the knowledge possessed by O'Neil at that time."

 § 651. Admissions and Declarations 

Declarations made by officers or agents with respect to a matter within the scope of their apparent authority and in the line of their duty, with reference to an existing state of affairs, are admissible in evidence as part of the res gestae,65 or as admissions or declarations of the corporation. Declarations of past occurrences are not binding on the corporation where not part of the res gestae.67 The declarations or admissions generally are not admissible in evidence against the corporation unless they were made in the course of the transaction, so as to constitute part of the res gestae.68 However, an officer, due to the position he holds, may be impliedly authorized to bind the corporation by admissions of liability.69 Declarations of agents are not binding when not made during the continuance of the agency, and at the time of the transaction.70 If the declaration is in ex-

§ 652. Action on Quantum Meruit where Agent Exceeds Author ity Even though the agent exceeds his authority as agent of the corporation, evidence that he made the contract on behalf of the corporation is admissible where the corporation is sued on a quantum meruit to show that the services were rendered for the defendant corporation.87 

§ 653. Provisions of Rule 93 Apply to Corporations Rule 93 of the Rules of Civil Procedure, Vernon's Tex.Rules 

Civ.Proc., provides in part: "A pleading setting up any of the following matters, unless the truth of such matters appear of record, shall be verified by affidavit: "h. Denial of the execution by himself or by his authority of any instrument in writing, upon which any pleading is founded, in whole or in part, and charged to have been executed by him or by his authority, and not alleged to be lost or destroyed. 

Where such instrument in writing is charged to have been executed by a person then deceased, the affidavit will be sufficient if it state that the affiant has reason to believe and does believe that such instrument was not executed by the decedent or by his authority. In the absence of such a sworn plea, the instrument shall be received in evidence as fully proved." "i. That the contract sued upon is usurious."
